9 Life tables and survivorship types 9.1 Background Life tables are powerful analytical tools used in various fields to understand and quantify mortality patterns and life expectancy within populations. Originating in population biology and demography, life tables have found extensive applications in epidemiology, human mortality studies, and even product life-cycle management. By systematically tracking and analysing the survival and mortality rates of individuals within specific cohorts, life tables reveal essential information about population dynamics, age-specific risks, and the factors that influence longevity. When they also record reproduction, they tell us how fast a population grows. The basic algebra used in life tables is explained in Neal, in the chapters Life Tables and Growth of Age-Structured and Stage-Structured Populations, and in the lecture “Life tables and age-structured population growth”. This practical uses the same notation as Neal and the lecture (see the table below). Gotelli’s A Primer of Ecology (optional) covers the same material with different symbols: \(g_x\) for \(p_x\), \(b_x\) for \(m_x\) and \(G\) for \(T\). In addition to providing valuable insights into mortality patterns and life expectancy, life tables also allow us to consider mortality patterns in the context of distinct survivorship types that result from the way mortality risk changes over the life course. Three primary survivorship types are commonly identified, based on survivorship curves (\(l_x\)) plotted on a log scale: Type I (convex curve): mortality is low early in life and increases with age. Most individuals survive to old age, and most deaths occur in older age groups. Type I survivorship is seen in humans and other long-lived species with strong parental care and low early-life mortality. Type II (straight line): mortality is constant with age, so individuals have about the same chance of dying at any age. Some small mammals and many birds come close to this pattern. Type III (concave curve): mortality is high early in life and decreases with age. Survival is low in the early stages of life, but those that survive the vulnerable period are likely to live a long time. Type III survivorship is typical of species that produce many offspring with little parental care, such as many fish and trees. Real species are often mixtures: for example, Dall sheep and many birds have high juvenile mortality (Type III-like), followed by mortality that rises with age in adults (Type I-like). By identifying and understanding these survivorship types, researchers gain critical insights into the demographic structure of populations and the selective pressures that influence survival and longevity. Learning outcomes: Increased competence in using Excel formulae for mathematical modelling. Competence in using mathematical models in Excel to strengthen your own understanding of biological processes. Building a cohort life table, and interpreting survivorship (\(l_x\)), survival probability (\(p_x\)), probability of death (\(q_x\)) and life expectancy (\(e_x\)). Calculating the net reproductive rate (\(R_0\)), generation time (\(T\)) and the capacity for increase (\(r_c = \ln(R_0)/T\)), an approximation to the intrinsic rate of increase \(r_m\). Understanding the three types of survivorship curve and how they relate to the way mortality changes with age. Understanding why changes in reproduction early in life matter more than changes late in life (the declining “force of selection”). 9.2 Notation Symbol Meaning Calculation \(x\) Age at the start of the interval (\(x = 0\) means age 0 to 1) \(S_x\) Number alive at the start of age \(x\) counted \(l_x\) Survivorship: probability of surviving from birth to age \(x\) \(S_x/S_0\) \(p_x\) Survival probability: probability of surviving from age \(x\) to \(x+1\) \(S_{x+1}/S_x\), or \(l_{x+1}/l_x\) \(q_x\) Probability of dying between age \(x\) and \(x+1\) \(1 - p_x\) \(e_x\) Life expectancy: further years expected at age \(x\) \(\left(\sum_{y \ge x} l_y\right)/l_x - 0.5\) \(\mu_x\) Force of mortality: the instantaneous death rate of individuals still alive at age \(x\) (a rate, not a probability) if \(\mu\) is constant over the year, \(q_x = 1 - e^{-\mu_x}\) \(m_x\) Female offspring per female aged \(x\) \(R_0\) Net reproductive rate: female offspring per female per lifetime (per generation) \(\sum l_x m_x\) \(T\) Generation time: mean age of mothers when their daughters are born \(\sum x l_x m_x / R_0\) \(r_c\) Capacity for increase: approximate population growth rate per year (an approximation to \(r_m\)) \(\ln(R_0)/T\) \(r_m\) Intrinsic rate of increase per year (exact, from the Euler-Lotka equation); \(\lambda = e^{r_m}\) solve \(\sum e^{-r_m x} l_x m_x = 1\) 9.3 Worked example The Worked example sheet in the spreadsheet is the life table from the lecture: a cohort of 500 newborn females, with \(S_x\) = 500, 400, 200, 50 and 0 at ages 0 to 4, and \(m_x\) = 0, 2, 3, 1 and 0. Click on the cells to see the formulas. For example: Survivorship: \(l_1 = 400/500 = 0.8\) Survival probability from age 1 to 2: \(p_1 = 200/400 = 0.5\), so \(q_1 = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5\) Life expectancy at birth: \(e_0 = (1 + 0.8 + 0.4 + 0.1)/1 - 0.5 = 1.8\) years Net reproductive rate: \(R_0 = 0 + 1.6 + 1.2 + 0.1 = 2.9\) Generation time: \(T = (1 \times 1.6 + 2 \times 1.2 + 3 \times 0.1)/2.9 = 4.3/2.9 = 1.48\) years Capacity for increase: \(r_c = \ln(2.9)/1.48 = 0.72\) per year, so \(\lambda \approx e^{r_c} = 2.05\) Note that \(r_c = \ln(R_0)/T\) is an approximation to the intrinsic rate of increase, \(r_m\). The exact value for this life table (\(r_m = 0.776\), \(\lambda = 2.17\)) comes from the Euler-Lotka equation or from a matrix model (next practical). The spreadsheet labels this quantity “r (approx.)”. 9.4 Your task Download and open the Excel file Life_Tables_Exercises.xlsx. The file has three worksheets: “Life table”, “Survivorship Curves” and “Worked example”. 9.4.1 Life table Let’s start with “Life table”. The aim now is to use Excel as a modelling tool to produce a life table. I have provided some initial data collected from a cohort of animals. I know how many individuals start each year (i.e. how many “enter an interval”) and therefore I can see how many survive each year (i.e. how many “enter the next interval”). I also know how many female offspring (on average) are produced by each female of each age (\(m_x\)). Start by calculating survivorship (\(l_x\)). Survivorship is the probability of surviving from birth to a particular age. Therefore, at age 0, \(l_0 = 1\), since everyone is alive at this point. The next value (\(l_1\)) must be calculated based on the number alive at that point. In this case it is \(352/500 = 0.704\). You must generalise this calculation into a formula that can be dragged to fill column D in the worksheet. In algebraic form, the equation is \(l_x = S_x/S_0\). Tip You need to understand the use of the $ symbol in Excel, and how to drag the selected area to place the formula in the column. Next, you can calculate the age-specific survival probability, \(p_x\). Note that this is different from \(l_x\). Survival probability is simply the probability that an individual will survive its current age class, i.e. the probability that an individual currently aged 2 will survive to become age 3. In this case, it is \(254/298 = 0.852\). The calculation is \(p_x = l_{x+1}/l_x\), or \(S_{x+1}/S_x\). From there you can calculate the age-specific probability of death, \(q_x\). This is simply \(1 - p_x\): the probabilities of survival and death must sum to 1. Then calculate life expectancy, \(e_x\), in column I: add up the \(l_x\) values from age \(x\) to the end of the table, divide by \(l_x\), and subtract 0.5 (because, on average, individuals that die during a year die halfway through it). For example, in the worked example \(e_1 = (0.8 + 0.4 + 0.1)/0.8 - 0.5 = 1.125\) years. Tip =SUM(D3:$D$13)/D3-0.5 in cell I3 can be dragged down the column. Now complete the remaining columns, \(l_x m_x\) and \(l_x m_x x\), and use them to calculate (a) the net reproductive rate, \(R_0 = \sum l_x m_x\); (b) the generation time, \(T = \sum x l_x m_x / R_0\); and (c) the capacity for increase, \(r_c = \ln(R_0)/T\), which approximates the population growth rate per year. Is this population growing, stationary or shrinking? Refer to the sheet “Worked example” if you get stuck (click on the cells to see the formulae used there). 9.4.1.1 Declining force of selection (optional, if time) This experiment is optional here: you will do a fuller version in the practical Trade-offs and the declining force of selection. Do it if you have finished the rest of the life table and the survivorship curves. The force of selection describes the relative importance of events that happen during the life course for fitness (measured, for example, by \(R_0\) or \(r_m\)). To investigate this you can do a computer “experiment” by altering reproduction at different ages. You can think of these as “what if?” experiments, e.g. “What if there was a mutation that added 1 to reproduction at age 1, or at age 2, etc.?” Before you start, predict: will adding one daughter at age 2 or at age 8 have the bigger effect on \(R_0\)? Why? Add 1 to \(m_x\) at one age at a time, from age 1 to age 10 (put it back before moving to the next age), and record the new value of \(R_0\). Do not include age 0: newborns cannot breed at birth. Graph your results as age vs. change in \(R_0\). What you should see is that changes early in life matter more than changes later in life. (Adding one daughter at age \(x\) raises \(R_0\) by exactly \(l_x\): a female must survive to age \(x\) to have that extra daughter.) Use \(R_0\), not \(r_c\), for this experiment. The approximation \(r_c = \ln(R_0)/T\) can even fall when reproduction is added late in life, because \(T\) increases; the exact \(r_m\) always increases, but by less and less with age. 9.4.2 Survivorship curves In the second part of this class we focus on the Survivorship Curves worksheet. The aim here is to explore how different types of organisms with different ways of life (“life history strategies”) can have qualitatively different kinds of life tables. The most important thing to observe is the difference in survivorship curves (\(l_x\)). These differences become very obvious when you plot the log-transformed survivorship against age. In the Excel worksheet, I have placed tables showing the fate of cohorts of three populations of different species. Your job now is to calculate the survivorship curve (\(l_x\)) for these species, and take the natural log (using the formula =LN(C3) for the first population, =LN(J3) for the second population, etc.). You should see that the graphs automatically fill up with lines. These show Type I, II and III survivorship. Next, calculate the age-specific probability of death (\(q_x\)) and of survival (\(p_x\)). These are the proportions of individuals that enter the age interval that do not and do survive to the end of the interval, respectively. You can calculate them as =1-(B4/B3) and =B4/B3 for the first row of the first population. Plot graphs of these. Make sure that you are (1) able to “diagnose” survivorship type from looking at a graph of \(\ln(l_x)\) vs \(x\); and (2) able to sketch a cartoon of the mortality trajectory if shown one of these survivorship curves. 9.5 Questions What are the three main types of survivorship curves, and which organisms typically exhibit each type? What does a net reproductive rate (\(R_0\)) of less than 1 signify for a population? How does the shape of a survivorship curve reflect trade-offs in life history strategies, typically? How is survivorship (\(l_x\)) different from survival probability (\(p_x\))? How does altering reproduction or survival/mortality at different ages affect \(R_0\) and population growth rate? Two populations have the same \(R_0\), but one has a shorter generation time. Which grows faster per year, and why? The probability of dying in a year, \(q_x\), can never be greater than 1, but the force of mortality, \(\mu_x\) (see the Notation table and the lecture), can. Why? 9.6 Takeaways Life tables summarise age-specific survival and reproduction in a compact, comparable way. Survivorship type reflects how mortality changes with age, and so different life history strategies. \(R_0\) is growth per generation; dividing \(\ln(R_0)\) by the generation time \(T\) gives the capacity for increase, \(r_c\), an approximation to the growth rate per year, \(r_m\). Early-life changes usually have the greatest impact on \(R_0\) and population growth.

10 Matrix population modelling 10.1 Background Matrix population models are powerful and widely used tools in population ecology for studying the dynamics of structured populations. Unlike simple growth models that assume every individual is the same, they take into account variation in vital rates (survival, growth and reproduction) across different life stages or age classes. They are particularly well suited to species with distinct life stages, such as plants with seedlings, juveniles and adults, or animals with different age classes. A matrix population model uses a transition matrix to describe how individuals move between stages, and how many new individuals each stage contributes, over a fixed time step. By incorporating demographic data and life-history traits, these models give a more realistic picture of population dynamics. They are widely used to project the future trajectory of a population under stated assumptions, and to assess how vulnerable it is to environmental change and management actions. In this practical, we will assume that one matrix projection corresponds to one year. Each matrix element therefore represents survival, growth, or reproduction over a one-year interval. This practical aims to give you a good understanding of the basics of their construction and use. The background reading is Neal’s chapter Growth of Age-Structured and Stage-Structured Populations. Learning outcomes: Competence in constructing life cycle diagrams to represent the life history of real (or theoretical) organisms. Understanding how to parameterise life-cycle diagrams and use them to produce a matrix population model. Competence in using R to calculate a population growth rate and project a population. Understanding how to connect these results to a management question. Understanding the logic of “in silico experiments” to investigate a biological question (mathematical modelling). 10.2 Your task First, think of an organism you would like to model the dynamics of. It could be a mammal, a bird, a fish, insect or tree … real or fantasy. Think about their life cycle, and draw it as a life cycle diagram with circles indicating the stages and arrows representing transitions between stages (e.g. growth) and reproduction. Keep it simple: aim for 2-3 stages and no more than about 7 arrows. Your diagram must include at least one reproduction arrow and at least one survival arrow. If your model is stage-based, consider whether individuals can stay in the same stage from one year to the next (an arrow that loops back to the same circle). Things to think about: Is it age based or stage based? How many stages are there? Can you simplify (e.g. instead of age in years, you could use life stage) If using stages, how are stages defined? E.g. by size, by development, etc. Are the survival and fecundity higher in earlier or later life? Does the organism ever skip stages? Can the organism move “backwards” through the life cycle? Next to the arrows, write values for survival probability and fecundity using your biological knowledge. It is fine to use “ballpark” estimates. Read the box below before you choose your fecundity values: a reproduction arrow is not simply the number of babies. What goes on a reproduction arrow? A matrix entry tells you how many individuals will be in a stage at the next census (next year’s count) for each individual in a stage now. So a reproduction arrow is the number of newborns that will be counted next year per individual this year. That includes whatever survival is needed for those newborns to be counted: If you count the population just after breeding (a post-breeding census), the parent must survive the year to breed again before the next count. The entry is the parent’s survival × the number of offspring it then produces. For example, an individual that survives the year with probability 0.8 and then has 2 offspring contributes 0.8 × 2 = 1.6 newborns to next year’s count. If you count just before breeding (a pre-breeding census), the newborns must survive from birth until the next count. The entry is the number of offspring × their first-year survival. Putting the raw number of babies straight into the matrix is the most common mistake in building matrix models (see the lecture, and the chapter “Pre- and Post-reproduction census” for a worked comparison). Demographers call this matrix entry fertility (Neal: the fertility coefficient); here we use the everyday word fecundity for the same thing. The model also follows females only (counting daughters), and assumes there is no shortage of mates. Sanity check your numbers Survival and stage-transition probabilities must be between 0 and 1. Fecundity (new individuals counted at the next census, per individual per year) can be greater than 1. For individuals starting in a given stage, the survival and transition probabilities leaving that stage cannot add up to more than 1. For example, 0.8 staying in the same stage plus 0.7 moving to the next stage is impossible, because it adds up to 1.5. (Fecundity does not count towards this total, because newborns are added to the population rather than being a fate of the parent.) Here’s an example for a fictional organism. Figure 10.1: Life cycle diagram of the example organism. Now you can turn this diagram into a matrix population model by filling in a square of survival/fecundity values. The life cycle shown above looks like this (below). The matrix describes transitions from time \(t\) to time \(t + 1\), where one time step corresponds to one year. Interpretation note: columns are stages at time \(t\) (from) and rows are stages at time \(t+1\) (to). To place each arrow in the matrix, ask two questions: FROM which stage does the arrow start? This gives the column. TO which stage does the arrow point? This gives the row. Before you touch R, fill in the blank table below on paper (or in your notes) for your own organism. Name your stages along the top and down the side, then write each arrow’s value in the correct cell. Leave a cell as 0 if there is no arrow. TO ↓ / FROM → Stage 1 Stage 2 Stage 3 Stage 1 Stage 2 Stage 3 Check your work: every arrow is one non-zero matrix element. Count the arrows in your life cycle diagram, then count the non-zero cells in your table. The two numbers must match. If they don’t, you have either missed an arrow or put a value in the wrong cell. Also check the column totals against the sanity check above. For the example organism, the diagram has 7 arrows (including the loops), and the matrix below has 7 non-zero cells. \[ A = \begin{bmatrix}0.3&8&2 \\0.1&0.5&0 \\0&0.4&0.4 \\\end{bmatrix} \] 10.3 Using R for matrix modelling Working with matrices is very tedious in Excel. However, in R you can use this information to predict the future dynamics of the population, and estimate the population growth rate. Open up RStudio, and let’s see if we can predict future dynamics. First you will need to install a package called popdemo. 10.3.1 Package setup If you are running this chapter in a fresh R session, you might need to install and/or load the popdemo package. install.packages("popdemo") You only need to install packages once. After that you can load the package for use by using the library function. library(popdemo) You can put your matrix into R like in the example below (change the numbers to match YOUR model). If your model has fewer, or more, stages then you will need to modify the code a bit. Ask for help if you get stuck. A <- matrix(c( 0.3, 8.00, 2.00, 0.1, 0.50, 0.00, 0.0, 0.40, 0.40 ), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE) stage_names <- c("Juvenile", "Adult", "Senescent") dimnames(A) <- list(stage_names, stage_names) A ## Juvenile Adult Senescent ## Juvenile 0.3 8.0 2.0 ## Adult 0.1 0.5 0.0 ## Senescent 0.0 0.4 0.4 Important: interpret matrix elements over the chosen time step In matrix population models, all transitions occur over a fixed time interval. In this practical, we use a 1-year time step, so: survival probabilities are annual fecundity is offspring per individual per year \(\lambda\) is growth per year 10.4 Projecting the population And now you can use the project function to project what happens to the population, then plot it. Look at what happens if you log or don’t log the y-axis. First you need to define an initial starting population structure. In my example, I have 3 stages, so I have 3 values for the initial population sizes. 10.4.1 What the projection does Let \(\mathbf{n}_t\) be the vector of stage abundances at time \(t\). The population at the next time step is found by multiplying the matrix by that vector: \[ \mathbf{n}_{t+1} = \mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{n}_t \] Each row of \(\mathbf{A}\) answers the question “where do the individuals in this stage next year come from?”: multiply each entry in the row by the number of individuals in the matching from stage (column), then add them up. Using the example matrix and starting population of 10, 5 and 3 individuals in the juvenile, adult and senescent stages: \[ \begin{bmatrix} n_J \\ n_A \\ n_S \end{bmatrix}_{t=1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 & 8.0 & 2.0 \\ 0.1 & 0.5 & 0.0 \\ 0.0 & 0.4 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} (0.3 \times 10) + (8.0 \times 5) + (2.0 \times 3) \\ (0.1 \times 10) + (0.5 \times 5) + (0.0 \times 3) \\ (0.0 \times 10) + (0.4 \times 5) + (0.4 \times 3) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 49 \\ 3.5 \\ 3.2 \end{bmatrix} \] So after one year there are 49 juveniles (mostly newborns produced by adults), 3.5 adults and 3.2 senescent individuals. To project two years ahead, we simply repeat the multiplication using the new vector. R does this for us with the %*% operator for matrix multiplication: initial <- c(10, 5, 3) A %*% initial ## [,1] ## Juvenile 49.0 ## Adult 3.5 ## Senescent 3.2 The popdemo function project repeats this step as many times as we ask. Here I use it to do a population projection for 10 years (10 time steps). Each step represents one annual cycle of survival, growth, and reproduction. Predict first. Before you run the projection for your own organism, write down your answers to these questions: Do you expect your population to increase, decrease or stay roughly stable? Why? Which stage do you expect to become the most abundant? Then run the projection and compare the result with your prediction. If it surprises you, work out why: look at which matrix elements are large and which are small. pr <- popdemo::project(A, vector = initial, time = 10) Take a look at pr, the projected population. This gives you the total population size, and below that the population sizes in each stage. pr ## 1 deterministic population projection over 10 time intervals. ## ## [1] 18.0000 55.7000 58.4300 85.2570 111.5643 151.4946 203.2634 273.8278 ## [9] 368.4012 495.8572 667.3121 You can access the population sizes of the different stages using vec(pr). vec(pr) ## Juvenile Adult Senescent ## [1,] 10.0000 5.00000 3.000000 ## [2,] 49.0000 3.50000 3.200000 ## [3,] 49.1000 6.65000 2.680000 ## [4,] 73.2900 8.23500 3.732000 ## [5,] 95.3310 11.44650 4.786800 ## [6,] 129.7449 15.25635 6.493320 ## [7,] 173.9609 20.60267 8.699868 ## [8,] 234.4093 27.69742 11.721013 ## [9,] 315.3442 37.28964 15.767375 ## [10,] 424.4552 50.17924 21.222808 ## [11,] 571.2161 67.53514 28.560821 Let’s plot this… pop <- vec(pr) matplot(pop, type = "l", log = "y") legend("topleft", legend = colnames(pop), col = 1:ncol(pop), lty = 1:ncol(pop)) For the example matrix, the population increases exponentially. Does your own population behave as you predicted? The population growth rate is the so-called “dominant eigenvalue” of the matrix A. 10.4.2 Does the starting population matter? Now try the projection again, but with a very different starting population, for example nearly all individuals in the youngest stage, or nearly all in the oldest stage. Keep the matrix the same and change only initial: initial_2 <- c(100, 0, 0) # change to suit your own life cycle pr_2 <- popdemo::project(A, vector = initial_2, time = 10) pop_2 <- vec(pr_2) matplot(pop_2, type = "l", log = "y") Predict, then compare. Before you run it: will the early part of the trajectory look the same as before? Will the late part? After you run it: what changes? What eventually becomes the same? Hint: look at the slopes of the lines on the log scale, and at the vertical gaps between them, once the first few years have passed. 10.4.3 Growth rate and stable stage distribution We can ask R for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix. The dominant eigenvalue is the population growth rate (\(\lambda\)). The corresponding eigenvector gives the stable stage distribution (SSD): the expected proportion of individuals in each stage class once the population has settled into its long-term pattern. This is exactly what your projections with different starting populations were converging towards. Predict first. Look at your projection plot. Is \(\lambda\) above 1, below 1, or about 1? Roughly how steep is the line on the log scale? Which stage do you think will have the highest SSD? Because our projection interval is one year, \(\lambda\) represents the annual population growth rate. You can see that in this case, using my example values the population is growing 34.6% per year. eigs(A, what = c("lambda", "ss")) ## $lambda ## [1] 1.345824 ## ## $ss ## [1] 0.85599732 0.10120281 0.04279987 10.5 Elasticity Elasticity analysis asks how responsive the population growth rate (\(\lambda\)) is to a small proportional change in each transition of the matrix. A transition with a high elasticity is one where a given percentage change produces a relatively large percentage change in \(\lambda\). The elasticities of all the matrix elements sum to one, so each can be read as that transition’s share of the total influence on \(\lambda\). This is useful in management and conservation when we ask questions like, “which parts of the lifecycle should we focus on to preserve the population?”. The mathematics are beyond this course, and R can calculate the elasticities for us. Predict first. Looking at your own matrix, which single element do you think has the highest elasticity, i.e. which one would change \(\lambda\) most, in proportional terms, if you changed it by the same percentage? Write it down before running the code. popdemo::elas(A) ## Juvenile Adult Senescent ## Juvenile 0.09517264 0.30005511 0.03172421 ## Adult 0.33177932 0.19612796 0.00000000 ## Senescent 0.00000000 0.03172421 0.01341654 Which transition has the highest elasticity, and what does that tell you about your organism’s life cycle? Was your prediction correct? If not, why do you think the biology of your organism led you to the wrong guess? Note that a high elasticity means \(\lambda\) responds strongly to a proportional change in that transition, which is not the same as saying it is easy or practical to change in the real world. Elasticity is not the same as sensitivity. Sensitivity measures the change in \(\lambda\) for a small absolute change in a matrix element (e.g. adding 0.01), whereas elasticity measures the proportional change in \(\lambda\) for a proportional change in the element (e.g. a 1% increase). Because elasticity rescales by the size of each element, small probabilities tend to have a high sensitivity but a lower elasticity, and large fecundities the reverse, so the two rankings can differ. You can compare them: popdemo::sens(A) ## [,1] [,2] [,3] ## [1,] 0.426952 0.05047766 0.02134760 ## [2,] 4.465165 0.52790728 0.00000000 ## [3,] 0.000000 0.10673799 0.04514076 For the example matrix, adult fecundity has a low sensitivity (0.05) but one of the highest elasticities (0.30), because it is a large number (8), so a 1% change in it is a large absolute change. Juvenile to adult (0.1) has the highest sensitivity (4.47) and also the highest elasticity (0.33). 10.6 In silico experiments: changing the life cycle Now that we have a model, we can use it as an experimental system. The idea is very simple: you run “experiments” on your matrix model (in silico, i.e. on the computer) by asking “what if” questions. For example, what would happen if we could increase survival of the juveniles by 20%? what would happen if adults are hunted more, and thus have a decreased survival by 60%? what would happen if we provided supplemental food to reproducing females, and increase fecundity by 50%? etc. Use your imagination! For each “what if” question, follow the same pattern: predict what will happen to \(\lambda\), change the matrix, observe the new \(\lambda\), and explain the difference in biological terms. In practice, we do that simply by modifying the matrix model. In the following, I am looking at the effect of increasing fecundity in adult and senescent individuals by 50%: A_mod <- matrix(c( 0.3, 8.00*1.5, 2.00*1.5, 0.1, 0.50, 0.00, 0.0, 0.40, 0.40 ), byrow = TRUE, nrow = 3, dimnames = list(stage_names, stage_names) ) popdemo::eigs(A, what = "lambda") # original ## [1] 1.345824 popdemo::eigs(A_mod, what = "lambda") # modified ## [1] 1.546586 popdemo::elas(A_mod) ## Juvenile Adult Senescent ## Juvenile 0.08514005 0.32540118 0.028380016 ## Adult 0.35378119 0.16901684 0.000000000 ## Senescent 0.00000000 0.02838002 0.009900705 10.7 Your investigation Now it is time to work with your own organism. Rather than just running every function once, you will carry out a small investigation of a biological question. Project and describe. Do a projection for your organism, and calculate and interpret \(\lambda\), the stable stage distribution and the elasticities (remember to write down your predictions first). Choose a question. Pick a “what if” question about your organism. For example: What happens if juvenile survival improves? What happens if adults reproduce more? What happens in a bad year (e.g. lower survival in all stages)? What if reproduction increases at the cost of adult survival? Predict. Before changing the model, write down your prediction for what will happen to \(\lambda\), and why. Change the model. Modify the appropriate matrix element(s) in a copy of your matrix (e.g. A_mod), so that you keep the original for comparison. Compare. Calculate \(\lambda\) for both matrices. Was your prediction right? Explain. Explain the result in biological terms. Use your elasticity results to help: does the change you made involve a transition with high or low elasticity? 10.7.1 An evolutionary experiment (homework, optional) If you run out of time in class, do this section at home. A model answer is in the Solutions. You can think of lambda (population growth rate) as being a measure of fitness. Imagine that some of your population had a mutation that caused them to have, say, 1 extra baby, but at the expense of reduced survival in one of the younger stages. Would this mutation persist in the population? First, predict: increasing fecundity is beneficial and decreasing survival is costly. Which effect do you think will win? Then modify the matrix, calculate \(\lambda\) for the mutant life history, and compare it with \(\lambda\) for the original. Does the mutant have a higher or lower \(\lambda\)? What does that suggest about selection on this trade-off? (Comparing \(\lambda\) like this treats it as fitness, which works when growth is density-independent, as it is in this model. With density dependence, as in the logistic growth chapters, things are more complicated.) 10.7.2 Questions In the graph showing log-transformed population size through time, what is the significance of the lines being straight after the transient phase? Explain how an elasticity analysis of a matrix model can be used to inform the management of a threatened species. What are some of the assumptions of a matrix population model? (Hint: some are similar to the assumptions of exponential/geometric growth models. Think about the environment, vital rates, migration and population density.) 10.8 Takeaways Matrix models link life history to population growth through structured vital rates. The dominant eigenvalue \(\lambda\) summarises long-term growth, while its eigenvector gives the stable stage distribution. Elasticity analysis and in silico experiments turn models into management and evolutionary experiments.

11 Pre- and Post-reproduction census 11.1 Background 11.2 Learning outcomes 11.3 Worked example 11.4 A common mistake 11.5 Your task 11.6 Takeaways

11 Pre- and Post-reproduction census 11.1 Background Population growth estimates depend on when the census is taken relative to reproduction. A pre-breeding census counts individuals just before reproduction; a post-breeding census counts them just after reproduction. This changes how survival and fertility are represented in the projection matrix, even if the underlying biology is the same. Provided the conversion between the two census types is done correctly, the population growth rate (\(\lambda\)) they produce is identical: census timing is just a bookkeeping convention, not a biological difference. However, it is easy to get the conversion wrong, and doing so does change your estimate of \(\lambda\). This chapter shows both: a correct conversion (same \(\lambda\)), and a common mistake (different \(\lambda\)). The background reading is the chapter Growth of Age-Structured and Stage-Structured Populations in Neal, which builds a Leslie matrix for a post-breeding census. This chapter follows on from the fecundity box in “Matrix population modelling”. 11.2 Learning outcomes Learning outcomes: Explain the difference between pre-breeding and post-breeding census models. Convert a post-breeding matrix to a pre-breeding matrix. Recognise that a correct conversion leaves \(\lambda\) unchanged, and explain why. Identify how a mis-specified survival or fertility term changes the resulting \(\lambda\) estimate. 11.3 Worked example 11.3.1 The life history We use a simple bird-like life history, with the same notation as in the life tables practical. Individuals breed for the first time at age 2, breed again at age 3, and none survive beyond age 3. We follow females only, so \(m_x\) counts daughters. Parameter Value Meaning \(p_0\) 0.2 Survival from birth (age 0) to age 1 (first-year survival) \(p_1\) 0.9 Survival from age 1 to age 2 \(p_2\) 0.6 Survival from age 2 to age 3 \(m_1\) 0 Daughters per female aged 1 (age-1 birds do not breed) \(m_2\) 3.0 Daughters per female aged 2 \(m_3\) 6.0 Daughters per female aged 3 Breeding happens once a year, in a short breeding season (a “birth pulse”). The only question is whether we count the population just after or just before that breeding season. Each choice gives a different set of age classes: Post-breeding census (A1) Pre-breeding census (A2) When we count Just after breeding: this year’s newborns are included Just before breeding: this year’s newborns are not born yet Age classes in the matrix Ages 0, 1, 2 Ages 1, 2, 3 Survival arrows (sub-diagonal) Age 0 → 1 (\(p_0\)), age 1 → 2 (\(p_1\)) Age 1 → 2 (\(p_1\)), age 2 → 3 (\(p_2\)) Fertility arrows (top row) From age 1: \(p_1 m_2\); from age 2: \(p_2 m_3\) From age 2: \(m_2 p_0\); from age 3: \(m_3 p_0\) Whose survival is in the fertility The parent’s: it must survive the year and then breed at the next breeding season The newborns’: they must survive from birth to the next census (\(p_0\)) Life cycle 0 → 1 → 2, with fertility arrows from 1 and 2 back to 0 1 → 2 → 3, with fertility arrows from 2 and 3 back to 1 Notice that in the post-breeding census the oldest class is age 2: those individuals survive (with \(p_2\)), breed at age 3 just before the next census, and then die, so they appear only through their fertility. In the pre-breeding census the youngest class is age 1: newborns are never counted at age 0. 11.3.2 Post-breeding census We start with the post-breeding census matrix. Individuals are counted right after breeding, so the fertility of an individual counted at age \(x\) is \(p_x m_{x+1}\): it must survive the year (\(p_x\)), and then breed at age \(x+1\), just before the next census, where its newborns are counted at age 0. For example, a bird counted at age 1 contributes \(p_1 m_2 = 0.9 \times 3 = 2.7\) newborns to next year’s count. p0 <- 0.2 p1 <- 0.9 p2 <- 0.6 m2 <- 3.0 m3 <- 6.0 A1 <- matrix(c(0.0, m2 * p1, m3 * p2, p0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0,p1,0), byrow = TRUE, nrow = 3) A1 ## [,1] [,2] [,3] ## [1,] 0.0 2.7 3.6 ## [2,] 0.2 0.0 0.0 ## [3,] 0.0 0.9 0.0 11.3.3 Pre-breeding census Now let’s correctly convert this to a pre-breeding census matrix. Individuals are counted just before breeding, so two things change: The age classes are now ages 1, 2 and 3, so the survival arrows are the survival from age 1 to 2 (\(p_1\)) and from age 2 to 3 (\(p_2\)). First-year survival, \(p_0\), is no longer on the sub-diagonal. The fertility term is no longer scaled by the parent’s survival. A parent counted at age \(x\) is about to breed, so it is alive at breeding by construction (its survival up to this point is already in the sub-diagonal). What must be added instead is the survival of its newborns from birth to the next census, \(p_0\). So the fertility of an individual counted at age \(x\) is \(m_x p_0\). A2 <- matrix(c(0.0, m2 * p0, m3 * p0, p1, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0,p2,0), byrow = TRUE, nrow = 3) A2 ## [,1] [,2] [,3] ## [1,] 0.0 0.6 1.2 ## [2,] 0.9 0.0 0.0 ## [3,] 0.0 0.6 0.0 Either way, first-year survival \(p_0\) appears once in every route from birth to reproduction. In A1 it is on the sub-diagonal; in A2 it is inside the fertilities. 11.3.4 Comparing the two Compare population growth rates. This uses the eigs function from the popdemo R package (install it with install.packages("popdemo") if you have not already done so in “Matrix population modelling”). (popdemo::eigs(A1, what = "lambda")) ## [1] 1.070261 (popdemo::eigs(A2, what = "lambda")) ## [1] 1.070261 Notice that \(\lambda\) is exactly identical for A1 and A2. This is not a coincidence or a rounding effect. Both matrices have the same characteristic equation, \[ \lambda^3 = p_0 p_1 m_2 \lambda + p_0 p_1 p_2 m_3, \] so they must have the same \(\lambda\). Each term is one route through the life cycle: survive to age 2 and breed (\(p_0 p_1 m_2\)), or survive to age 3 and breed (\(p_0 p_1 p_2 m_3\)). The conversion only changes how the same survival and reproduction are arranged in the matrix; it does not change the biology, so it cannot change the population’s growth rate. The net reproductive rate, \(R_0 = \sum l_x m_x\), is also identical, because it is calculated from the same life table (\(l_1 = p_0\), \(l_2 = p_0 p_1\), \(l_3 = p_0 p_1 p_2\)): l2 <- p0 * p1 l3 <- p0 * p1 * p2 (R0 <- l2 * m2 + l3 * m3) ## [1] 1.188 Not everything is invariant, though. Because the two matrices count different age classes, the stable age distribution and the reproductive values are different: for example, in a post-breeding census most of the population is newborns (age 0), whereas a pre-breeding census never counts newborns at all. The sensitivities of \(\lambda\) to individual matrix elements also differ. Only \(\lambda\) (and quantities derived from it) and \(R_0\) are guaranteed to be the same. popdemo::eigs(A1, what = "ss") # stable age distribution, ages 0, 1, 2 ## [1] 0.7440408 0.1390391 0.1169202 popdemo::eigs(A2, what = "ss") # stable age distribution, ages 1, 2, 3 ## [1] 0.4324619 0.3636641 0.2038740 11.4 A common mistake It is easy to get the pre-breeding conversion partly right and partly wrong. A very common error is to correctly shift the survival transitions to the new age classes, but forget to also change the fertility term, i.e. to keep scaling fertility by the parent’s own survival (\(p_1\), \(p_2\)) instead of switching to the newborns’ survival (\(p_0\)): A3 <- matrix(c(0.0, m2 * p1, m3 * p2, p1, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0,p2,0), byrow = TRUE, nrow = 3) (popdemo::eigs(A3, what = "lambda")) ## [1] 1.863632 This looks like a small, easy-to-miss slip: only the fertility row is “wrong”, and the matrix still looks like a sensible pre-breeding matrix. But it produces a substantially different (and incorrect) estimate of \(\lambda\), compared to the correctly converted A2. 11.5 Your task Confirm that A1 and A2 give exactly the same \(\lambda\). Explain, in your own words, why a correct change of census timing should not change the underlying population growth rate. Compare A2 (correct pre-breeding matrix) and A3 (the common mistake). Which specific matrix entries differ, and why does that particular mistake push \(\lambda\) so far from the correct value? (Hint: look for \(p_0\) in each matrix.) Modify one survival probability (e.g. p1) and re-build A1, A2 and A3. Does the correct conversion (A1 vs A2) still agree? Does the size of the error from the mistake (A2 vs A3) grow, shrink, or stay about the same? Now try changing p0 instead. What do you notice? 11.6 Takeaways Census timing (pre- vs post-breeding) changes which age classes are counted, and how fertility and survival are encoded in the matrix. A correctly done conversion between the two gives exactly the same \(\lambda\) and \(R_0\): timing alone is a bookkeeping choice, not a biological difference. In a post-breeding census the fertility includes the parent’s survival over the year (\(p_x m_{x+1}\)); in a pre-breeding census it includes the newborns’ first-year survival (\(m_x p_0\)). The stable age distribution, reproductive values and sensitivities do depend on census timing, so always say which census a matrix uses. Small errors in how survival or fertility terms are calculated for a given census type are easy to make and can substantially bias your \(\lambda\) estimate. The general lesson extends beyond census timing: applying the wrong calculation will bias your estimates, even if the matrix “looks” reasonable.

12 Life Table Response Experiments 12.1 Background 12.2 Learning outcomes 12.3 Set up 12.4 A worked example 12.5 Retrospective vs prospective analyses 12.6 Your task 12.7 Takeaways

12 Life Table Response Experiments 12.1 Background A Life Table Response Experiment (LTRE), in matrix population modelling, is a technique used to analyse how differences in demographic parameters between two or more populations or “treatments” contribute to the observed difference in their population growth rate (\(\lambda\)). It answers the question: why do these populations have different growth rates? Which of the differences in survival, growth or fertility account for most of the difference in \(\lambda\)? The method compares matrix models of the populations in question and decomposes the difference in growth rate between the models into contributions from the individual matrix elements. Each contribution is (roughly) the difference in that element multiplied by how sensitive \(\lambda\) is to that element. LTRE is a retrospective analysis (Caswell’s terminology): it looks back at differences that have already happened, and explains an observed difference in \(\lambda\). Sensitivity and elasticity analysis, and in silico experiments like those in “Matrix population modelling”, are prospective: they ask what would happen to \(\lambda\) if we changed a vital rate in the future. The two kinds of question need different tools, and we come back to this distinction at the end of the chapter. The background reading is the chapter Growth of Age-Structured and Stage-Structured Populations in Neal. Sensitivity was introduced in the lecture; we compute it below. 12.2 Learning outcomes Learning outcomes: Explain the purpose of an LTRE, and the difference between a retrospective analysis (LTRE) and a prospective one (sensitivity, elasticity, in silico experiments). Calculate the sensitivity of \(\lambda\) to each matrix element, and the LTRE contribution of each element as (difference in element) × (sensitivity at the midpoint matrix). Check that the contributions add up (approximately) to the observed difference in \(\lambda\), and explain why the match is not exact. Interpret LTRE output biologically, including the sign of each contribution. 12.3 Set up For the core LTRE analysis you need popbio (for the LTRE function) and popdemo (for the eigs function used to compare growth rates). If you have not installed them already, do so now. install.packages(c("popbio", "popdemo")) library(popbio) library(popdemo) 12.4 A worked example In this example, we consider a two-stage matrix model to analyse, say, squirrel populations in two different geographic locations. The life cycle has juveniles (J) and adults (A). Each year, a juvenile can survive and stay a juvenile, or survive and mature into an adult; an adult can survive (and stay adult) and also produces juveniles (the fertility: juveniles counted at the next census per adult). The reference population, from Location A, lives in an area with favourable environmental conditions. The treatment population, from Location B, experiences worse conditions in spring. This particularly affects juveniles, which are much less likely to survive and mature, and adults produce fewer young (mothers in poor condition produce fewer young). Adult survival, on the other hand, is a little higher at Location B. Matrix element Meaning Reference (Location A) Treatment (Location B) \(a_{11}\) (top left) Juvenile survives and stays juvenile 0.1 0.1 \(a_{21}\) (bottom left) Juvenile survives and matures to adult 0.5 0.2 \(a_{12}\) (top right) Fertility: juveniles produced per adult 2.3 1.3 \(a_{22}\) (bottom right) Adult survives 0.6 0.7 The two matrices can be created in R as follows. Compare the values in the matrices with the values in the life cycle diagrams below. A_ref <- matrix(c(0.1,2.3, 0.5,0.6), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE) A_treat <- matrix(c(0.1,1.3, 0.2,0.7), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE) Figure 12.1: Life cycle diagrams for the reference population (Location A, left) and the treatment population (Location B, right). J = juvenile, A = adult. Arrows show survival and maturation probabilities, and the fertility (arrow from A to J). 12.4.1 Comparing matrices Before we dig into the formal LTRE, it is useful to compare the two matrices, A_ref and A_treat, to see how they are different from each other. We can check what overall difference there is between the matrices in a couple of ways. Firstly, we can examine the differences in the individual transition rates between the matrices by subtracting one from the other. A_ref - A_treat ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 0.0 1.0 ## [2,] 0.3 -0.1 Next, we can ask what impact these differences have on the population growth rate (lambda). Note that putting the command in parentheses tells R to both create the new object (e.g. lambda_A_ref) and print the result to the screen. (lambda_A_ref <- popdemo::eigs(A_ref, what = "lambda")) ## [1] 1.451136 (lambda_A_treat <- popdemo::eigs(A_treat, what = "lambda")) ## [1] 0.991608 The reference population is growing (\(\lambda > 1\)), whereas \(\lambda\) for the treatment population is just below 1, so the Location B population is slowly declining. We could express this as a difference, or as a proportional difference. The difference in growth rates between the matrices is 0.46. (lambdaDiff <- lambda_A_ref - lambda_A_treat) ## [1] 0.4595278 This is a 32% reduction, compared to the reference matrix. (lambdaDiff/lambda_A_ref) * 100 ## [1] 31.66677 So far, so good. We can see that \(\lambda\) is lower at Location B, but we don’t know exactly why. There are 3 changes in the matrix. Which of these changes is most instrumental in driving the change in the population growth rate? 12.4.2 Sensitivity: how much does \(\lambda\) change when one element changes? To answer this, we need to know how strongly \(\lambda\) responds to each matrix element. This is the sensitivity of \(\lambda\) to element \(a_{ij}\), written \(s_{ij}\): the change in \(\lambda\) for a small absolute change in \(a_{ij}\) (the slope of \(\lambda\) against \(a_{ij}\)). Elasticity, which you met in “Matrix population modelling”, is the proportional version of the same idea. Sensitivities can be calculated from two eigenvectors of the matrix: the stable stage distribution \(\mathbf{w}\) (the right eigenvector) and the reproductive values \(\mathbf{v}\) (the left eigenvector, which is the right eigenvector of the transposed matrix). The formula is \[ s_{ij} = \frac{v_i \, w_j}{\sum_k v_k w_k}. \] So \(\lambda\) is most sensitive to transitions into stages with high reproductive value (\(v_i\)) from stages that are common in the stable stage distribution (\(w_j\)). In base R: sensitivity <- function(M) { # Right eigenvector: stable stage distribution w eig_right <- eigen(M) w <- Re(eig_right$vectors[, which.max(Re(eig_right$values))]) # Left eigenvector: reproductive values v (eigenvector of the transposed matrix) eig_left <- eigen(t(M)) v <- Re(eig_left$vectors[, which.max(Re(eig_left$values))]) # s_ij = v_i * w_j / sum(v * w) outer(v, w) / sum(v * w) } sensitivity(A_ref) ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 0.3864808 0.2270383 ## [2,] 1.0443762 0.6135192 (The popbio package has a function sensitivity() that does the same thing; here you can see what it does.) 12.4.3 Contributions from individual matrix elements The LTRE splits the observed difference in \(\lambda\) into one contribution per matrix element. The contribution of element \(a_{ij}\) is \[ c_{ij} = \left(a_{ij}^{\mathrm{treat}} - a_{ij}^{\mathrm{ref}}\right) \times s_{ij}\left(\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{mid}}\right), \qquad \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{mid}} = \frac{\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{ref}} + \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{treat}}}{2}, \] that is, how much the element differs, multiplied by how much \(\lambda\) responds to that element. The sensitivity is calculated from the matrix halfway between the two populations (the midpoint matrix), because the sensitivities of the two populations are not the same, and the midpoint is a fair compromise. A large contribution can come from a large difference in an element, from a high sensitivity, or from both. We can calculate the contributions by hand: A_mid <- (A_ref + A_treat) / 2 (contributions <- (A_treat - A_ref) * sensitivity(A_mid)) ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 0.0000000 -0.20832964 ## [2,] -0.3214229 0.06636876 The LTRE function in the popbio package does exactly this calculation. Note the order of the arguments: treatment first, then reference. popbio::LTRE(A_treat, A_ref) ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 0.0000000 -0.20832964 ## [2,] -0.3214229 0.06636876 The contributions should add up to the observed difference in \(\lambda\) (treatment minus reference): sum(popbio::LTRE(A_treat, A_ref)) ## [1] -0.4633838 lambda_A_treat - lambda_A_ref ## [1] -0.4595278 The two numbers are very close, but not identical (-0.463 vs -0.460). The LTRE treats \(\lambda\) as if it changed in a straight line with each element, with a slope equal to the sensitivity at the midpoint matrix. In reality the sensitivities change as the elements change, so this linear approximation is only approximately right. It is very good when the differences between the matrices are small, and gets worse when they are large. 12.4.4 Interpreting the contributions Contributions are in the same units as \(\lambda\). A negative contribution means that difference in the element lowers \(\lambda\) in the treatment population relative to the reference; a positive contribution means it raises \(\lambda\). Here, the juvenile stasis element contributes nothing, because it is the same (0.1) in both populations. The other three differences all contribute: The lower probability of juveniles maturing into adults (0.5 → 0.2, bottom left) makes the largest contribution (-0.321). The difference is only 0.3, but \(\lambda\) is very sensitive to this element. The lower fertility (2.3 → 1.3, top right) contributes -0.208. The difference in the element is much larger (1.0), but \(\lambda\) is much less sensitive to it. The slightly higher adult survival at Location B (0.6 → 0.7, bottom right) makes a small positive contribution (0.066), which partly offsets the other two. So the main reason the Location B population has a lower growth rate (and is declining) is that fewer juveniles survive and mature into adults; the reduced fertility is the second most important reason. 12.5 Retrospective vs prospective analyses It is tempting to read an LTRE as a management recommendation (“juvenile maturation made the largest contribution, so managers should improve juvenile maturation”). That is not what an LTRE tells you. Following Caswell, it helps to separate two kinds of question: Retrospective (LTRE): Why do these observed populations differ in \(\lambda\)? The LTRE takes differences in vital rates that have already happened and shares out the observed difference in \(\lambda\) among them. A contribution is large if the element did differ a lot, if \(\lambda\) is sensitive to it, or both. Prospective (sensitivity, elasticity, in silico experiments): What would happen to \(\lambda\) if we changed a vital rate? These analyses do not depend on how much the rates have varied in the past. They are the tools for exploring management options, together with knowledge of which rates can actually be changed, and by how much. The answers can differ. A vital rate can make a large LTRE contribution simply because it happened to vary a lot between places (for example because of weather), even if managers cannot change it. And a vital rate with a high sensitivity or elasticity can make no LTRE contribution at all, if it did not differ between the populations: in our example \(\lambda\) has a sensitivity of 0.336 to juvenile stasis at the midpoint matrix, but juvenile stasis contributes nothing because it is 0.1 in both populations. The two approaches complement each other. LTRE is useful for understanding what has caused observed differences between populations, years or experimental treatments (and so for generating hypotheses about the causes), and it can handle several vital rates differing at the same time. To ask what management actions would do, use prospective tools. 12.6 Your task Before running any more code, look at the table of matrix elements and the sensitivities. Predict the sign of each LTRE contribution, and which one will be largest. Then compare your prediction with the output above. Check for yourself that the contributions sum approximately to \(\lambda_{\mathrm{treat}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}\). Modify one element in A_treat (for example, set the treatment fertility to 1.8 instead of 1.3, or the treatment maturation probability to 0.4 instead of 0.2). Predict which LTRE contribution will change most, and in which direction. Re-run the contributions (by hand and with popbio::LTRE) and check your prediction. Explain the change using “difference in element × sensitivity”. Explain, in two or three sentences, why the LTRE result does not on its own tell a manager which vital rate to target. 12.7 Takeaways LTRE is retrospective: it decomposes an observed difference in \(\lambda\) into contributions from specific matrix elements. Each contribution is (difference in the element) × (sensitivity of \(\lambda\) to that element, at the midpoint matrix), and the contributions sum approximately to the observed difference in \(\lambda\). Sensitivity and elasticity analyses are prospective: they ask what would happen if a vital rate changed, and are the right tools for exploring management options.

13 How many eggs should a bird lay? 13.1 Background 13.2 Before you start: predict 13.3 Your task 13.4 Assumptions 13.5 Questions 13.6 Takeaways

13 How many eggs should a bird lay? 13.1 Background Trade-offs are inherent compromises in biology, where allocating limited resources to one trait may come at the expense of another. Organisms face these trade-offs when making crucial life-history decisions. One classic example is the British ornithologist David Lack’s clutch size trade-off. Parents can feed only so many chicks, so the more eggs a bird lays, the less food each chick gets and the lower its chance of surviving. Lack proposed that clutch size evolves to the number from which, on average, the most young survive. In other words, although it may be beneficial to have many offspring, the survival of those offspring will decline if they cannot be cared for. Understanding such trade-offs sheds light on the fascinating strategies that organisms employ to optimise their fitness and evolutionary success. Further reading: Neal’s chapter Evolution of Life Histories. Learning outcomes: Calculate the expected number of surviving offspring from clutch size and chick survival. Explain how a trade-off between offspring number and offspring survival produces an intermediate optimum. Predict how the optimum changes when the environment, or the cost of breeding to the parents, changes. 13.2 Before you start: predict Before you calculate anything, make a prediction and write it down: will a big bird that lays 10 eggs raise more surviving chicks than one that lays 4 eggs, or fewer? Why? You will check your prediction below. 13.3 Your task The big bird (Bigus canarius) (Fig 13.1) can lay up to 10 eggs per breeding season. If there is only 1 egg, the probability that the parents can adequately feed the chick and ensure it survives is very high (0.9). However, as the number of siblings increases, the amount of energy and food that the parents can dedicate to caring for each chick decreases, and the probability of survival therefore declines . With a clutch size of 10 eggs, there is so little food per chick that the survival rates are close to zero. Figure 13.1: Big bird, Bigus canarius A recent study gathered data on chick survival probability as a function of number of eggs in the nest. These are given in the table below. Eggs Survival probability 1 0.90 2 0.85 3 0.82 4 0.70 5 0.50 6 0.30 7 0.22 8 0.15 9 0.10 10 0.05 Use these data to plot a graph in Excel with number of eggs on the x-axis and survival probability on the y-axis. Now, in another column in Excel, calculate, given the chick survival probability, what the expected number of surviving chicks will be for a big bird laying between 1 and 10 eggs2. Plot your result on another graph with number of eggs on the x-axis and number of surviving offspring on the y-axis. What do you notice? What is the optimum number of eggs to lay? Advanced: What happens to the optimum as you change the relationship between clutch size and survival? Field observations of the big bird show that most females lay 3 eggs. Keep this in mind for the questions below. 13.4 Assumptions This simple model assumes that every egg hatches, that every chick in a nest has the same chance of surviving, that we count only one breeding season, and that laying and raising more eggs has no cost to the parents’ own survival. Question 3 relaxes the last assumption. 13.5 Questions What is Lack’s hypothesis? Does the big bird’s optimum support it, given that most big birds lay 3 eggs? In a good food year, each chick’s survival probability in clutches of 5 or more eggs is 0.2 higher (for example, 0.50 becomes 0.70). Recalculate. What is the best clutch size now, and why? Raising chicks is costly for the parents. Suppose the probability that a parent survives to breed again next year is \(0.8 - 0.08 \times \text{eggs}\) (so 0.72 with 1 egg, and 0.48 with 4 eggs). On average, a parent then breeds \(1 / (1 - \text{parent survival})\) times in its life. Calculate the number of surviving chicks over a parent’s whole life for each clutch size. Does the best clutch size change? What does this mean for Lack’s hypothesis? (Discussion) Birds also trade off the number of eggs against the size of each egg. What would you need to add to this model to study that trade-off? 13.6 Takeaways Trade-offs often produce intermediate optimal strategies. Expected reproductive success depends on both offspring number and survival probability. If raising young costs the parents’ future survival, the best clutch is smaller than the one that produces the most surviving young in a single season. This may require some thought!↩︎

14 Trade-offs and the declining force of selection 14.1 Background 14.2 Before you start: predict 14.3 Your task 14.4 Exploring different life history strategies 14.5 Questions 14.6 Takeaways

14 Trade-offs and the declining force of selection Why does evolution care less and less about you as you age? Because fewer individuals survive to late ages, selection acts more weakly on late life, and trade-offs then let early benefits win over late costs. 14.1 Background An important kind of trade off are those which occur between processes in early and late life. For example, it may be beneficial to increase reproduction at younger ages, but this might lead to increased risk of death at older ages. A mechanism for this could be that limited resources are allocated to producing offspring rather than maintaining/repairing the body. The balance of the trade off between these early and late life processes is shaped by the force of selection: how much a small change in survival or reproduction at a given age changes fitness. Crucially, from the age of first reproduction onwards, the force of selection tends to decline with age, meaning that late-life processes are not as important as early-life processes. Medawar (1952) pointed out that because few individuals survive to old age, harmful mutations whose effects appear only late in life are hardly removed by selection, so they can build up in a population: this is mutation accumulation. Hamilton (1966) showed mathematically why the force of selection on survival and reproduction declines with age once reproduction has begun. It also means that a mutation giving a modest reproductive advantage at an early age, alongside a harmful or even deadly effect late in life, can be “seen” by natural selection as advantageous. This idea is called antagonistic pleiotropy (Williams 1957): one gene with a good effect early in life and a bad effect later. Further reading: Neal’s chapter Evolution of Life Histories. References: Medawar, P. B. (1952) An Unsolved Problem of Biology. H. K. Lewis, London. Williams, G. C. (1957) Pleiotropy, natural selection, and the evolution of senescence. Evolution 11: 398-411. Hamilton, W. D. (1966) The moulding of senescence by natural selection. Journal of Theoretical Biology 12: 12-45. This highlights the significance of early-late life trade-offs and their role in shaping ageing patterns in various organisms. Understanding this concept is essential for comprehending life history evolution, ageing, and longevity across species. The aim of this exercise is to gain an understanding of early-life late-life trade offs and to understand why events early in life tend to be much more important to evolution than those that happen later in life. Learning outcomes: Calculate how a change in fertility or survival at a given age changes fitness (\(R_0\)). Explain why the force of selection declines with age, and why this lets genes with early benefits and late costs spread. Explain why survival after reproduction has ended has little or no effect on fitness in this model. 14.2 Before you start: predict Recall that fitness can be measured as \(R_0 = \sum l_x m_x\), where \(l_x\) is the probability of surviving from birth to age \(x\), and \(m_x\) is the number of daughters produced per female at age \(x\) (as in Life tables and survivorship types). Before you open the spreadsheet, make a prediction and write it down: will one extra offspring at age 1 or one extra offspring at age 20 raise \(R_0\) more? Why? You will check your prediction in the tasks below. 14.3 Your task Open the Excel file TradeOffsAndForceOfSelection.xlsx. This file shows a simplified life table, following a cohort of 1000 individuals for a fictional creature. Survival rates from year to year are set to be 0.8 (i.e. 80% make it through to the next year). This fixed, constant survival rate leads to an exponentially declining survival curve, illustrated with a chart in the Excel file. Fertility (\(m_x\), the number of babies produced per year; assume these are daughters per female) is set to be 10 per year. In the spreadsheet, the Survival value in each row is the probability of surviving into that age from the age before. So setting Survival to 0 in the age-25 row means that nobody reaches age 25. (The Survival value in the age-1 row is not used: the cohort starts at age 1.) The product of survivorship (\(l_x\)) and fertility (\(m_x\)), \(l_x m_x\), is the expected number of offspring produced at age \(x\) by a newborn. The sum of these values, \(\sum l_x m_x\), is the net reproductive rate, \(R_0\): the population’s growth per generation (see the practical Life tables and survivorship types). \(R_0\) is a good measure of the fitness of a life history strategy when the population is roughly stable in size (stationary, or regulated around an equilibrium). A caveat. This fictional life table has \(R_0 \approx 50\), which would make the population grow about 10.8-fold per year (\(\lambda \approx 10.8\), from the Euler-Lotka equation). In a growing population the right fitness measure is \(r_m\) (or \(\lambda\)), and it weights early reproduction even more heavily than \(R_0\) does: an offspring produced early is itself breeding while later offspring are still to come. For this life table, matching the effect of one extra offspring at age 1 would need about 2.4 extra offspring at age 5 if fitness is \(R_0\), but about 46,000 if fitness is \(r_m\). So treat the numbers below as an illustration: the qualitative message (early life matters more than late life) holds, and is even stronger, in growing populations. Note that the initial \(R_0\) is 49.81 14.4 Exploring different life history strategies We will now use this data to explore how alternative life history strategies affect fitness. Consider a trade-off between early reproduction and late life survival (i.e. via resources allocated to body maintenance). In this scenario the species could increase reproduction early in life by allocating more energy to making babies. However, resources are limited and this will come at the expense of survival at a later date. A mechanism for this could be that the body no longer fixes cancers so effectively. Simulate this by adding 1 to fertility (\(m_x\)) at age 1 (the benefit), but setting Survival to 0 in the age-25 row, so that all die before age 25 (the cost). What is the fitness of this strategy? By setting Survival to 0 in earlier rows instead, determine how many years of life could be lost before this cost is no longer worth bearing. Is this surprising? Now reset everything (\(m_x\) =10; survival = 0.8). Recall what fitness was when you added 1 to \(m_x\) at age 1 (50.81). If, instead of adding to \(m_x\) at age 1 you were to increase \(m_x\) at age 25, how much would you need to increase \(m_x\) to reach this figure? What about at age 20? Age 15? Age 10? Age 5? Plot the increase required vs. age (make a new worksheet/ark in Excel). What do you notice? Reset everything again (\(m_x\) =10; survival = 0.8). Set \(m_x\) from age 15 onwards to be 0. Now alter survival rate after this point (at ages 15-25). What happens to fitness? 14.5 Questions Explain the concept of the declining force of selection in the context of life history evolution and ageing. How does this phenomenon contribute to the evolution of life history strategies in different organisms? Use concepts of life history evolution, including the force of selection, to explain why age-related diseases are common in humans. How would predation risk influence the early-late life trade off in resource allocation to reproduction vs. body maintenance? In this model, survival after the last reproduction has no effect on fitness. Why might survival after reproduction still matter for killer whales or humans? 14.6 Takeaways The force of selection declines with age, making early-life traits more influential. Small early-life advantages can outweigh large late-life costs. Trade-offs between reproduction and survival shape ageing and life history strategies.
