15 Matrix Population Models (MPMs): Projection and Simulation 15.1 Learning outcomes 15.2 What is a matrix population model? 15.3 The projection interval (\(\Delta t\)) 15.4 The population vector 15.5 The projection matrix 15.6 A simple 3-stage model 15.7 Projection: projecting \(\mathbf{n}_t\) forward 15.8 Define vital rates and build \(\mathbf{A}\) 15.9 Define an initial population vector \(\mathbf{n}_0\) 15.10 One-step projection 15.11 Project for many years (deterministic) 15.12 Long-term growth rate (\(\lambda\)) 15.13 Simulation: adding stochasticity and management actions 15.14 Your task 15.15 Takeaways 15.16 Notes and extensions

15 Matrix Population Models (MPMs): Projection and Simulation This short tutorial introduces matrix population models (MPMs) and shows two closely related uses: Projection: how a population vector is projected forward through time using a matrix. Simulation: how the same structure can be used to explore scenarios (e.g. culling) and quantify uncertainty. The examples use a simple 3-stage life cycle. The goal is to be clear about: the projection interval (time step, \(\Delta t\)), how survival/transition and reproduction appear in the matrix, how to project a population vector \(\mathbf{n}_t\), how to convert the deterministic model into a basic stochastic simulation. The background reading is the chapter Growth of Age-Structured and Stage-Structured Populations in Neal. The chapter “Matrix population modelling” covers building a matrix, projection and \(\lambda\) in more detail, using the popdemo package; here we do everything in base R. 15.1 Learning outcomes Learning outcomes: Explain why the vital rates in a matrix must match the projection interval \(\Delta t\). Build a stage-structured projection matrix in base R, project a population forward and calculate \(\lambda\) with eigen(). Explain the difference between a deterministic projection and a stochastic simulation with demographic stochasticity. Write a simulation once as a function, and use it to run replicate simulations and summarise their uncertainty. Use simulation to compare management scenarios (proportional harvest, fixed quotas, contraception) and explain the results in terms of the life cycle. 15.2 What is a matrix population model? An MPM describes how a structured population changes over discrete time steps. 15.3 The projection interval (\(\Delta t\)) MPMs are defined for a particular projection interval \(\Delta t\) (the time step between updates). Common choices are: \(\Delta t = 1\) year (very common in ecology) \(\Delta t = 1\) month (or other shorter steps) Key rule: the vital rates you put in the matrix must match the chosen \(\Delta t\). If \(\Delta t\) is one year, use annual survival and annual fertility/recruitment. If \(\Delta t\) is one month, use monthly survival and monthly recruitment. A common mistake is mixing time scales (e.g. monthly survival with yearly reproduction). 15.4 The population vector Let \(\mathbf{n}_t\) be a vector of abundances at time \(t\) (measured in units of \(\Delta t\)): \[ \mathbf{n}_t = \begin{bmatrix} n_{1,t} \\ n_{2,t} \\ \vdots \\ n_{k,t} \end{bmatrix} \] Each element is the number (or density) in a class (age/stage/size/etc.). 15.5 The projection matrix Let \(\mathbf{A}\) be a square matrix of vital rates. The basic model is: \[ \mathbf{n}_{t+\Delta t} = \mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{n}_t \] Interpretation of entries: Survival / transition: individuals moving between classes (including remaining in the same class) Reproduction: production of new individuals (often into the first class) 15.6 A simple 3-stage model We will use three stages: Juvenile (J) Subadult (S) Adult (A) The life-cycle assumptions (per \(\Delta t = 1\) year) are: Adults produce juveniles: \(F_A\) juveniles per adult per year (recruits to J). This is a fertility: the number of new juveniles counted at the next census per adult, so it already includes the survival needed to reach that count, not just the number born (see the fecundity box in the chapter “Matrix population modelling”). Juveniles that survive and grow move to Subadult with probability \(G_J\). Subadults either: survive and remain subadult with probability \(P_S\), or survive and grow to adult with probability \(G_S\). Adults survive and remain adult with probability \(P_A\). A common stage-structured (Lefkovitch) matrix is: \[ \mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & F_A \\ G_J & P_S & 0 \\ 0 & G_S & P_A \end{bmatrix} \] 15.7 Projection: projecting \(\mathbf{n}_t\) forward 15.8 Define vital rates and build \(\mathbf{A}\) # Vital rates for a 1-year projection interval F_A <- 1.2 # recruits (juveniles) per adult per year G_J <- 0.35 # juvenile -> subadult (survive + grow) P_S <- 0.55 # subadult -> subadult (survive + stay) G_S <- 0.25 # subadult -> adult (survive + grow) P_A <- 0.80 # adult -> adult (survive + stay) # Build the projection matrix (rows = stage at t+1, cols = stage at t) A <- matrix( c(0, 0, F_A, G_J, P_S, 0, 0, G_S, P_A), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE ) dimnames(A) <- list( c("Juvenile", "Subadult", "Adult"), c("Juvenile", "Subadult", "Adult") ) # Print matrix so we can check entries A ## Juvenile Subadult Adult ## Juvenile 0.00 0.00 1.2 ## Subadult 0.35 0.55 0.0 ## Adult 0.00 0.25 0.8 15.9 Define an initial population vector \(\mathbf{n}_0\) # Initial population vector (year 0) n0 <- c(Juvenile = 50, Subadult = 30, Adult = 20) n0 ## Juvenile Subadult Adult ## 50 30 20 15.10 One-step projection # Deterministic one-step update n1 <- A %*% n0 n1 ## [,1] ## Juvenile 24.0 ## Subadult 34.0 ## Adult 23.5 Given the stage abundances at time \(t\), multiplying by \(\mathbf{A}\) gives the expected abundances at time \(t+1\) (because \(\Delta t=1\) year here). 15.11 Project for many years (deterministic) # Number of projection steps years <- 30 # Matrix to store yearly stage abundances nmat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = years + 1, ncol = length(n0)) colnames(nmat) <- names(n0) # Set initial year nmat[1, ] <- n0 # Project forward one year at a time for (t in 1:years) { nmat[t + 1, ] <- as.numeric(A %*% nmat[t, ]) } head(nmat, 6) ## Juvenile Subadult Adult ## [1,] 50.0000 30.00000 20.00000 ## [2,] 24.0000 34.00000 23.50000 ## [3,] 28.2000 27.10000 27.30000 ## [4,] 32.7600 24.77500 28.61500 ## [5,] 34.3380 25.09225 29.08575 ## [6,] 34.9029 25.81904 29.54166 15.11.1 Plot totals and stage trajectories # Total abundance each year totalN <- rowSums(nmat) # Plot total abundance plot( 0:years, totalN, type = "l", xlab = "Year", ylab = "Total population size" ) # Plot stage-specific abundances matplot( 0:years, nmat, type = "l", lty = 1, xlab = "Year", ylab = "Abundance" ) legend("topleft", legend = colnames(nmat), lty = 1, bty = "n") 15.12 Long-term growth rate (\(\lambda\)) For a constant matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), the asymptotic growth rate is the dominant eigenvalue \(\lambda\). # Eigenvalues of the projection matrix eig <- eigen(A) # Dominant eigenvalue is asymptotic growth rate lambda lambda <- Re(eig$values[which.max(Re(eig$values))]) lambda ## [1] 1.01942 If \(\lambda > 1\): growth (on average) per time step If \(\lambda = 1\): stationary If \(\lambda < 1\): decline Here \(\lambda\) is only just above 1 (1.019): the population is expected to grow by about 2% per year. Keep this in mind for the management scenarios below: a population that is only just growing does not need much extra mortality to tip it into decline. 15.13 Simulation: adding stochasticity and management actions Deterministic projection treats the model output as exact expectations. In reality: births and deaths vary (demographic stochasticity), vital rates vary across years (environmental stochasticity), management can intervene (culling, supplementation, etc.). Below is a transparent stochastic simulation that: simulates reproduction with Poisson variation, simulates survival/transitions with binomial variation, allows a simple culling intervention. This simulation includes demographic stochasticity only: the matrix (the vital rates) is the same every year, and the randomness comes from the fact that a whole number of individuals survive, grow or are born, by chance. Environmental stochasticity (good and bad years, with different vital rates) is covered in the chapter “Stochastic population growth”, and in an optional exercise at the end of this chapter. 15.13.1 Writing the simulation once, as a function We are going to run the same simulation many times, with and without culling, so we write it once as a function. The function: Reads the vital rates from the matrix A (so if you change the matrix, the simulation changes too). Creates an output matrix with one row per year and one column per stage, and fills row 1 with the initial stage abundances (n0). For each year, reads the current stage counts (nJ, nS, nA). We do not call these J, S and A: the name A is already taken by the projection matrix, and overwriting it would silently break everything that uses the matrix afterwards. If the year has reached cull_start, removes individuals from the target stage: a proportion cull_prop (each individual is removed with that probability), plus a fixed number cull_n. Both are 0 by default (no culling). Draws the number of births and transitions using random distributions: births from adults: Poisson, survival/transition events: Binomial. Writes the resulting stage counts into the next row, and returns the whole trajectory. The stored counts are the census counts before any cull. The cull is applied to the working counts only, just before breeding and survival. simulate_once <- function(A, n0, years, cull_stage = "Adult", cull_prop = 0, cull_n = 0, cull_start = 10) { # Step 1: read the vital rates from the projection matrix F_A <- A["Juvenile", "Adult"] G_J <- A["Subadult", "Juvenile"] P_S <- A["Subadult", "Subadult"] G_S <- A["Adult", "Subadult"] P_A <- A["Adult", "Adult"] # Step 2: a matrix to store the trajectory, with year 0 in row 1 out <- matrix(0L, nrow = years + 1, ncol = 3) colnames(out) <- c("Juvenile", "Subadult", "Adult") out[1, ] <- as.integer(n0[c("Juvenile", "Subadult", "Adult")]) for (t in 1:years) { year <- t - 1 # row t holds year t - 1 # Step 3: current stage counts at the census n_now <- out[t, ] # Step 4: culling, once the start year has been reached if (year >= cull_start) { removed <- rbinom(1, size = n_now[cull_stage], prob = cull_prop) + cull_n removed <- min(removed, n_now[cull_stage]) # cannot remove more than are there n_now[cull_stage] <- n_now[cull_stage] - removed } nJ <- n_now["Juvenile"] nS <- n_now["Subadult"] nA <- n_now["Adult"] # Step 5: births, survival and transitions newJ <- rpois(1, lambda = F_A * nA) # births from adults J_to_S <- rbinom(1, size = nJ, prob = G_J) # juvenile -> subadult S_stay <- rbinom(1, size = nS, prob = P_S) # subadult stays subadult S_remaining <- nS - S_stay # the rest either grow or die p_grow_cond <- if ((1 - P_S) > 0) G_S / (1 - P_S) else 0 S_to_A <- rbinom(1, size = S_remaining, prob = p_grow_cond) A_surv <- rbinom(1, size = nA, prob = P_A) # adult survival # Step 6: write next year's abundances out[t + 1, "Juvenile"] <- newJ out[t + 1, "Subadult"] <- J_to_S + S_stay out[t + 1, "Adult"] <- S_to_A + A_surv } out } The subadult step needs a little explanation. A subadult has three possible fates: stay subadult (\(P_S\)), grow to adult (\(G_S\)) or die (\(1 - P_S - G_S\)). We first draw how many stay. Among the rest, the probability of growing (rather than dying) is \(G_S / (1 - P_S)\), so on average a fraction \(G_S\) of all subadults grow, as in the matrix. 15.13.2 One simulated trajectory (no culling) Each run draws new random numbers, so your trajectory will differ from the one shown here. Run the chunk a few times to see how much it varies. sim1 <- simulate_once(A, n0, years) # Plot the total population trajectory plot(0:years, rowSums(sim1), type = "l", xlab = "Year", ylab = "Total population size (simulated)") We can calculate the realised \(\lambda\) for this trajectory. This is the average yearly multiplication rate over the whole run, \((N_T / N_0)^{1/T}\), where \(N_0\) and \(N_T\) are the total population sizes at the start and at the end, after \(T\) years. tot_no <- rowSums(sim1) (realised_lambda_no <- (tot_no[years + 1] / tot_no[1])^(1 / years)) ## [1] 1.029897 This is a finite-horizon, trajectory-specific estimate. Different runs give different values, scattered around the deterministic \(\lambda\) (1.019). (In many ecology texts the long-run stochastic growth rate is written \(\lambda_s\); that is related to, but not the same as, a single-run realised value.) If the population goes extinct, \(N_T = 0\) and so the realised \(\lambda\) is 0. It is better to report extinction separately, as we do below with many replicates. 15.13.3 Add a culling intervention Example: from year 10 onwards, harvest 10% of the adults each year (each adult has a probability of 0.1 of being removed). This is a proportional harvest: the number removed goes up and down with the number of adults. A proportional harvest of adults has the same effect as multiplying the adult column of the matrix by 0.9 (only 90% of adults are left to breed and survive). So we can predict its long-term effect with a deterministic calculation before we simulate it: A_harvest <- A A_harvest[, "Adult"] <- A_harvest[, "Adult"] * 0.9 (lambda_harvest <- max(Re(eigen(A_harvest)$values))) ## [1] 0.9600498 With a 10% adult harvest, \(\lambda\) falls from 1.019 to 0.96, so once harvesting starts the population should change from slowly growing to declining by about 4% per year. Now the simulation: sim_cull <- simulate_once(A, n0, years, cull_stage = "Adult", cull_prop = 0.1, cull_start = 10) # Compare trajectories: solid = no culling, dashed = culling plot(0:years, rowSums(sim1), type = "l", xlab = "Year", ylab = "Total population size", ylim = range(c(rowSums(sim1), rowSums(sim_cull)))) lines(0:years, rowSums(sim_cull), lty = 2) legend("topleft", legend = c("No culling", "Culling: 10% of adults/year from year 10"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n") # Realised lambda from each simulated trajectory tot_cu <- rowSums(sim_cull) realised_lambda_cu <- (tot_cu[years + 1] / tot_cu[1])^(1 / years) data.frame( scenario = c("No culling", "Culling"), final_N = c(tot_no[years + 1], tot_cu[years + 1]), realised_lambda = c(realised_lambda_no, realised_lambda_cu) ) ## scenario final_N realised_lambda ## 1 No culling 242 1.0298971 ## 2 Culling 55 0.9802693 Interpretation: realised \(\lambda > 1\): the population grew over the simulated period, \(0 <\) realised \(\lambda < 1\): it declined, realised \(\lambda = 0\): it went extinct at some point in the simulated period. These are just two runs, and with only about 100 individuals chance plays a large part. The realised \(\lambda\) for the culling run is also averaged over the whole 30 years, including the first 10 years without culling. To compare the scenarios properly, we need many replicates. 15.13.4 Many replicates (uncertainty bands) A single run is one possible realisation. We typically run many replicates and summarise. Here we run two sets of replicates (no culling vs culling), then compute the median and 10-90% interval for each year. Note: different studies may use different interval widths (for example, 95% intervals) depending on purpose and reporting conventions. # Number of Monte Carlo replicates nreps <- 200 # Store total abundance per year (rows) for each replicate (columns) totals_no <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = years + 1, ncol = nreps) totals_cull <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = years + 1, ncol = nreps) for (rep in 1:nreps) { # Scenario A: no culling totals_no[, rep] <- rowSums(simulate_once(A, n0, years)) # Scenario B: 10% of adults harvested each year from year 10 totals_cull[, rep] <- rowSums(simulate_once(A, n0, years, cull_stage = "Adult", cull_prop = 0.1)) } # Summarise each year across replicates (median and 10-90% interval) summarise_reps <- function(totals) { data.frame( year = 0:(nrow(totals) - 1), median = apply(totals, 1, median), lo = apply(totals, 1, quantile, probs = 0.1), hi = apply(totals, 1, quantile, probs = 0.9) ) } sum_no <- summarise_reps(totals_no) sum_cu <- summarise_reps(totals_cull) # Scenario A vs Scenario B: compare summaries in one figure plot(sum_no$year, sum_no$median, type = "n", xlab = "Year", ylab = "Total population size", ylim = range(c(sum_no$lo, sum_no$hi, sum_cu$lo, sum_cu$hi))) # Ribbon for no-culling uncertainty (10-90%) polygon( x = c(sum_no$year, rev(sum_no$year)), y = c(sum_no$lo, rev(sum_no$hi)), col = grDevices::adjustcolor("steelblue", alpha.f = 0.25), border = NA ) # Ribbon for culling uncertainty (10-90%) polygon( x = c(sum_cu$year, rev(sum_cu$year)), y = c(sum_cu$lo, rev(sum_cu$hi)), col = grDevices::adjustcolor("firebrick", alpha.f = 0.25), border = NA ) # Median trajectories on top of ribbons lines(sum_no$year, sum_no$median, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue4") lines(sum_cu$year, sum_cu$median, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "firebrick4") legend("topleft", legend = c("No culling (median)", "No culling (10-90%)", "Culling (median)", "Culling (10-90%)"), lty = c(1, NA, 2, NA), lwd = c(2, NA, 2, NA), pch = c(NA, 15, NA, 15), col = c("steelblue4", grDevices::adjustcolor("steelblue", alpha.f = 0.5), "firebrick4", grDevices::adjustcolor("firebrick", alpha.f = 0.5)), pt.cex = c(1, 1.5, 1, 1.5), bty = "n") Two useful summaries of the replicates are the median final population size and the proportion of replicates that went extinct (an estimate of the probability of extinction within 30 years): data.frame( scenario = c("No culling", "Culling 10% of adults"), median_final_N = c(median(totals_no[years + 1, ]), median(totals_cull[years + 1, ])), prob_extinct = c(mean(totals_no[years + 1, ] == 0), mean(totals_cull[years + 1, ] == 0)) ) ## scenario median_final_N prob_extinct ## 1 No culling 137.0 0 ## 2 Culling 10% of adults 40.5 0 Notice that even without culling a few replicates can go extinct by chance, although \(\lambda > 1\): demographic stochasticity matters in small populations. 15.14 Your task 15.14.1 Exercise 1: Projection interval sanity check In the tutorial, \(\Delta t = 1\) year. Write one sentence explaining what that means. Suppose you wanted \(\Delta t = 1\) month. What changes would you need to make to the interpretation of: \(P_A\)? \(F_A\)? Name one real reason you might prefer monthly time steps over yearly ones. 15.14.2 Exercise 2: Change one vital rate and re-run projections Reduce adult survival from \(P_A = 0.80\) to \(P_A = 0.70\). Rebuild A, then recompute: the deterministic projection plot, \(\lambda\). Does the population grow or decline now? How can you tell? Run simulate_once() with the new matrix. Do you need to change the function? Why not? Hint: change P_A in the chunk that defines the vital rates, then re-run the chunks from there onwards (building A, the projection loop and eigen()). 15.14.3 Exercise 3: Culling as management Change the harvest from 10% to 20% of adults per year. Before you run it, predict \(\lambda\) under the new harvest using the deterministic calculation (multiply the adult column of A by 0.8). Then run the replicates and compare the median trajectory, the uncertainty bands and the probability of extinction. Now use a fixed quota instead: remove exactly 5 adults per year from year 10 (cull_prop = 0, cull_n = 5). How does the probability of extinction compare with the 10% harvest? Why is a fixed quota riskier for a small population than a proportional harvest? To identify which stage is most impactful, run the same culling intensity for each stage separately (juveniles, subadults, adults: change cull_stage), then compare results. Do this both for a fixed quota of 5 individuals per year and for a 10% harvest. Which stage has the largest effect, and why? Hint for question 3: ask how many future juveniles an individual in each stage is “worth”. The left eigenvector of A (the reproductive values) does this for you: v <- Re(eigen(t(A))$vectors[, 1]); v / v[1]. 15.14.4 Exercise 4: Contraception treatment (reduced fertility) Design a second management treatment where fertility is reduced instead of removing individuals. Keep survival/transition rates unchanged, but reduce fertility from year 10 with a 90% effective contraceptive treatment (multiply F_A by 0.1 from year 10 onwards). Implement this by adding an argument fert_mult to simulate_once() (with default fert_mult = 1), and using F_A * fert_mult instead of F_A in the births step from year cull_start onwards. Run replicate simulations for: baseline (no treatment), culling treatment (10% of adults per year), contraception treatment. Compare all three scenarios in one figure and discuss which treatment gives the largest reduction in population growth. Also predict the long-term \(\lambda\) for the contraception treatment with a deterministic calculation. 15.14.5 Exercise 5 (optional): Environmental stochasticity So far the vital rates are the same every year. Make adult survival vary between years: in each year, with probability 0.5 the year is “good” (\(P_A = 0.9\)) and otherwise it is “bad” (\(P_A = 0.7\)). The average is still 0.8. Modify a copy of simulate_once() to draw the type of year at the start of each year, and compare the spread of the replicate trajectories with the original simulation. 15.15 Takeaways Every rate in a matrix model refers to the projection interval \(\Delta t\): survival, growth and fertility must all be per \(\Delta t\). Deterministic projection gives the expected trajectory and, for a constant matrix, the long-term growth rate \(\lambda\) (the dominant eigenvalue). A stochastic simulation with the same vital rates shows the range of outcomes that chance alone produces. In small populations this includes extinction, even when \(\lambda > 1\). Writing the simulation once as a function makes it easy to run many replicates and to compare scenarios fairly. A proportional harvest is equivalent to changing the matrix, so its long-term effect on \(\lambda\) can be predicted before simulating. A fixed quota is much riskier for a small population, because the proportion removed rises as the population shrinks. Removing individuals from different stages has very different effects: individuals in stages with high reproductive value (here adults) matter most. 15.16 Notes and extensions If you include juvenile stasis (juveniles surviving but remaining juveniles), add a \(P_J\) term and include it in the matrix and simulation. The deterministic matrix model is most useful for structure and long-term behaviour (\(\lambda\), stable stage structure, elasticities). Stochastic simulations are most useful for short-term variability and scenario exploration (management, uncertainty, risk).

16 Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium 16.1 Background 16.2 Assumptions of Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium 16.3 Worked example 16.4 Your task 16.5 Takeaways

16 Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium Learning outcomes. By the end of this practical you should be able to: Explain the difference between alleles and genotypes. Calculate expected genotype frequencies from allele frequencies, and allele frequencies from the frequency of a recessive genotype. Estimate allele frequencies from observed genotype counts and compare the observed counts with those expected under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE). List the assumptions of HWE and explain what a departure from HWE might, and might not, tell you. 16.1 Background Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is a fundamental concept in population genetics for understanding the genetic dynamics of populations. Named after British mathematician G.H. Hardy and German physician Wilhelm Weinberg, this principle describes the stable genetic proportions in a population under specific conditions of no evolution. In an idealised population, where mating is random, genetic mutations are absent, natural selection is not acting, and there is no gene flow or genetic drift, the frequencies of alleles and genotypes remain constant across generations. The Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium provides a baseline against which real populations can be compared, allowing researchers to detect factors that may cause deviations from this equilibrium and, in turn, understand the forces driving evolution and genetic changes within populations. In this practical we will learn more about HWE and practise solving some HWE-related problems. Reading: Neal, chapter The Hardy-Weinberg Principle. Neal writes the two alleles as \(A_1\) and \(A_2\); here we use A and a. The key formulae of the Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium are: Equation 1: \(p + q = 1\) and Equation 2: \(p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1\). Let’s first consider where these equations come from. First, Equation 1. In a diploid organism, each individual carries two alleles for a particular gene. Let’s consider a gene with two alleles, A and a. In a given population: Symbol Meaning \(p\) Frequency of allele A \(q\) Frequency of allele a The sum of the frequencies of these two alleles in the population must equal 1, as they are the only two possibilities for this gene, so \(p+q=1\). Note that dominance affects the phenotype, not the allele frequency. A dominant allele can be rare and a recessive allele can be common. When genotype counts are available, we can calculate allele frequencies directly by counting allele copies: \[ p = \frac{2n_{AA} + n_{Aa}}{2N}, \qquad q = \frac{2n_{aa} + n_{Aa}}{2N}. \] Here, \(n_{AA}\), \(n_{Aa}\) and \(n_{aa}\) are the numbers of individuals with each genotype, and \(N = n_{AA} + n_{Aa} + n_{aa}\). Each homozygote contributes two copies of the same allele, while each heterozygote contributes one copy of each allele. These calculations do not require HWE. Once we know \(p\) and \(q\), we can calculate the expected genotype counts under HWE as \(Np^2\), \(N(2pq)\) and \(Nq^2\), and compare them with the observed counts. Equation 1 serves as the foundational stepping stone for Equation 2. In Equation 1, we establish the sum of allele frequencies, \(p\) and \(q\), in the gene pool. This equation sets the stage for the more complex Equation 2, where we translate these allele frequencies into genotype frequencies for the population. We can derive Equation 2 from the gene pool and random mating. Consider a zygote formed by two gametes, one from the father and one from the mother, each drawn at random from the gene pool (the random union of gametes). A gamete carries A with probability \(p\) and a with probability \(q\), so the possible combinations (father’s allele first) are: \(p \times p = p^2\) (AA) \(q \times q = q^2\) (aa) \(p \times q = pq\) (Aa) \(q \times p = pq\) (aA) Notice that we have two \(pq\) terms (Aa and aA). The order of alleles doesn’t matter, so they are summed together: \(2pq\). So, the total probability for all possible combinations is: \(p^2 + 2pq + q^2\). This must equal 1 (100% probability), which gives us Equation 2: \(p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1\). Note that this identity is true for any value of \(p\): it is just \((p + q)^2 = 1\). What HWE claims is something stronger, namely that the genotype frequencies in the population actually equal \(p^2\), \(2pq\) and \(q^2\). In these formulae, \(p^2\) is the frequency of the homozygous AA genotype, \(q^2\) is the frequency of the homozygous aa genotype and \(2pq\) is the frequency of the heterozygous Aa genotype. From these equations we can produce the following plot, which shows the expected genotype frequencies at HWE for any allele frequency. HWE can occur at any allele frequency, but once the allele frequency is known, the expected genotype frequencies are fixed by Equation 2. (It is a common misconception that the three genotypes should occur in a 1:2:1 ratio, or that allele frequencies should tend towards 50% \(p\) and 50% \(q\).) Given a small amount of information it is possible to figure out what the allele and genotype frequencies should be if the population is at HWE. If a population is NOT at HWE, that is a signal worth investigating. It may mean that one of the assumptions below is violated, but apparent departures can also arise from genotyping errors or simple chance in a small sample. Figure 16.1: The Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium. The lines show the expected genotype frequencies at HWE for each allele frequency, p. 16.2 Assumptions of Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium For a population to be in Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium, certain assumptions must be met: Random mating: There is no preference in mate selection based on genotype. No mutation: Alleles do not change into other alleles, so mutation does not alter allele frequencies. Very large population size: Random sampling has a negligible effect on allele frequencies (genetic drift). No gene flow: Migration does not transfer alleles into or out of the population’s breeding gene pool. No natural selection: All genotypes in the population have an equal chance of reproductive success. These assumptions do two different jobs. Random mating is what produces the Hardy-Weinberg genotype proportions (\(p^2 : 2pq : q^2\)) in each generation. The other four (no mutation, no drift, no gene flow and no selection) are what keep the allele frequencies themselves constant from one generation to the next. Any deviation from these assumptions could result in a population that is not in Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium. 16.3 Worked example Unless a problem states otherwise, assume that the population is at HWE. This matters: working back from the frequency of a recessive genotype to an allele frequency (as below) is only valid if the population is at HWE. Suppose 16% of individuals have the recessive genotype, aa, so \(q^2 = 0.16\). What proportion of the population would we expect to be heterozygous? Calculate \(q = \sqrt{0.16} \approx 0.4\). Calculate \(p = 1 - q \approx 0.6\). Calculate the heterozygote frequency: \(2pq \approx 2(0.6)(0.4) \approx 0.48\). We therefore expect about 48% of individuals to be heterozygous (Aa), assuming the population is at HWE. 16.4 Your task Tackle the following problems, using the HWE theory outlined above. Worked solutions are given in Section 26.16. 16.4.1 Problem #1. A population has two alleles, A and a, at a gene of interest. The frequency of allele A is 0.8. Assuming the population is at HWE, calculate the following: The frequency of allele a. The expected frequencies of the genotypes AA, Aa and aa. The frequencies of the two possible phenotypes if A is completely dominant over a. 16.4.2 PROBLEM #2. Sickle-cell disease is caused by the HbS allele of the haemoglobin gene; the normal allele is HbA. People with genotype AA have normal red blood cells but are vulnerable to severe malaria. People with genotype SS have sickle-cell disease, which is often fatal without treatment. Carriers (AS) are usually healthy and are protected against severe malaria, so in malarial regions they survive better than either homozygote. If 9% of babies in a population are born with sickle-cell disease (SS), what percentage are carriers (AS)? 16.4.3 Problem #3. You genotype a sample of 200 individuals from a population at a gene with two alleles, A and a. You find 90 AA, 70 Aa and 40 aa individuals. This time, do not assume the population is at HWE: assess whether the observed counts match HWE expectations. A descriptive comparison is sufficient for this exercise; a formal statistical test is an optional extension (see the box below). Calculate the frequencies of alleles A and a from the genotype counts. (Hint: 200 diploid individuals carry 400 allele copies, and each heterozygote carries one copy of each allele.) Calculate the expected number of each genotype if the population were at HWE. Compare the observed and expected counts. Is there an excess or a deficit of heterozygotes? Suggest some reasons why a population might show this pattern. Optional extension: a formal test. Neal tests for departures from HWE with a \(\chi^2\) (chi-square) test. For each genotype, calculate \((O - E)^2/E\), where \(O\) is the observed and \(E\) the expected count, and add the three values to get \(\chi^2\). Compare your value with the critical value of the \(\chi^2\) distribution for the correct degrees of freedom (3.84 for \(P = 0.05\) and 10.83 for \(P = 0.001\) with 1 degree of freedom; in R, pchisq(your_value, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE) gives the \(P\) value). Think carefully about the degrees of freedom. There are three genotype classes, but how many independent pieces of information did you take from the data to calculate the expected counts? Why is the answer 1 degree of freedom, not 2? 16.4.4 Problem #4. Within a population of butterflies, brown (B) is completely dominant over white (b), and 40% of all butterflies are white. Assuming the population is at HWE, calculate the following: The percentage of butterflies in the population that are heterozygous. The frequency of homozygous dominant individuals. Extension: Of the brown butterflies, what proportion would you expect to be heterozygous? (Think carefully about what the denominator should be.) 16.5 Takeaways Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium provides a baseline for detecting evolutionary forces. Allele frequencies (\(p\), \(q\)) determine genotype frequencies (\(p^2\), \(2pq\), \(q^2\)). Comparing observed genotype counts with HWE expectations can reveal a departure from HWE. A departure identifies a pattern worth investigating (for example, a violated assumption, genotyping error or chance in a small sample), not its cause.

17 The Gene Pool Model 17.1 Background 17.2 Your task 17.3 Part 1: A simple model 17.4 Part 2: Simulation of allele frequency through time 17.5 Part 3: Many populations 17.6 Part 4: Bottlenecks and founder effects 17.7 Conclusions 17.8 Takeaways

17 The Gene Pool Model Learning outcomes. By the end of this practical you should be able to: Explain why genetic drift is stronger in small populations than in large ones. Estimate the probability that an allele is fixed from replicate simulations, and show that for a neutral allele it equals the allele’s starting frequency. Predict the fate of a new neutral mutation (starting frequency \(1/(2N)\)). Describe how bottlenecks and founder events change allele frequencies and genetic diversity. Use a simple simulation in R to explore a biological process. This practical comes before the lecture on genetic drift, on purpose: you will discover the main results of drift by simulation, and the lecture will then explain and quantify them. Sections marked “optional” are best revisited after the drift lecture. Reading: Neal, chapter Genetic Drift and Effective Population Size. 17.1 Background A central goal in evolutionary biology is to understand variation (including genetic variation) and how it changes through time. One important idea is the “gene pool,” which contains all the different versions of genes (alleles) within a group of organisms. These alleles influence phenotypic traits and other characteristics. To grasp how populations evolve, we need to understand how allele frequencies change in a population. Over time, genetic diversity changes as the relative numbers of alleles change. Some alleles may be lost from the population while others may become “fixed”: the allele is the only one left, so every individual in the population carries it. When no other process is acting, allele frequencies still change by chance. This is genetic drift. The main factor that determines the strength of drift is population size. In small populations, “sampling error” means that, just by chance, large changes often occur in allele frequencies. In large populations, dramatic changes are much less likely. Two related concepts are critical in understanding genetic drift: bottlenecks and founder effects. A genetic bottleneck occurs when a population is dramatically reduced in size, for example by an environmental catastrophe. During a bottleneck, allele frequencies (and genetic diversity) can change dramatically because of sampling effects. A founder effect is a similar scenario, where a small group (a sample from the population) establishes a new population. Because the new population starts from a small sample of the ancestral population, it can have a rather different genetic composition from the ancestral population. 17.2 Your task In this practical, you will use R to simulate how allele frequencies change in a population over generations. By changing population size, starting frequency and the history of the population, you will see how drift behaves in different situations. The practical has four parts. The core path (about 45 minutes) is Parts 1 to 3 plus the bottleneck simulation in Part 4; the rest is optional, for the end of the session or at home. The gene pool (5 minutes). Build a gene pool and see that the gene pool in the next generation is a sample of the current one. Drift through time (10 minutes). Project allele frequency through time and investigate the importance of population size. Many populations (15 minutes). Repeat the simulation many times to estimate the probability that an allele is fixed or lost, including for a rare (new) allele. Bottlenecks (15 minutes). Modify the code to simulate a population that passes through a period of small size. Optional: tracking genetic diversity (Part 3), effective population size and founder effects (Part 4), and the Challenge at the end. Before you start, make a prediction. Imagine two populations, each starting with allele A at a frequency of 0.5. One has 20 individuals and the other has 1000. Sketch what you expect the frequency of A to look like over 100 generations in each population. Which population do you expect to lose one of its alleles first? Keep your sketch, and compare it with your simulations in Part 2. 17.2.1 The model and its assumptions Our model is a simple version of the Wright-Fisher model of population genetics. It assumes: a single locus with two alleles, A and a; a constant number of diploid individuals, N, so the gene pool contains 2N alleles; non-overlapping generations: all adults are replaced by their offspring each generation; random mating, so each new allele is a random draw from the parents’ gene pool; no selection, no mutation and no migration. So the only thing that changes allele frequencies is chance. Keep these assumptions in mind: we come back to them at the end. 17.3 Part 1: A simple model We will first aim to get an understanding of what a gene pool is, using a simple model. We will use R to make a gene pool, then look at how allele frequency in the gene pool changes over a single generation. 17.3.1 The gene pool To establish the gene pool we first set the population size. I set this to be reasonably large, at 500 individuals. pop_size <- 500 There are two alleles (gene variants) per individual: one allele came from the father, and one from the mother. Therefore, the gene pool contains 2 x N alleles (in this case, 1000 alleles). pool_size <- pop_size * 2 I now set the initial allele frequency to be 0.5. You can use other values, but 0.5 is best to start with. initial_frequency_A <- 0.5 initial_frequency_a <- 1 - initial_frequency_A We can now calculate the number of A and a alleles, by multiplying the frequency by the pool size and rounding the result to the closest whole number. number_A <- round(initial_frequency_A * pool_size) number_a <- round(initial_frequency_a * pool_size) Following this, the gene pool can be filled like this. What we are saying here is “repeat A, number_A times, then repeat a number_a times”. gene_pool <- c(rep("A", number_A), rep("a", number_a)) We can count the alleles in the initial gene pool with table: table(gene_pool) ## gene_pool ## a A ## 500 500 We can express these numbers as allele frequencies (i.e. as proportions of the total) by wrapping the table command with prop.table like this: prop.table(table(gene_pool)) ## gene_pool ## a A ## 0.5 0.5 17.3.2 Projecting allele frequency over one time step Let’s assume the population size remains constant at N = 500. During the next time step (i.e. 1 generation), the individuals in the population mate with each other randomly. We can use the sample function to simulate this. This code is saying “sample, from the gene pool, 1000 alleles, with replacement”. We need to sample \(2 \times\) the population size because each individual contains two alleles. We sample with replacement because any allele in the parents’ gene pool can be passed on to more than one offspring (or to none). new_gene_pool <- sample(gene_pool, 2 * pop_size, replace = TRUE) Let’s look at the allele frequency in the new gene pool. It should be similar, but probably not exactly the same as the initial gene pool. prop.table(table(new_gene_pool)) ## new_gene_pool ## a A ## 0.491 0.509 There are still 500 individuals, but the allele frequencies are (probably) not exactly the same as in the initial gene pool. The reason is that the new gene pool is a random sample, not simply a carbon copy. Try to vary the population size and do this several times at small and large population sizes. You should notice that the frequencies are more similar to the starting frequency, and to each other, when you repeat this for large population sizes than for small population sizes. 17.4 Part 2: Simulation of allele frequency through time To simulate the passage of time, we need to do this sampling procedure many times. We can do this using a loop in R. In our loop, we repeat the gene pool sampling process once per generation. Each time we go through the loop, we sample alleles from the old gene pool at time \(t\) to create a new gene pool for time \(t+1\). Each time through the loop we also calculate the allele frequency of A, so we can track how it changes through time. Let’s set up a simulation that runs for 100 generations, starting with a small population of 20 individuals. You can copy and paste this code, which is a complete gene pool model. # Set the population size and number of generations pop_size <- 20 n_gen <- 100 # Set up an empty vector of length n_gen to contain results allele_freq_A <- rep(NA, n_gen) # Put in an initial value for frequency of A allele_freq_A[1] <- 0.5 # Establish the initial gene pool and name it gene_pool_time_n # This part looks complicated, but it just condenses the code # from Part 1 into one line. gene_pool_time_n <- c( rep("A", round(2 * allele_freq_A[1] * pop_size)), rep("a", round(2 * (1 - allele_freq_A[1]) * pop_size)) ) for (i in 2:n_gen) { # Sample 2N alleles, with replacement, to make the next generation gene_pool_time_n_plus_1 <- sample(gene_pool_time_n, pop_size * 2, replace = TRUE ) # Calculate the frequency of A in the new gene pool gene_pool_table <- table(factor(gene_pool_time_n_plus_1, levels = c("A", "a"))) allele_freq_A[i] <- gene_pool_table["A"] / sum(gene_pool_table) # Replace the old gene pool with the new one. gene_pool_time_n <- gene_pool_time_n_plus_1 } Now we can plot this result (Figure 17.1). plot(1:n_gen, allele_freq_A, type = "l", xlab = "Generation", ylab = "Frequency of allele A", ylim = c(0, 1)) Figure 17.1: Simulation of allele frequency through time in a population of 20 individuals Tip: make a new script and paste the code loop along with the plot command so that you can run both together easily. Run the code several times with pop_size <- 20, then several times with pop_size <- 1000. Compare the results with the prediction you made at the start. How does population size affect the variation through time in allele frequencies? Why do you see these patterns? With 20 individuals, does A always end up fixed (frequency 1), or is it sometimes lost (frequency 0)? When the population size is large (say 1000), can you see an allele become fixed within 100 generations? Do you think it could happen if you ran the simulation for much longer? (Try n_gen <- 3000. It may take a little while to run.) 17.5 Part 3: Many populations A single run of the simulation is like watching a single population. To answer questions about probability (for example, “how likely is it that A is fixed?”) we need to watch many populations: we run the same simulation many times and count the outcomes. To make this easy, we first wrap the loop from Part 2 into a function. A function is a reusable piece of code: you give it some inputs (here, population size, number of generations and the starting frequency of A), and it returns the frequency of A in every generation. simulate_gene_pool <- function(pop_size, n_gen, initial_freq_A) { allele_freq_A <- rep(NA, n_gen) allele_freq_A[1] <- initial_freq_A gene_pool_time_n <- c( rep("A", round(2 * initial_freq_A * pop_size)), rep("a", round(2 * (1 - initial_freq_A) * pop_size)) ) for (i in 2:n_gen) { gene_pool_time_n_plus_1 <- sample(gene_pool_time_n, pop_size * 2, replace = TRUE ) gene_pool_table <- table(factor(gene_pool_time_n_plus_1, levels = c("A", "a"))) allele_freq_A[i] <- gene_pool_table["A"] / sum(gene_pool_table) gene_pool_time_n <- gene_pool_time_n_plus_1 } return(allele_freq_A) } Now we can use replicate to run the function many times. Here we simulate 20 populations, each of 20 individuals, for 100 generations. The result is a matrix with one row per generation and one column per population. The matplot function plots each column as a separate line (Figure 17.2). n_gen <- 100 results <- replicate(20, simulate_gene_pool(pop_size = 20, n_gen = n_gen, initial_freq_A = 0.5)) matplot(1:n_gen, results, type = "l", lty = 1, xlab = "Generation", ylab = "Frequency of allele A", ylim = c(0, 1)) Figure 17.2: Twenty replicate populations of 20 individuals, each starting with allele A at a frequency of 0.5 We can count the outcomes by looking at the last row of the matrix (the final generation): final_freq <- results[n_gen, ] sum(final_freq == 1) # number of populations where A is fixed ## [1] 11 sum(final_freq == 0) # number of populations where A is lost ## [1] 7 Use this code to investigate the following questions: What proportion of the populations have lost one of their alleles (i.e. A is fixed or lost) by generation 100 when N = 20? When N = 100? When N = 1000? Of the populations where one allele was fixed, in what proportion was it A? Does this proportion depend on population size? (You may need more than 20 replicates to see this clearly.) So what does population size change: which allele is fixed, or how quickly variation is lost? 17.5.1 Rare alleles and new mutations A brand-new mutation starts as a single copy in the gene pool, so its starting frequency is \(1/(2N)\). Let’s see what happens to it. Here we run 200 populations of 20 individuals, each starting with one copy of A (frequency \(1/40\)), for 300 generations (long enough for nearly all of them to be fixed or lost). pop_size <- 20 results_rare <- replicate(200, simulate_gene_pool(pop_size = pop_size, n_gen = 300, initial_freq_A = 1 / (2 * pop_size))) final_freq_rare <- results_rare[300, ] mean(final_freq_rare == 1) # proportion of populations where A was fixed ## [1] 0.015 mean(final_freq_rare == 0) # proportion of populations where A was lost ## [1] 0.985 Are rare alleles more or less likely to be lost than common ones? Compare the proportion of populations where the new allele was fixed with \(1/(2N)\). What does this tell you about the fate of most new mutations? Try a few different starting frequencies (e.g. 0.1, 0.25, 0.75). Can you find a simple rule linking the starting frequency of a neutral allele to its probability of fixation? You can use this template: change p0 and run it again. Record your results in a small table (starting frequency, proportion of populations where A was fixed). p0 <- 0.25 results_p0 <- replicate(200, simulate_gene_pool(pop_size = 20, n_gen = 300, initial_freq_A = p0)) mean(results_p0[300, ] == 1) # proportion of populations where A was fixed With 200 replicates, expect your proportions to differ from the “true” probability by a few percentage points just by chance. Going further (optional): tracking genetic diversity. In the mutation lecture we measured genetic diversity with expected heterozygosity, \(H_e = 2pq\). Theory predicts that drift reduces \(H_e\) by a factor of \(1 - 1/(2N)\) every generation, so that \(H_t = H_0 (1 - 1/(2N))^t\). The code below calculates \(H_e\) for each generation of each population, averages it across 500 populations of 20 individuals (an average over only 20 populations is too noisy), and adds the theoretical curve in red. Note that the first row of results is generation \(t = 0\), so the theoretical curve uses t <- 0:(n_gen - 1). Does your simulation agree with the theory? n_gen <- 100 results <- replicate(500, simulate_gene_pool(pop_size = 20, n_gen = n_gen, initial_freq_A = 0.5)) He <- rowMeans(2 * results * (1 - results)) # mean He in each generation t <- 0:(n_gen - 1) plot(t, He, type = "l", ylim = c(0, 0.5), xlab = "Generation", ylab = "Mean expected heterozygosity") lines(t, 0.5 * (1 - 1 / (2 * 20))^t, col = "red") 17.6 Part 4: Bottlenecks and founder effects Next, modify the code to simulate a genetic bottleneck, when a population goes through a period of small population size. Start from the code in Part 2, set pop_size <- 1000 at the top before the initial gene pool is built (otherwise the gene pool starts with only 40 alleles, which is itself a hidden founder event), and add this code at the start of the loop (inside the curly brackets), so that the population size is reset each generation: if (i %in% 30:50) { pop_size <- 10 } else { pop_size <- 1000 } This code means, “…if the generation is between 30 and 50, make the population size 10, otherwise make the population size 1000”. In other words, the population goes through a bottleneck of 10 individuals for 21 generations (30 to 50 inclusive). You can modify this code to change the length and severity of the bottleneck. Figure 17.3 shows an example of what your plot of a bottleneck simulation might look like. I have added some lines to show where the bottleneck starts and ends. Here is the complete code, which you can also simply copy: # Set the starting population size and number of generations pop_size <- 1000 n_gen <- 100 # Set up an empty vector of length n_gen to contain results allele_freq_A <- rep(NA, n_gen) # Put in an initial value for frequency of A allele_freq_A[1] <- 0.5 # Establish the initial gene pool and name it gene_pool_time_n gene_pool_time_n <- c( rep("A", round(2 * allele_freq_A[1] * pop_size)), rep("a", round(2 * (1 - allele_freq_A[1]) * pop_size)) ) for (i in 2:n_gen) { # Set the population size for this generation if (i %in% 30:50) { pop_size <- 10 } else { pop_size <- 1000 } gene_pool_time_n_plus_1 <- sample(gene_pool_time_n, pop_size * 2, replace = TRUE ) gene_pool_table <- table(factor(gene_pool_time_n_plus_1, levels = c("A", "a"))) allele_freq_A[i] <- gene_pool_table["A"] / sum(gene_pool_table) # Replace the old gene pool with the new one. gene_pool_time_n <- gene_pool_time_n_plus_1 } plot(1:n_gen, allele_freq_A, type = "l", xlab = "Generation", ylab = "Frequency of allele A", ylim = c(0, 1)) abline(v = 30, col = "red", lty = 3) abline(v = 50, col = "red", lty = 3) text(40, 0.95, "bottleneck", col = "red") Figure 17.3: Simulation of a genetic bottleneck: 1000 individuals, falling to 10 individuals in generations 30 to 50 Run the bottleneck simulation several times, and answer the following questions: How does a genetic bottleneck influence the genetic composition of the population? How might a genetic bottleneck affect the probability that one allele is fixed and the other lost? What happens to allele frequency after the bottleneck, when the population is large again? Does the population “recover” its original allele frequency? Does the severity of the bottleneck (i.e. its length and the population size during it) matter? Optional (revisit after the drift lecture): effective population size. Over the 100 generations of the bottleneck run, the census population size averages about 790 (79 generations at 1000 and 21 at 10). Yet the population loses diversity like a much smaller one. For drift, what matters is the effective population size, \(N_e\), the size of an idealised population that would lose diversity at the same rate. When \(N\) changes over time, \(N_e\) is approximately the harmonic mean of \(N\), which is dominated by the small values: \[N_e \approx \frac{t}{\sum_{i=1}^{t} 1/N_i}\] Calculate the arithmetic mean and the harmonic mean of \(N\) for your bottleneck run. Here is one way to do it in R: N <- rep(1000, 100) # population size in each of the 100 generations N[30:50] <- 10 # the bottleneck mean(N) # arithmetic mean 1 / mean(1 / N) # harmonic mean, approximately Ne What does the difference between the two tell you about the importance of short periods of small population size? 17.6.1 Founder effects (optional) A founder effect is like a bottleneck at the very start of a new population. To simulate it, take a large source population (1000 individuals, frequency of A = 0.5) and found a new population from just 10 individuals (20 alleles) drawn at random from it. Repeat this 50 times, as if 50 islands were each colonised by a different group of 10 founders: source_pool <- c(rep("A", 1000), rep("a", 1000)) founder_freq_A <- replicate(50, { founders <- sample(source_pool, 2 * 10, replace = FALSE) mean(founders == "A") }) hist(founder_freq_A, breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.05), xlab = "Frequency of allele A in the founded population", main = "") abline(v = 0.5, col = "red", lty = 3) Figure 17.4: Frequency of allele A in 50 new populations, each founded by 10 individuals from a source population where the frequency of A is 0.5 How different are the new populations from the source population, and from each other? How would this change with 50 founders instead of 10? Optional: use simulate_gene_pool() with initial_freq_A set to one of these founder frequencies to follow a founded population forward in time. 17.7 Conclusions You should now have a good idea of what a gene pool model is, the importance of population size, the concept of sampling from a population, and how bottlenecks and founder effects change genetic composition. Let’s finish with some more general questions: What are the limitations of this simulation? Look back at the list of assumptions in “The model and its assumptions”. Which real-world processes and complexities are missing? Why is genetic diversity important to a population, for example in a conservation context? Can you think of real-life scenarios where understanding gene pool dynamics would be valuable, such as in conservation biology or medical genetics? 17.8 Takeaways Genetic drift is stronger in small populations because sampling error is larger. Drift does not favour either allele: a neutral allele’s probability of fixation equals its starting frequency. Population size changes how quickly variation is lost. Most new mutations (starting at \(1/(2N)\)) are lost by chance. Bottlenecks and founder effects can rapidly reshape allele frequencies, and the change persists after the population becomes large again. Challenge (optional): Can you think of a way to simulate the genetics of a population that is steadily shrinking through time? Try it.

18 Neutral or Adaptive Evolution in Humans: What Drives Evolution of Our Traits? 18.1 Background 18.2 Key idea 18.3 Your task (30 minutes) 18.4 Discussion (10 minutes) 18.5 Takeaways

18 Neutral or Adaptive Evolution in Humans: What Drives Evolution of Our Traits? 18.1 Background Understanding the role of natural selection and genetic drift in human traits requires a look at several key aspects: Heritable variation: a trait can only evolve (by drift or by selection) if individuals differ in it and some of those differences are inherited. Selection vs drift: selection acts when variation in a trait is correlated with variation in survival or reproduction. Drift is chance change in allele frequencies, and it acts in every finite population. Role of environment: the environment can change the strength, and even the direction, of selection on a trait. First ask: is the variation heritable? Some traits vary a lot but are hardly inherited at all. For example, the fine texture of the iris and the detailed ridge patterns (minutiae) of fingerprints differ even between identical twins: they are mostly the result of chance events during development. Variation like this cannot evolve by drift or by selection, because it is not passed on. Neutral and adaptive evolution are two ends of a continuum. In the lecture on genetic drift we defined neutral evolution. Suppose a trait varies, individuals vary in reproductive success, and the trait is inherited, but the trait is not (or only very weakly) correlated with reproductive success. The trait still evolves, but by chance: this is neutral evolution, caused by genetic drift. When the correlation between the trait and reproductive success is strong, we get adaptive evolution, caused by natural selection. Most traits lie somewhere in between. Population size also decides where a trait sits on this continuum. Drift acts on the alleles that affect a trait, and its strength per generation is about \(1/(2N_e)\), where \(N_e\) is the effective population size. Selection on those alleles is effective only when the selective advantage, \(s\), is clearly larger than roughly \(1/(2N_e)\). So weak selection that is effective in a large population can be swamped by drift in a small one. Whether a trait evolves “neutrally” therefore depends on population size as well as on the environment. When selection is moderate or strong, a trait tends to be held close to some optimal value (stabilising selection) or to change in a consistent direction (directional selection): adaptive evolution. When selection is weak or absent, the alleles that affect the trait change in frequency at random, and the trait drifts: neutral evolution. Both require heritable variation to begin with: if there is little heritable variation, the trait will not respond much even if selection is strong. Finally, the strength of selection depends on the environment. A trait may be important in some environments but not others, and may be selected for in one environment but against in another. For example, the skin pigment melanin protects against intense ultraviolet (UV) radiation, including UV damage to the vitamin folate, so darker skin is favoured where UV is intense. Where UV is weak, lighter skin allows more vitamin D to be made in the skin (Jablonski & Chaplin 2010, PNAS). Ancient DNA shows that some of the main light-skin alleles became common in Europe only within roughly the last 8,000 years (Mathieson et al. 2015, Nature). Exactly which selective pressures mattered most, and when, is still debated. The objective of this exercise is to develop an intuitive understanding of the effect of selection and genetic drift on traits. Figure 18.1: Two present-day human environments: Hadza men returning from a hunt in the dry savanna woodland of northern Tanzania (left) and Nyhavn in Copenhagen (right). Both photographs show people living today: all living human populations are equally evolved, and all are still subject to natural selection. How would selection on each trait differ between these environments? Photos: Andreas Lederer (left) and Jorge Láscar (right), both CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Learning outcomes: Decide whether a trait can evolve at all, by asking whether its variation is heritable. Place traits on the continuum from neutral evolution (genetic drift) to adaptive evolution (natural selection), and justify each placement with evidence or reasoning. Explain how the environment (foraging societies vs modern industrialised countries such as Denmark) and population size change the strength of selection on a trait. Predict which differences between human populations gene flow would erase, and which local selection could maintain. Use correct scientific terminology when arguing for your categorisation in a group. 18.2 Key idea Traits like resistance to infectious disease are likely to face strong selection in environments where the disease is common. Heritable variation with little or no effect on survival or reproduction (for example, many DNA differences at synonymous sites, which do not change the protein) is more likely to change by drift. 18.3 Your task (30 minutes) You are given a short list of eight human traits (below). They were chosen to cover the whole range, from traits that are probably drifting, through traits with little heritable variation, to traits under strong selection in some environments but not others. In small groups: Write the traits on PostIt notes. Discuss and categorise the traits based on the strength of natural selection in foraging (hunter-gatherer) societies, like those in which most of human evolution took place (10 minutes). Repeat the exercise for modern industrialised societies like Denmark (10 minutes). In Denmark today, most people survive to adulthood, so ask how each trait might affect the number of children people have: selection still acts, but now mainly through differences in reproduction rather than survival. Gene flow between populations (10 minutes). Human populations exchange migrants, and gene flow pulls their allele frequencies together. In the lecture on migration and gene flow we saw that very few migrants (about one per generation) are enough to stop drift making populations very different, but that local selection can keep populations different if it is strong compared with the migration rate (\(s\) larger than \(m\)). For each trait, ask: Does the trait differ between human populations living in different environments? Would gene flow erase those differences (as expected for neutral traits), or could local selection hold them apart? Good places to start: skin pigmentation and UV; lactase persistence (digesting milk sugar as an adult), which became common in populations that keep milk-producing animals; and the sickle-cell allele (HbS), which protects carriers against malaria. Remember that most human genetic variation is found within populations rather than between them. For steps 2 and 3, order the traits from those likely influenced by GENETIC DRIFT to those evolving through ADAPTIVE EVOLUTION via NATURAL SELECTION. For each trait, start with the question “is the variation heritable?”. 18.3.1 The traits Trait Description Metabolic efficiency How effectively your body converts food into energy. Eyesight acuity Sharpness of vision. Height Standing height. Birth canal (pelvic) shape The shape of the bony opening through which a baby is born. Resistance to bubonic plague Immunity or resilience against bubonic plague. Eye colour The colour of the iris (brown, green, blue and so on). Earwax type Wet or dry earwax, set by a single DNA change; dry earwax is common in East Asia and rare in Europe and Africa. Face symmetry The balance and proportionality of facial features. 18.4 Discussion (10 minutes) After the exercise, discuss as a class: Were there any traits that were categorised differently between the two types of societies? Why? Which traits did you decide had little or no heritable variation, and so could not evolve by drift or by selection? Which differences between human populations would gene flow erase, and which are maintained by local selection? Did the exercise challenge any preconceived notions you had about trait evolution? Can you think of any other traits that would be interesting to add to this exercise? 18.5 Takeaways A trait can only evolve if its variation is heritable. Neutral and adaptive evolution are two ends of a continuum: where a trait sits depends on how strongly it affects survival or reproduction, and on population size (\(s\) compared with \(1/(2N_e)\)). Selection strength depends on environment and context, not just on the trait itself, and different environments can reverse which traits are favoured. Humans are still evolving: in industrialised societies, selection acts mainly through differences in the number of children. Gene flow erases neutral differences between populations, but local selection can maintain differences in traits such as skin pigmentation.

19 Writing Short Answers 19.1 What examiners look for 19.2 Paragraph structure 19.3 Mark three answers yourself 19.4 Now write your own (15 minutes) 19.5 Takeaways

19 Writing Short Answers The final exam has two parts: multiple-choice questions and short-answer questions. A short-answer question needs a paragraph or two of written text. It tests whether you understand the key terms and concepts, and whether you can communicate that understanding clearly. Knowing the material is not enough: you need to show the examiner that you know it. In this session you will look at what makes a good short answer, mark three example answers yourself, and then write and mark an answer of your own. Learning outcomes: Break a question into its parts, and use its verbs (define, describe, explain, compare) to decide what each part needs. Plan an answer before writing it. Write paragraphs with a topic sentence, supporting sentences and a concluding sentence. Use precise terminology and specific examples. Mark an answer against a rubric, and use the rubric to improve your own writing. 19.1 What examiners look for Read the question, then read it again. Most questions have several parts. Underline each one and answer every part: a missing part costs marks however good the rest is. Look at the verbs. Define asks for a precise meaning. Describe asks what happens. Explain asks why or how it happens. Compare asks for similarities and differences, side by side. Contrast asks for differences only. Plan first. Spend a couple of minutes listing the points you will make for each part. A plan stops you writing everything you know about the topic and missing what was asked. Answer first. Your first sentence should answer the question directly. Background can come afterwards, if it is needed at all. An examiner should not have to hunt for your point. Use the right terms, and use them correctly. Precise terms are clearer than everyday descriptions, and they show the examiner you understand the concept. Give specific examples. “A bird” or “a plant” is not a specific example. “Copper-tolerant common bent grass on a small copper mine in Wales” is. The examples from the lectures and the textbook are ideal, because you know what was found and why it matters. Keep to time. A long answer to one question can cost you a whole question elsewhere. Compare these two definitions: Gene flow is the movement of alleles from one population into the gene pool of another, through immigrants that breed there or gametes, such as pollen, that fertilise there. Gene flow is when animals move to a new place and take their genes with them. The first is precise and complete. The second describes migration, misses the point that immigrants must breed, and leaves out plants altogether. 19.2 Paragraph structure Paragraphs in scientific writing follow a simple pattern: A topic sentence that states the main idea of the paragraph, and tells the reader what to expect. An examiner who reads only your topic sentences should be able to see your whole answer. One or more supporting sentences that explain, give evidence or give examples. Each one should back up the topic sentence: if it does not, it belongs in another paragraph. A concluding sentence that says what follows from the point, qualifies it, or links to the next paragraph. Do not just repeat the topic sentence: that costs time and earns nothing. In a short paragraph you can leave the concluding sentence out. One paragraph should make one main point. Make it long enough to make and support that point, and no longer. 19.2.1 A worked example Question. Compare how haploid and diploid genetic systems affect the response to selection. Give an example of a trait under selection in each, and explain how the genetic system affects the speed of evolutionary change. (1) Haploid systems respond to selection more quickly than diploid systems, because in a diploid an allele can be hidden from selection in heterozygotes. (2) In a haploid organism every allele is expressed, so selection acts on a new advantageous mutation as soon as it appears. (3) For example, drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a haploid bacterium, can evolve within a single patient, helped by short generation times and very large population sizes. (4) In a haploid, then, the speed of change is set by the strength of selection and the supply of new mutations, not by dominance. (5) In a diploid, the speed of change depends on dominance, and a favoured dominant allele spreads fastest while it is rare. (6) This is because it is expressed in heterozygotes, which carry almost all the copies of a rare allele: the dominant carbonaria allele of the peppered moth rose from about 1% to 99% of moths near Manchester in about 50 generations, which needs selection of about s = 0.3 against the pale form. (7) However, a dominant allele slows down near fixation, because the last copies of the recessive allele hide in heterozygotes. (8) A favoured recessive allele shows the opposite pattern. (9) While it is rare it occurs almost only in heterozygotes, where it is not expressed, so it can take thousands of generations to start spreading, but once it is common it goes to fixation quickly. (10) Dominance therefore decides whether change in a diploid is slow at the start or at the end, a delay that haploids never have. How the answer is built: The first sentence answers the question: haploids respond faster, and it says why. One point per paragraph: haploids; dominant alleles in diploids; recessive alleles in diploids. Topic sentences (1, 5 and 8): read on their own, they outline the whole answer. Supporting sentences back up their topic sentence, and each claim has a specific example with numbers (tuberculosis; the peppered moth). Concluding sentences (4, 7 and 10) each add something: what follows (4), a qualification (7), and a link back to the comparison (10). None of them just repeats its topic sentence. Together, the three paragraphs answer every part of the question: they compare the two systems, give an example of each, and explain how each system affects the speed of change. 19.3 Mark three answers yourself Here is a short-answer question with its marking rubric, followed by three student answers. Mark each answer using the rubric on your own, then agree marks with a partner. The examiner’s marks are shown in the practical session, and a full explanation is posted on itslearning (Resources › Practice Exams) after the session. Where your marks differ from the examiner’s, work out why. Question. Define gene flow and explain how it differs from migration. Explain how gene flow can both help and hinder a population’s adaptation to local conditions, giving a specific example. Explain why very few migrants per generation are enough to stop populations diverging by genetic drift, but many more are needed to swamp local adaptation. Rubric (10 points) Criterion 2 points 1 point 0 points 1. Definition Gene flow is the movement of alleles into another population’s gene pool, by immigrants that breed there or by gametes (such as pollen) that fertilise there Partly right: talks about genes moving, but vague about how they enter the gene pool Incorrect, or describes only the movement of individuals 2. Differs from migration Explains that migration is the movement of individuals, and that it causes gene flow only if the migrants or their gametes take part in breeding Says the two differ, but not why Treats them as the same thing, or missing 3. Local adaptation Explains both how gene flow can help (bringing in variation, genetic rescue) and how it can hinder (bringing in alleles suited to other environments), with a specific example Only one side, or no specific example Incorrect or missing 4. Drift versus selection Explains that a number of migrants (about one per generation) is enough to stop divergence by drift whatever the population size, but that gene flow swamps selection only when the migration rate \(m\) is similar to or larger than \(s\) States the result without explaining it, or explains only one half Incorrect or missing 5. Structure The first sentence of each part answers it; one point per paragraph, each with a topic sentence; correct terminology Mostly clear, but loosely structured, repetitive or imprecise Disorganised A factual error in a criterion caps that criterion at 1 point. Material the question does not ask for earns nothing, however accurate it is. 19.3.1 Answer A Gene flow is the process where animals from one area move to another area and bring their genes with them. One of the main ways gene flow happens is through movement, for example when birds fly to a different place and then mate with the local birds. Gene flow can make a population less unique, because when animals from different areas mix, the local traits get diluted. For example, if birds with colourful feathers mate with birds with dull feathers, you might end up with fewer colourful birds. Drift is random, so it can be stopped by a few migrants, but selection is stronger, so more migrants are needed to stop it. 19.3.2 Answer B Gene flow is the movement of alleles from one population into the gene pool of another. It happens only when the incoming individuals or gametes take part in reproduction: a migrant that arrives but does not breed adds nothing to the gene pool. Migration, the movement of individuals, is therefore not the same as gene flow. Sockeye salmon migrate thousands of kilometres at sea, yet because they return to breed in the stream where they hatched, there is little gene flow between river populations. Gene flow happens by two main routes. Animals that disperse from where they were born and breed in another population carry their alleles with them. Plants do not move as adults, so their gene flow happens mainly through pollen, carried by wind or insects, and through seeds. Gene flow can both help and hinder local adaptation. It helps by bringing back genetic variation that a small, isolated population has lost: when eight female pumas from Texas were released into the inbred Florida panther population in 1995, heterozygosity increased, signs of inbreeding depression became rarer and the population grew (genetic rescue). It hinders by bringing in alleles that suit other environments. Common bent grass on a small copper mine in Wales is copper tolerant, but non-tolerant pollen blows onto the mine, so seed produced there is less tolerant than the adults, and copper then kills the non-tolerant seedlings. Downwind, tolerant pollen blowing off the mine produces tolerant seedlings on normal soil, where tolerance is costly. Drift and selection respond to gene flow differently. The strength of drift is about \(1/(2N)\) per generation, so drift is weaker in large populations, while gene flow pulls a population back towards the others by the proportion \(m\) each generation. The two balance when \(Nm\) is about 1, so about one migrant per generation is enough to stop drift making populations very different, whatever their size. Selection, in contrast, changes allele frequencies by a proportion set by the selection coefficient \(s\), so gene flow swamps local adaptation only when \(m\) is similar to or larger than \(s\). Populations can therefore exchange enough migrants to stop divergence by drift and still stay locally adapted, as the grass on the copper mine shows. 19.3.3 Answer C Gene flow is about how animals move to new places, like birds flying south for winter. So, the mechanisms are migration and movement, because that’s how animals and people move around. Gene flow doesn’t let animals adapt, because they are always moving, so they can’t get used to one place. For example, if a penguin moves to a desert, it can’t adapt because it’s too hot and there’s no water. Drift happens in small populations and selection happens in big ones, so how many migrants you need depends on the size of the population. 19.4 Now write your own (15 minutes) Answer the question below without notes, in about 15 minutes, as you would in the exam. Aim for about 250 words: three short paragraphs is enough for full marks. Plan for a couple of minutes first. Write in a document on your laptop. There is nothing to hand in. Question. Adaptive and neutral evolution are two fundamental modes of evolutionary change. (i) Explain the difference between them, giving two ways in which they differ. (ii) Give one example of each, and explain why it fits. Rubric (10 points) Criterion 2 points 1 point 0 points 1. Adaptive evolution A change in allele frequencies caused by natural selection, consistent in direction, that produces adaptations Vague (for example, “organisms adapt to their environment”), or the cause is missing Incorrect or missing 2. Neutral evolution A change in allele frequencies caused by genetic drift, in variants with little or no effect on fitness, random in direction Partly right, or the cause is missing Incorrect (for example, “neutral means no change”) or missing 3. Where they differ States at least two differences: in direction, in outcome, or in what controls them (the selection coefficient \(s\) versus drift, about \(1/(2N_e)\)) One difference, or differences implied but never stated None 4. Examples, explained A specific example of each, in a heritable trait, each with an explanation of why it fits Both examples named but not explained, or only one explained No suitable examples 5. Structure The first sentence answers the question; one point per paragraph, each with a topic sentence; correct terminology Mostly clear, but loosely structured, repetitive or imprecise Disorganised A factual error in a criterion caps that criterion at 1 point. When the time is up, swap laptops with a neighbour (or email them your answer) and mark each other’s answer with the rubric. Give a mark for each criterion, and add one sentence on the change that would gain the most marks. If you would rather not share your answer, mark your own instead. After the session, compare both answers with the model answer posted on itslearning (Resources › Practice Exams). This practice does not count towards your final grade. 19.5 Takeaways Answer every part of the question, and let the verbs tell you what each part needs. Plan before you write. Answer the question in your first sentence. One main point per paragraph: a topic sentence, support, and an ending that adds something rather than repeating the topic sentence. Use precise terms, and back every general claim with a specific example. Marking other people’s answers against a rubric is one of the quickest ways to improve your own.
