20 Heritability from a linear regression 20.1 Background 20.2 Before you start: predict 20.3 Your Task 20.4 Takeaways

20 Heritability from a linear regression 20.1 Background Heritability measures how much of the variation in a trait within a population is due to additive genetic differences between individuals. It is a proportion, between 0 and 1, and it tells us how closely offspring resemble their parents. Heritability matters in plant and animal breeding, in medicine and in conservation, because it determines how fast a trait can respond to selection. Narrow-sense heritability (Neal writes it \(h^2_N\)) is a ratio of two variances: the additive genetic variance divided by the total phenotypic variance. \(h^2 = \frac{V_A}{V_P}\) Only the additive part of the genetic variance counts, because parents pass on alleles, not whole genotypes. Effects that depend on particular combinations of alleles (dominance and interactions between genes) are broken up every generation, so they do not make offspring resemble their parents in a predictable way. The rest of the phenotypic variance is mainly environmental. If we ignore non-additive genetic effects, as we do in this practical, \(V_P = V_A + V_E\), where \(V_E\) is the environmental variance. A heritability close to 1 means that most of the variation among individuals is additive genetic, so offspring closely resemble their parents. A heritability close to 0 means that parents’ trait values tell us little about their offspring’s: the variation is mostly due to the environment, to chance, or to non-additive genetic effects. Heritability is not a fixed property of a trait. It belongs to a particular population in a particular environment, because it changes whenever either variance changes: More environmental variation (a patchier habitat, more variable weather or food) increases \(V_P\) and so lowers \(h^2\), even if \(V_A\) is unchanged. Selection removes unfavourable alleles and so reduces \(V_A\). A trait under strong, persistent selection can end up with low heritability. (Traits closely related to fitness also tend to have low heritability because their environmental variance is large; see the lecture.) Genetic architecture (how many genes affect the trait, and how large their effects are) differs between traits and species. We can estimate heritability from the resemblance between parents and offspring. If we plot the offspring value in each family (one offspring, or the mean of several) against the mid-parent value (the mean of the two parents), the slope of the regression line estimates \(h^2\). If you only know one parent, the slope estimates \(h^2/2\), because each parent passes on only half of its alleles. Using the mean of several offspring per family gives a more precise estimate, but one offspring per family (as in this practical) also works. This is the method used in the lecture for East’s tobacco plants and for Darwin’s finches. Reading: Neal, chapter Polygenic Inheritance and Quantitative Genetics. Reference Wray, N. & Visscher, P. (2008) Estimating trait heritability. Nature Education 1(1):29 Learning Outcomes: Estimate narrow-sense heritability, with its uncertainty, from a mid-parent–offspring regression in R. Use heritability and phenotypic variance to estimate additive genetic variance, and explain why heritability can differ between populations. Evaluate the assumptions behind regression estimates of heritability. 20.2 Before you start: predict Imagine plotting offspring wing length against mid-parent wing length. What slope would you expect if offspring were, on average, exactly like their parents? What slope would you expect if offspring were no more like their own parents than like any other bird in the population? What does a slope between these two tell you? Write down your answers, then check them against your results at the end. 20.3 Your Task 20.3.1 Estimating heritability (15 minutes) You are provided with two datasets for wing length (mm) in a small songbird. Each row is one family: Midparent_value is the mean wing length of the two parents, and Offspring_value is the wing length of one of their offspring, measured as an adult. Each dataset contains 100 families. Data set 1 Data set 2 Download the first data set and import it into R (RStudio). The starter code assumes you have saved it in a folder called data inside your project; change the path if you saved it somewhere else. Plot the data, with mid-parent value on the x-axis and offspring value on the y-axis. Fit a linear regression model of the form y ~ x. Look at the slope of the relationship: this is your estimate of the heritability. Use confint() to find its 95% confidence interval. Starter code in R: pop_1 <- read.csv("data/heritability_pop1.csv") plot(pop_1$Midparent_value, pop_1$Offspring_value, xlab = "Mid-parent wing length (mm)", ylab = "Offspring wing length (mm)") mod1 <- lm(Offspring_value ~ Midparent_value, data = pop_1) abline(mod1, col = "red") summary(mod1) coef(mod1)[2] # slope = heritability estimate confint(mod1)[2, ] # 95% confidence interval for the slope Reading a confidence interval: the 95% confidence interval is the range of values for \(h^2\) that are compatible with your data. The narrower it is, the more precise your estimate. If the interval includes zero, the data cannot rule out \(h^2 = 0\), but that does not show that \(h^2\) is zero: the upper limit tells you how large it could plausibly be. Questions What is your estimate of \(h^2\), and how precise is it? What does this heritability tell us about the variation in wing length in this population? What does it not tell us about any one bird? What else might explain the remaining variation? Calculate \(V_P\) as the variance of the offspring values (var(pop_1$Offspring_value)). Now calculate var(pop_1$Midparent_value) and compare the two. Why is the variance of the mid-parent values only about half of \(V_P\), and so why should we not use it as \(V_P\)? (Hint: each mid-parent value is the mean of two birds.) Calculate the additive genetic variance, \(V_A = h^2 \times V_P\). Imagine a breeder selects parents whose mean wing length is 2 mm above the population mean. Use the breeder’s equation, \(R = h^2 S\), to predict the change in mean wing length in the next generation. 20.3.2 Comparative Analysis (10 minutes) Now analyse the second data set. It is for the same trait in the same species, but from a different population living in a different environment. Repeat steps 1 to 4, and calculate \(V_P\) and \(V_A\) for this population too. Copy this table into your notes and fill it in for both populations. Population 1 Population 2 \(h^2\) 95% confidence interval \(V_P\) (mm²) \(V_A\) (mm²) \(V_P - V_A\) (mm²), an estimate of \(V_E\) Questions How does the heritability compare with population 1? Do the two confidence intervals overlap? Use your table to compare \(V_A\) and \(V_P - V_A\) between the two populations. Which differs more, and what does that suggest about the cause of the difference in heritability? Can you suggest environmental differences between the two populations that could explain this? For the same selection differential (\(S\) = 2 mm), which population would respond faster to selection? Can you think of any real-world applications where understanding heritability would be important? 20.3.3 Assumptions (10 minutes) Estimating heritability from a mid-parent–offspring regression assumes the following. Additive genetic effects: the slope estimates the additive genetic variance only. Dominance and interactions between genes do not make offspring resemble parents, and the method does not account for genotype-by-environment interactions. No shared environment: parents and offspring do not resemble each other for non-genetic reasons. If they share a territory, food supply or parental care, the heritability will be overestimated. Cross-fostering experiments (swapping eggs or chicks between nests) break this link. Correct parentage: the measured parents are the genetic parents. In many birds, some chicks are sired by a male other than the social father (extra-pair paternity), which makes the heritability look lower than it is. Linearity: the relationship between parent and offspring trait values is a straight line. Measurement accuracy: measurement error in the parents’ values makes the slope shallower, so heritability is underestimated; error in the offspring values makes the estimate less precise. Random mating: mates do not choose each other on the basis of the trait (no assortative mating). Representative sample: the families measured are a random sample of the population. If the offspring measured are only those that survived a harsh winter, for example, selection on wing length can bias the estimate. Independence: each family contributes one data point. Using the same parents in several families, or several offspring from one family as separate data points, violates this. Questions For shared environment, correct parentage and measurement accuracy: give a specific example of how each assumption could be violated in a wild bird population, and explain why that would make the heritability estimate too high or too low. Optional extension: do the same for the other five assumptions. Some have no clear direction, or cause a different problem (for example, a confidence interval that is too narrow), and one may surprise you. 20.4 Takeaways The slope of offspring on mid-parent estimates narrow-sense heritability, \(h^2 = V_A/V_P\); report it with its uncertainty. Heritability belongs to a population in an environment: two populations with the same additive genetic variance can have very different heritabilities if their environments differ. High heritability does not mean a trait is fixed or unaffected by the environment.

21 Lotka-Volterra competition 21.1 Background: the model and its isoclines 21.2 Key idea 21.3 Your task 21.4 Takeaways

21 Lotka-Volterra competition The Lotka-Volterra competition model is a foundational tool in ecology for understanding interspecific competition, or competition between different species for shared resources such as food, space, and nesting sites. It examines how population sizes change in a shared environment by considering factors like interaction strength and environmental carrying capacities. The model is closely linked to the idea of “competitive exclusion”: two species with identical ecological roles cannot coexist indefinitely, and eventually one will exclude the other. This principle comes mainly from experiments, especially Gause’s work with yeasts and Paramecium in the 1930s, rather than from the model itself. In the basic model, two truly identical species do not exclude each other at all (see the fifth case below). The model also explores the role of both inter- and intra-specific competition. It identifies conditions for species coexistence, influenced by parameters like competition coefficients and carrying capacities. These insights are vital for understanding community structure, species interactions, and ecological stability. In a two-species system there are four general outcomes: Predictable Exclusion of Species 1 by Species 2: Species 2 outcompetes and excludes species 1 from the environment. Predictable Exclusion of Species 2 by Species 1: Species 1 outcompetes and excludes species 2 from the environment. Exclusion Dependent on Initial Densities: Depending on the starting numbers of each species, either one could exclude the other. Stable Coexistence: Both species may reach a stable equilibrium where they coexist without one excluding the other. Neal also describes a fifth, knife-edge case, in which the two isoclines lie exactly on top of each other (see below). The model suggests that stable coexistence is possible if each species limits its own population growth more than it affects the other species. Overlapping niches could lead to competitive exclusion, influenced by their competition coefficients and carrying capacities. Learning outcomes: Competence in constructing an Excel-based population model. Understanding how the Lotka-Volterra competition model works. Understanding the competition coefficients \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), and using the isocline intercepts (\(K_1\), \(K_1/\alpha\), \(K_2\), \(K_2/\beta\)) to predict the outcome of competition. 21.1 Background: the model and its isoclines We use the notation of Neal (Interspecific Competition). Each species grows logistically, but its growth is also slowed by the other species: \[\frac{dN_1}{dt} = r_1 N_1 \frac{K_1 - N_1 - \alpha N_2}{K_1}\] \[\frac{dN_2}{dt} = r_2 N_2 \frac{K_2 - N_2 - \beta N_1}{K_2}\] \(\alpha\) is the per capita effect of species 2 on species 1, measured relative to the effect of species 1 on itself. If \(\alpha = 0.5\), two individuals of species 2 have the same effect on species 1 as one individual of species 1. \(\beta\) is the per capita effect of species 1 on species 2, measured in the same way. Species 1 stops growing when \(N_1 = K_1 - \alpha N_2\). This straight line is the zero isocline (zero net growth isocline) of species 1. On a graph with \(N_1\) on the x-axis and \(N_2\) on the y-axis it crosses the x-axis at \(K_1\) (no species 2 present) and the y-axis at \(K_1/\alpha\) (so many individuals of species 2 that species 1 cannot grow at all). In the same way, the isocline of species 2, \(N_2 = K_2 - \beta N_1\), crosses the y-axis at \(K_2\) and the x-axis at \(K_2/\beta\). Each species increases when the populations are below (to the left of) its own isocline and decreases above it. The outcome depends on how the two isoclines are arranged (Fig. 21.1): Arrangement of the intercepts Outcome \(K_1 > K_2/\beta\) and \(K_1/\alpha > K_2\) (species 1’s isocline lies outside species 2’s) Species 1 excludes species 2 \(K_2 > K_1/\alpha\) and \(K_2/\beta > K_1\) (species 2’s isocline lies outside species 1’s) Species 2 excludes species 1 \(K_1 < K_2/\beta\) and \(K_2 < K_1/\alpha\) (the isoclines cross) Stable coexistence at the crossing point \(K_1 > K_2/\beta\) and \(K_2 > K_1/\alpha\) (the isoclines cross the other way) Unstable equilibrium: either species can win, depending on the starting densities Figure 21.1: The four general arrangements of the Lotka-Volterra competition isoclines. Solid line: species 1 (intercepts \(K_1\) and \(K_1/\alpha\)). Dashed line: species 2 (intercepts \(K_2\) and \(K_2/\beta\)). Filled circle: stable equilibrium; open circle: unstable equilibrium. In the fifth case (Neal’s “coexistence at a range of equilibrium densities”), \(K_1 = K_2/\beta\) and \(K_2 = K_1/\alpha\), so the two isoclines lie exactly on top of each other. Every point on the shared line is an equilibrium, and the species coexist at whatever ratio they happen to reach. Two identical species (\(\alpha = \beta = 1\), \(K_1 = K_2\)) are an example. This case needs exactly matching values, so it is unlikely in nature. It also shows that the basic model does not, on its own, predict the exclusion of identical species: Gause observed exclusion in his Paramecium experiments, and Neal shows that an extra source of mortality (a “removal factor”) has to be added to the model to explain it. 21.2 Key idea Whether a coefficient is bigger or smaller than 1 does not decide the outcome on its own. What matters is how each competition coefficient compares with the ratio of the carrying capacities. The easiest way to see this is to ask whether each species can invade when it is rare and the other species is sitting at its carrying capacity. Species 1 can invade a population of species 2 at \(K_2\) if \(K_1 > \alpha K_2\), i.e. if \(\alpha < K_1/K_2\) (equivalently \(K_2 < K_1/\alpha\)). Species 2 can invade a population of species 1 at \(K_1\) if \(K_2 > \beta K_1\), i.e. if \(\beta < K_2/K_1\) (equivalently \(K_1 < K_2/\beta\)). Species 1 can invade? Species 2 can invade? Outcome Yes No Species 1 excludes species 2 No Yes Species 2 excludes species 1 Yes Yes Stable coexistence No No Exclusion, but which species wins depends on the starting densities These are the same conditions as in the isocline table above, written in a different way. For example, with \(K_1 = 3000\), \(\alpha = 1.25\), \(K_2 = 1000\) and \(\beta = 0.5\), species 2 has the stronger per capita effect (\(\alpha > 1\)), yet species 1 wins: species 1 can invade (\(1.25 < 3000/1000 = 3\)) but species 2 cannot (\(0.5 > 1000/3000 = 0.33\)). 21.3 Your task In this class (over TWO sessions) you will be working from a PDF available here to make a model exploring this idea. This PDF walks you through the creation of an Excel spreadsheet exploring interspecific competition and competitive exclusion using the Lotka-Volterra model. Notation and time steps in the PDF The PDF writes the competition coefficients as \(\alpha_{12}\) and \(\alpha_{21}\). In Neal’s notation (used in this book), \(\alpha_{12} = \alpha\) (effect of species 2 on species 1) and \(\alpha_{21} = \beta\) (effect of species 1 on species 2). The spreadsheet is a discrete-time version of the model: \(N_{1,t+1} = N_{1,t} + R_1 N_{1,t}(K_1 - N_{1,t} - \alpha N_{2,t})/K_1\), and the same for species 2. Its \(R\) is a rate per time step, not Neal’s continuous \(r\). Keep \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) at 1 or below, so that you see the Lotka-Volterra behaviour rather than the oscillations and chaos of the discrete logistic model (compare Deeper into logistic growth). Create the Excel spreadsheet by following the instructions in the PDF. Note on the PDF: the labels added to Figure 5 have the subscripts the wrong way round. The correct isocline intercepts are \(K_1\) and \(K_1/\alpha_{12}\) for species 1, and \(K_2\) and \(K_2/\alpha_{21}\) for species 2 (in Neal’s notation, \(K_1\), \(K_1/\alpha\), \(K_2\) and \(K_2/\beta\); see the Background above). In the first session, build the sheet and check it: with the PDF’s default values (\(R_1 = R_2 = 1\), \(K_1 = 1200\), \(\alpha = 0.75\), \(K_2 = 1000\), \(\beta = 0.5\), starting at \(N_1 = 100\), \(N_2 = 50\)) the two species should settle at \(N_1 = 720\), \(N_2 = 640\). Label the four isocline intercepts on your graph. In the second session, use the model to answer the questions below. For each parameter set you try, sketch the isoclines and predict the outcome first, then run the model to check. 21.3.1 The questions What parameter values will cause species 1 to exclude species 2 from the habitat? What do these values mean in ecological terms? What parameter values will reverse this outcome? What do these values mean in ecological terms? What parameter values will allow the two species to coexist indefinitely and stably? What do these values mean in ecological terms? Are there parameter values under which the outcome depends on initial population sizes or rates of population growth? What do these values mean in ecological terms? (Optional) Neal describes two pairs of flour beetles. Predict the outcome for each from the isoclines, then check with your sheet: (a) Rhizopertha (species 1, \(K_1 = 330\)) and Oryzaephilus (species 2, \(K_2 = 440\)), with \(\alpha = 0.235\) and \(\beta = 0.12\); (b) Tribolium confusum (species 1, \(K_1 = 220\)) and T. castaneum (species 2, \(K_2 = 340\)), with \(\alpha = 1\) and \(\beta = 2.2\). For (b), try several different starting densities. 21.4 Takeaways Competition outcomes depend on relative self-limitation vs. interspecific effects. The competition coefficients \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) encode how much one species suppresses the other. Coexistence occurs when each species limits itself more than it limits the other, in the scaled sense that \(\alpha < K_1/K_2\) and \(\beta < K_2/K_1\) (each species can invade when rare). Comparing a coefficient with 1 is not enough when the carrying capacities differ. The four isocline intercepts (\(K_1\), \(K_1/\alpha\), \(K_2\), \(K_2/\beta\)) are all you need to predict the outcome.

22 Lotka-Volterra predator-prey dynamics 22.1 Background 22.2 Key idea 22.3 Your task 22.4 Optional extras 22.5 R-version 22.6 Takeaways

22 Lotka-Volterra predator-prey dynamics 22.1 Background The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model (Lotka 1925; Volterra 1926) is a fundamental concept in ecological dynamics, used to study the dynamics between predator and prey populations. Rosenzweig and MacArthur (1963) later extended this basic model to incorporate prey carrying capacity and predator functional response. The model assumes that the predator’s population growth is directly influenced by the availability of its prey, while the prey’s population growth is affected by predation pressure. As predator numbers increase, the prey population declines, which, in turn, leads to a decrease in predator numbers due to reduced food availability. This cyclical pattern continues as predator and prey populations oscillate over time. The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model gives us a framework for understanding the dynamics of species interactions. In this class you will build and explore a Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model in Excel to gain insight into the ecology of interacting predators and prey. Learning outcomes: Competence in constructing an Excel-based population model. Understanding how the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model works, and how it is visualised. 22.2 Key idea The two isoclines (the lines where prey or predator numbers stop changing) are set by different parameters: the prey isocline by the prey’s growth rate and the predator’s attack rate, the predator isocline by the predator’s death rate and how efficiently it turns prey into offspring. Changing a parameter moves an isocline, and so moves the equilibrium point where they cross. Whether the populations then cycle more or less widely depends on how far the starting numbers are from that new equilibrium. Important: the spreadsheet is a discrete-time model In the lecture, the Lotka-Volterra model is written in continuous time (dH/dt, dP/dt). In that model the populations cycle for ever: the cycles neither grow nor shrink (they are neutrally stable), and their size depends only on the starting numbers. The spreadsheet instead updates the populations once per time step (N(t+1) = N(t) + change over one step), like the discrete logistic model in Deeper into logistic growth. Because each step uses the population sizes at the start of the step, the model always reacts a little too late, and the oscillations grow until one or both populations crash. This is a property of the discrete-time version (a time lag), not of predator-prey interactions in general. Keep this in mind when you answer the questions below, especially question 6. You can compare the two versions in the R chapters Continuous-time Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model in R and Discrete-time Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model in R. 22.3 Your task Follow the PDF worksheet (here), which guides you to build and explore a Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model in Excel. The model has parameters for the prey and for the predator, and you will explore how these parameters influence the dynamics of the populations. The worksheet is divided into four parts. We will mainly focus on Part 1 - the basic model - in the class. Symbols: worksheet vs Neal The worksheet uses different symbols from Neal (Predator-Prey Interactions), whose continuous model is \(dH/dt = rH - aHP\) and \(dP/dt = cHP - dP\). The worksheet’s equations are \(V_{t+1} = V_t + RV_t - aC_tV_t\) and \(C_{t+1} = C_t + afV_tC_t - qC_t\). Worksheet Neal Meaning \(V\) (“victim”) \(H\) Prey population \(C\) (“consumer”) \(P\) Predator population \(R\) \(r\) Prey growth rate (in the worksheet, per time step) \(a\) \(a\) Attack rate \(af\) (\(f\) = conversion efficiency) \(c\) Rate at which prey eaten become new predators \(q\) \(d\) Predator death (starvation) rate So the prey isocline \(C = R/a\) is Neal’s \(P = r/a\), and the predator isocline \(V = q/(af)\) is Neal’s \(H = d/c\). Correct formula for step 7 of the PDF The predator formula printed in the PDF is missing a minus sign. In cell C15 use: English Excel: =IF(C14+$H$8*$H$9*B14*C14-$H$7*C14>0,C14+$H$8*$H$9*B14*C14-$H$7*C14,0) Danish Excel: =HVIS(C14+$H$8*$H$9*B14*C14-$H$7*C14>0;C14+$H$8*$H$9*B14*C14-$H$7*C14;0) The prey formula in cell B15 (step 6) in Danish Excel is =HVIS(B14+$F$7*B14-$H$9*C14*B14>0;B14+$F$7*B14-$H$9*C14*B14;0), and MAX is MAKS. Your first rows should read 1050.000, 19.600 (time 1) and 1106.700, 19.286 (time 2). The sheet runs for 100 time steps. With the default values neither species goes extinct within that time, although the cycles clearly grow. To see the end of the story, copy the formulas further down (to row 314 gives 300 time steps): the prey hit zero at time step 220. After completing the Excel sheet, try to answer the following questions: In the spreadsheet model, does a larger prey population growth rate (R) increase or decrease the stability of the predator-prey interaction? What happens if the predators starve more quickly? Less quickly? What happens if the predator is more efficient at converting prey into offspring? Less efficient? What happens if the predator is better at finding prey? Worse? Is the behaviour of the model sensitive to starting populations? Begin with populations near the point where the isoclines cross, and move slowly farther out. What is the ultimate outcome of the predator-prey interaction in the spreadsheet, regardless of parameter values? Is this outcome caused by the biology or by the model being discrete-time (see the box above)? How does this compare to real predator and prey populations? What factors not included in the model may explain the differences between model predictions and reality? 22.4 Optional extras Part 2 modifies the basic model to include a refuge for the prey, part 3 adds a carrying capacity for the prey, and part 4 adds carrying capacities for both prey and predator. Feel free to continue to work on these if there is time, and if you are interested. Part 3 is particularly worth trying: prey self-limitation turns the expanding oscillations into damped ones that settle at an equilibrium. 22.5 R-version Two R versions are available: a continuous-time version (the model in the lecture) and a discrete-time version (the same model as this spreadsheet). 22.5.1 References Lotka, A. J. 1925. Elements of Physical Biology. Williams & Wilkins. Volterra, V. 1926. Variazioni e fluttuazioni del numero d’individui in specie animali conviventi. Memorie della Reale Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei 2: 31–113. Rosenzweig, M. L. and R. H. MacArthur. 1963. Graphical representation and stability conditions of predator-prey interactions. American Naturalist 97: 209–223. 22.6 Takeaways Predator-prey feedbacks can generate oscillations without external forcing. Parameter changes move the isoclines and the equilibrium; in the continuous model the size of the cycles is set by the starting numbers. The spreadsheet’s growing oscillations come from its discrete time steps; the continuous model gives neutrally stable cycles. Simple models highlight mechanisms but omit real-world constraints.

23 Continuous-time Lotka-Volterra Predator-Prey Model in R 23.1 Background 23.2 What you should see 23.3 Your task 23.4 Takeaways

23 Continuous-time Lotka-Volterra Predator-Prey Model in R 23.1 Background The Lotka-Volterra model describes the interaction between predators and prey. This document demonstrates how to program the continuous-time version of the model in R. Then, by varying the parameters you can explore its features, and visualise the dynamics of predator and prey populations over time. Learning outcomes: Use of R to investigate an ecological model. Understanding how the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model works, and how it is visualised. 23.2 What you should see With the default parameters, you should see: repeating oscillations in predator and prey abundances through time, with the predator peaks following the prey peaks a closed orbit in the phase plane around the coexistence equilibrium (the same loop is traced again and again) straight-line isoclines (ZNGIs) whose intersection is the coexistence equilibrium This is the same model as the Excel spreadsheet and the discrete-time R chapter, with the same parameter values, but solved in continuous time. Comparing the three shows which behaviour belongs to the biology and which to the time steps. 23.3 Your task In R/RStudio, you will create an R script that programs the continuous time version of the Lotka-Volterra model. You will then use this model to investigate how the model works and how varying the parameters affects the system. 23.3.1 Step 0: Create a new script Open RStudio and create a new script (File > New File > R Script). Save it with a useful name (File > Save). Type or copy/paste the following code, step-by-step, into the Script. Run the code, or parts of it, selecting the parts you want to run and clicking “Run”. 23.3.2 Step 1: Load Necessary Libraries We will use the deSolve package to solve the system of differential equations numerically. Note that you may need to install the package first using the command install.packages("deSolve"). library(deSolve) 23.3.3 Step 2: Define the Model The system of equations is defined as follows: Victim (prey) population growth: \(\frac{dV}{dt} = RV - aVC\) Consumer (predator) population growth: \(\frac{dC}{dt} = afVC - qC\) The function below implements these equations in R. predator_prey_model <- function(t, state, parameters) { with(as.list(c(state, parameters)), { dV <- R * V - a * V * C # Victim (prey) growth equation dC <- a * f * V * C - q * C # Consumer (predator) growth equation list(c(dV, dC)) }) } 23.3.4 Step 3: Set Parameters and Initial Conditions We set the parameters and initial conditions for the model. I use the same nomenclature as the PDF from the Excel exercise, and the same values. The parameters are as follows: R is the victim population growth rate, a is the attack rate of the predator, f is the conversion efficiency of the predator and q is the predator starvation (death) rate. Here R is an instantaneous rate (Neal’s r), because the model is in continuous time. The Neal textbook (chapter Predator-Prey Interactions) writes the same model as \(dH/dt = rH - aHP\) and \(dP/dt = cHP - dP\). The translation is: \(V = H\) (prey), \(C = P\) (predators), \(R = r\), \(a = a\), \(a \cdot f = c\) and \(q = d\). parameters <- c(R = 0.25, # Victim (prey) growth rate a = 0.01, # Attack rate f = 0.008, # Conversion efficiency q = 0.1) # Predator death rate initial_state <- c(V = 1000, # Initial victim population C = 20) # Initial consumer population 23.3.5 Step 4: Simulate the Model We simulate the model over a specified time period and store the results. time <- seq(0, 200, by = 0.1) # Time sequence output <- ode(y = initial_state, times = time, func = predator_prey_model, parms = parameters) output_df <- as.data.frame(output) 23.3.6 Step 5: Visualise the Dynamics How does the size of the two populations change through time? You should see that the amplitude and period change as the parameters change. Amplitude: Half the difference between a population’s peak and trough. It shows how much the population fluctuates. Period: The time it takes for a population to complete one full cycle of oscillation. i.e. the peak-to-peak distance. It indicates the speed of the population cycles. 23.3.6.1 Population Dynamics Over Time The plot below shows the changes in consumer and victim populations over time. # Make room in the right-hand margin for the second axis label par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 5)) # Plot victim population on the primary y-axis plot(output_df$time, output_df$V, type = "l", col = "blue", lwd = 2, ylab = "Victim Population (V)", xlab = "Time", main = "Predator-Prey Dynamics") # Add consumer population on a secondary y-axis par(new = TRUE) plot(output_df$time, output_df$C, type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "") axis(side = 4, col = "red", col.axis = "red") mtext("Consumer Population (C)", side = 4, line = 3, col = "red") # Add legend legend("topright", legend = c("Victim (V)", "Consumer (C)"), col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2) 23.3.6.2 Phase Plot with ZNGIs The phase plot shows the relationship between victim and consumer populations. Zero Net Growth Isoclines (ZNGIs) indicate where the growth rate of each population is zero. plot(output_df$V, output_df$C, type = "l", col = "purple", lwd = 2, xlab = "Victim (V)", ylab = "Consumer (C)", main = "Predator-Prey Dynamics with ZNGIs") # Consumer ZNGI: dC/dt = 0 when V = q / (a * f) (a vertical line) abline(v = parameters["q"] / (parameters["a"] * parameters["f"]), col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2) # Victim ZNGI: dV/dt = 0 when C = R / a (a horizontal line) abline(h = parameters["R"] / parameters["a"], col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2) # Add point for initial population sizes points(output_df$V[1], output_df$C[1], pch = 19, col = "black", cex = 1.5) # Add a direction arrow only if the final step has visible movement. n <- nrow(output_df) step_inches <- c( diff(grconvertX(output_df$V[c(n - 1, n)], from = "user", to = "inches")), diff(grconvertY(output_df$C[c(n - 1, n)], from = "user", to = "inches")) ) if (all(is.finite(step_inches)) && sqrt(sum(step_inches^2)) > 1e-3) { arrows(x0 = output_df$V[n - 1], y0 = output_df$C[n - 1], x1 = output_df$V[n], y1 = output_df$C[n], col = "purple", length = 0.1, lwd = 2) } 23.3.7 Questions Before you change anything, write down a prediction for each question (a sentence or a quick sketch), then run the code to check it. 1. Oscillations Run the simulation with the default parameters. Describe how the two populations change through time. Which peaks first, prey or predators, and why? In the phase plot, which way does the orbit go round (clockwise or anticlockwise)? Explain the direction using the four regions marked out by the isoclines. 2. Neutral stability and starting numbers Predict: what will happen if you start exactly at the equilibrium, \(V = 1250\), \(C = 25\)? And just next to it, at \(V = 1300\), \(C = 25\)? Now try starting values further away, e.g. \(V = 2000, C = 20\) and \(V = 1000, C = 40\). What happens to the amplitude and the period? Do the oscillations grow, shrink or stay the same over time? 3. Equilibrium and time-averages Calculate the equilibrium for the default parameters, using \[ V^* = \frac{q}{a \cdot f}, \quad C^* = \frac{R}{a}. \] The populations never settle at these values. Instead, compare them with the average population sizes over the simulation: mean(output_df$V) and mean(output_df$C). What do you find? 4. Moving the isoclines Predict which isocline (prey or predator) moves, and in which direction, if you double each of \(R\), \(a\), \(f\) and \(q\) in turn. Check your predictions on the phase plot. A pesticide kills both prey and predators: it lowers \(R\) and raises \(q\). Try \(R = 0.2\) and \(q = 0.12\). What happens to the average numbers of prey and predators? Is this what you would have guessed? (This is Volterra’s principle; see Neal’s Predator-Prey Interactions.) 5. Extinction and reality Start far from the equilibrium, at \(V = 1000\), \(C = 100\). What are the smallest prey and predator numbers reached? Can either population reach exactly zero in this model? What would happen to a real population at these numbers? Which assumptions of the model are unrealistic? Which real-world factors might stop the cycles continuing for ever? 23.3.8 Conclusion This document demonstrates how to implement and explore the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model in continuous time using R. By varying parameters and initial conditions, you can investigate how predator-prey dynamics are influenced by ecological factors. Notice that, unlike the discrete-time model (which has an implicit time lag of one time step and gives oscillations of increasing amplitude that end in extinction), the continuous-time model gives neutrally stable cycles: they neither grow nor shrink, and their size depends on the starting populations. To see the discrete-time version, take a look at the Excel exercise (here) or the R exercise here. The main findings of the continuous time model are as follows: Oscillatory Dynamics: Predator and prey populations exhibit cyclical oscillations. The prey population increases when predator numbers are low, while the predator population grows when prey is abundant, so predator peaks follow prey peaks. Neutral Stability: The oscillations are neutrally stable. They persist indefinitely without damping or amplification, and each pair of starting numbers gives its own orbit: the further from equilibrium you start, the larger the cycles. In the model neither population can ever reach exactly zero, but large orbits can take a population down to a fraction of one individual (for example, starting at \(V = 1000\), \(C = 100\) the predators fall to about 2 and the prey to about 8; with \(q = 1\) the predators fall to about 0.01). In a real population that would mean extinction. Equilibrium Points: There are two equilibria: The trivial equilibrium, where both predator and prey populations are zero. The coexistence equilibrium, \(V^* = q/(af)\) and \(C^* = R/a\). The populations cycle around it rather than settling at it, but the average population sizes over a cycle equal the equilibrium values. Parameter Dependence: The parameters set the position of the isoclines, and so the equilibrium: \(R\) and \(a\) move the prey isocline, \(q\), \(a\) and \(f\) move the predator isocline. The amplitude of the cycles is set by how far the starting numbers are from the equilibrium. For small cycles the period is approximately \(2\pi/\sqrt{Rq}\) (about 40 time units with the default parameters); large cycles take longer. Phase Plane Behaviour: Predator and prey populations follow closed orbits in the phase plane around the coexistence equilibrium, anticlockwise when prey are on the x-axis, under the assumption that the system remains undisturbed. 23.4 Takeaways Continuous-time predator-prey models generate sustained, neutrally stable cycles: their size is set by the starting numbers, not by the parameters alone. Equilibria and isoclines help explain why cycles form and how parameters shift them; the average population sizes over a cycle equal the equilibrium. Real ecosystems add damping, delays, and noise that change these dynamics.

24 Discrete-time Lotka-Volterra Predator-Prey Model in R 24.1 Key idea 24.2 Introduction 24.3 Step 1: Define the Model 24.4 Step 2: Set Parameters and Initial Conditions 24.5 Step 3: Simulate the Model 24.6 Step 4: Visualise the Dynamics 24.7 Your task 24.8 Conclusion 24.9 Takeaways

24 Discrete-time Lotka-Volterra Predator-Prey Model in R Learning outcomes: Implement and explore a discrete-time predator-prey model in R. Understand how time steps introduce delays and affect stability. Compare discrete-time dynamics to continuous-time dynamics. 24.1 Key idea With \(\Delta t = 1\), the phase plane typically shows expanding spirals, reflecting instability introduced by discrete time steps. 24.2 Introduction The Lotka-Volterra model describes the interaction between predators and prey. This document demonstrates how to program the discrete-time version of the model in R, explore its features, and visualise the dynamics of predator and prey populations over time. The time step (\(\Delta t\)) can be adjusted to explore the impact of a time delay in the system. In ecological systems, time delays can represent biological processes such as the time it takes for predators to respond to changes in prey density, for prey populations to recover after predation. If \(\Delta t\) is set to 1, this model is equivalent to a year-by-year model (as we have fitted in Excel in class), where the impact of predators on prey has a 1 year lag. i.e. the growth of predators, depends on the availability of prey 1 year ago and the growth of prey depends on the amount of predators 1 year ago. There are two ways to think about \(\Delta t\). With \(\Delta t = 1\) this is a model of populations that really do change in steps (e.g. one breeding season per year). With \(\Delta t\) very small, nothing biological has changed: we are simply calculating the continuous-time model more accurately, in many small steps. The parameters and the starting numbers are the same as in the Excel spreadsheet and the continuous-time R chapter. 24.3 Step 1: Define the Model The discrete-time equations are as follows: Victim (prey) population growth: \(V_{t+1} = V_t + \Delta t \cdot (R \cdot V_t - a \cdot C_t \cdot V_t)\) Consumer (predator) population growth: \(C_{t+1} = C_t + \Delta t \cdot (a \cdot f \cdot V_t \cdot C_t - q \cdot C_t)\) Note that, when \(\Delta t = 1\), the model is as follows: Victim (prey) population growth: \(V_{t+1} = V_t + R \cdot V_t - a \cdot C_t \cdot V_t\) Consumer (predator) population growth: \(C_{t+1} = C_t + a \cdot f \cdot V_t \cdot C_t - q \cdot C_t\) Compare these to Equations 1 and 2 in the Excel exercise PDF. The function below implements these equations in R. discrete_predator_prey_model <- function(time_steps, dt, initial_state, parameters) { # Initialise vectors to store populations time_steps <- round(time_steps) V <- numeric(time_steps + 1) C <- numeric(time_steps + 1) time <- seq(0, time_steps * dt, by = dt) # Set initial populations V[1] <- initial_state["V"] C[1] <- initial_state["C"] # Extract parameters R <- parameters["R"] a <- parameters["a"] f <- parameters["f"] q <- parameters["q"] # Loop through time steps to calculate populations for (t in 1:time_steps) { # max(0, ...) stops populations going negative (like IF() in Excel) V[t + 1] <- max(0, V[t] + dt * (R * V[t] - a * V[t] * C[t])) C[t + 1] <- max(0, C[t] + dt * (a * f * V[t] * C[t] - q * C[t])) } # Combine results into a data frame data.frame(time = time, V = V, C = C) } 24.4 Step 2: Set Parameters and Initial Conditions We set the parameters, initial conditions, the total time to simulate (total_time) and the time step (\(\Delta t\)). The number of steps is calculated from these, so that changing \(\Delta t\) always covers the same total time and the runs can be compared fairly. parameters <- c(R = 0.25, # Victim (prey) growth rate a = 0.01, # Attack rate f = 0.008, # Conversion efficiency q = 0.1) # Consumer (predator) death rate initial_state <- c(V = 1000, # Initial victim population C = 20) # Initial consumer population total_time <- 300 # Total time to simulate dt <- 1 # Time step (dt), 1 = a standard discrete model time_steps <- total_time / dt # Number of time steps needed to cover total_time 24.5 Step 3: Simulate the Model We simulate the model for the specified parameters and time steps. output_df <- discrete_predator_prey_model(time_steps = time_steps, dt = dt, initial_state = initial_state, parameters = parameters) 24.6 Step 4: Visualise the Dynamics 24.6.1 Population Dynamics Over Time The plot below shows the changes in consumer and victim populations over time. # Make room in the right-hand margin for the second axis label par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 5)) # Plot victim population on the primary y-axis plot(output_df$time, output_df$V, type = "l", col = "blue", lwd = 2, ylab = "Victim Population (V)", xlab = "Time", main = "Discrete Predator-Prey Dynamics") # Add consumer population on a secondary y-axis par(new = TRUE) plot(output_df$time, output_df$C, type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "") axis(side = 4, col = "red", col.axis = "red") mtext("Consumer Population (C)", side = 4, line = 3, col = "red") # Add legend legend("topright", legend = c("Victim (V)", "Consumer (C)"), col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2) 24.6.2 Phase Plot with ZNGIs The phase plot shows the relationship between victim and consumer populations. ### Phase Plot with ZNGIs, Initial Point, and Arrow plot(output_df$V, output_df$C, type = "l", col = "purple", lwd = 2, xlab = "Victim (V)", ylab = "Consumer (C)", main = "Discrete Predator-Prey Dynamics with ZNGIs") # Add Consumer ZNGI: no change in C when V = q / (a * f) (a vertical line) abline(v = parameters["q"] / (parameters["a"] * parameters["f"]), col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2) # Add Victim ZNGI: no change in V when C = R / a (a horizontal line) abline(h = parameters["R"] / parameters["a"], col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2) # Add point for initial population sizes points(output_df$V[1], output_df$C[1], pch = 19, col = "black", cex = 1.5) # Add a direction arrow only if the final step has visible movement. n <- nrow(output_df) step_inches <- c( diff(grconvertX(output_df$V[c(n - 1, n)], from = "user", to = "inches")), diff(grconvertY(output_df$C[c(n - 1, n)], from = "user", to = "inches")) ) if (all(is.finite(step_inches)) && sqrt(sum(step_inches^2)) > 1e-3) { arrows(x0 = output_df$V[n - 1], y0 = output_df$C[n - 1], x1 = output_df$V[n], y1 = output_df$C[n], col = "purple", length = 0.1, lwd = 2) } 24.7 Your task Before each run, predict what you will see (sketch the phase plot), then check. Run the model with the default settings (\(\Delta t = 1\), total_time = 300). How does the phase plot differ from the closed orbit in the continuous-time chapter? When does the first population hit zero? Find it with output_df$time[which(output_df$C == 0 | output_df$V == 0)[1]]. Decrease \(\Delta t\) to 0.1 (keep total_time = 300; the number of steps is recalculated for you, so re-run the parameter chunk as well as the simulation) and compare the phase plane behaviour to \(\Delta t = 1\). Then try \(\Delta t = 0.01\). Increase \(\Delta t\) to 2 and observe whether extinction happens faster. Change \(R\) or \(q\) (e.g. double one of them) with \(\Delta t = 1\). Does the spiral grow faster or slower? Now double \(a\) or \(f\) instead. Which parameters control how quickly the spiral grows? (Careful: changing \(a\) or \(f\) also moves the equilibrium, so the default start is then nearer to or further from it. Compare how fast the spiral widens, not only when it ends.) 24.8 Conclusion This document demonstrates how to implement and explore the discrete-time Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model. By adjusting the time step (\(\Delta t\)) and other parameters, you can investigate how predator-prey dynamics are influenced by ecological factors. With the default settings (\(\Delta t = 1\)), the time lag of one step makes the phase plot spiral outwards: the cycles grow until the prey are wiped out (they hit zero at \(t = 220\)), after which the predators starve and dwindle towards zero. Smaller time steps make the spiral grow more slowly, and with \(\Delta t = 0.01\) the orbit is almost closed, like the continuous-time model. Larger time steps make it grow faster: with \(\Delta t = 2\) the prey hit zero at \(t = 142\). Contrast this with the perpetual (neutrally stable) oscillations you get with the continuous-time model. 24.9 Takeaways Discrete time steps destabilise the predator-prey cycles of the continuous-time model: the populations react one step too late, so each cycle overshoots a little more than the last. Each time step, the distance from the equilibrium grows by a factor of about \(\sqrt{1 + \Delta t^2 R q}\). This depends on the prey growth rate, the predator death rate and the step length, but not on the attack rate or conversion efficiency. With the default values it is about 1.012 per step (roughly 1 % per step). Smaller \(\Delta t\) values bring the discrete model closer to the continuous-time behaviour.

25 Game theory: Hawks and doves 25.1 Background Game theory analyses interactions in which the payoff of a choice depends on what others choose. Maynard Smith and Price (1973) brought it into biology as evolutionary game theory, which does not assume that animals are rational. Instead, each individual follows a strategy, strategies are heritable, and payoffs are measured in fitness, so strategies that earn more spread through the population. One particularly fascinating example is the Hawk and Dove game. Representing two distinct strategies, the Hawk embodies aggression and assertiveness, always seeking to escalate conflicts and dominate opponents. On the other hand, the Dove adopts a more peaceful and conciliatory approach, aiming to avoid confrontations and achieve cooperative outcomes. By studying the Hawk and Dove strategies we can gain insights into understanding the delicate balance between competition and cooperation, shedding light on the dynamics of conflicts and the evolution of cooperative behaviour in both the natural world and human societies. The simple model unravels the intricacies of strategic decision-making, with profound implications across various fields, from biology and social sciences to economics and politics. In this activity, you play the role of the strategies: you will play the hawk and dove game with a single partner and then with multiple partners to observe the hypothetical costs and benefits of antagonistic or cooperative behaviour, respectively. The whole class enters results into one shared, live spreadsheet as you play, so we can watch the class-wide patterns emerge on screen in real time, round by round, instead of waiting until after class to see what happened. Learning outcomes: Understanding of the fundamental concepts of game theory and its application in analysing strategic interactions in competitive environments. Ability to apply game theory concepts to real-world contexts in biology, or politics. Appreciation of how simple models can be used to address complex biological or political decision making. Practice generating a testable prediction from a simple model before collecting data, then checking it against real, live class results. 25.2 Worked example 25.2.1 Inputs Benefit: \(B = 4\) Cost: \(C = 3\) 25.2.2 Steps Compute Hawk-Hawk payoff: \((B-C)/2\). Compute Hawk-Dove payoff to Hawk: \(B\) (and 0 to Dove). Compute Dove-Dove payoff: \(B/2\) to each player. 25.2.3 Output and interpretation Hawk-Hawk gives \(0.5\) each, Hawk-Dove gives 4 to Hawk and 0 to Dove, and Dove-Dove gives 2 each. Link to the lecture: when does a mix of Hawks and Doves evolve? The class game uses the lecture’s payoff matrix with the display cost set to zero (\(D = 0\)). This is also the matrix in Neal’s chapter “Animal Behaviour, Altruism and Limiting Aggression”, where Dove-Dove pays \(B/2 - D\). If \(B > C\) (as today, \(B = 4\), \(C = 3\)), Hawk earns more than Dove whatever the opponent plays, so in a one-off encounter the evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS) is pure Hawk. If \(C > B\), neither pure strategy is stable. The ESS is a mix, with Hawks at frequency \(p^* = B/C\), where Hawks and Doves earn the same on average. For example, with \(B = 4\) and \(C = 8\), \(p^* = 0.5\). (With a display cost, as in the lecture’s worked example, \(p^* = (B/2 + D)/(C/2 + D)\), which gives 7/12.) 25.3 Your task Before the activity starts, review the cost-benefit payoff table below to understand how to score the game. 25.4 The payoff table The general payoff table looks like this (payoff to Player 1): Player 1  Player 2 Hawk Dove Hawk \((B-C)/2\) \(B\) Dove \(0\) \(B/2\) You can determine the benefit by looking at the left column and choosing the row corresponding to the card you played. The box that corresponds to your partner’s choice is in the top row. For this game, B equals four (4), and C equals three (3). So depending on the cards played, player one (i.e., you) would gain a score of two (2), four (4), zero (0), or one-half (0.5). Like this: Player 1  Player 2 Hawk Dove Hawk 0.5 4 Dove 0 2 25.4.1 What does theory predict? Before you play, work through this with your partner. Because B (4) is bigger than C (3), Hawk beats Dove no matter what your opponent plays: against a Dove you get 4 (vs. 2 for playing Dove yourself), and against a Hawk you still get 0.5 (vs. 0 for playing Dove). So in a single, anonymous encounter, Hawk is the dominant strategy: theory predicts everyone should end up playing Hawk. But notice that mutual Hawk-Hawk (0.5 each) is worse for both of you than mutual Dove-Dove (2 each). That means this game has the same structure as the famous Prisoner’s Dilemma, with Hawk playing the role of “Defect”. One twist: if you and your partner take turns (Hawk/Dove one round, Dove/Hawk the next), you each average (4 + 0)/2 = 2 per round, exactly as much as mutual Dove-Dove. So with these payoffs, taking turns is just as good a way to “cooperate”. Prediction for Game Two (a new partner every round, i.e. effectively a series of one-off encounters): theory says Hawk should dominate and pay off best. Prediction for Game One (the same partner, 15 times in a row): think about what happens if you play Hawk against your partner. Might they retaliate next round? If you get stuck trading Hawk-Hawk for the rest of the game, is that better or worse than settling into mutual Dove-Dove? Could you and your partner do as well as mutual Dove in another way? Write down what you think will happen to the frequency of Hawk play and to mean payoff per round as the 15 rounds go on, before you start. Prediction for round 15: you both know the game ends after round 15, so there is no next round in which to be punished. What do you expect people to play in the last round? Keep your predictions: we’ll come back to them once the live results are in. 25.4.2 Hypotheses Building on the predictions above, the experimental hypothesis for this exercise is that, compared with changing partners (Game Two), playing a repeated partner (Game One) leads to: a lower frequency of Hawk play (overall, and declining over the 15 rounds), and a higher mean payoff per player per round, because pairs avoid costly Hawk-Hawk encounters. The null hypothesis is that neither the frequency of Hawk play nor the mean payoff per player differs between the repeated-partner and changing-partner games. Note what we are not testing: whether the more hawkish player in a pair earns more. Within any single round Hawk always earns more than Dove (0.5 > 0 against a Hawk, 4 > 2 against a Dove), so the more hawkish player in a pair always ends up with at least as high a total. What repeated play can change is how your partner responds, and so how much both of you earn. 25.4.3 Instructor setup (before class) (Read this section if you are running the session; students can skip ahead to “How today’s data collection works”.) To let the whole class see results build up live, set up one shared spreadsheet before class instead of the old per-round Google Form: Duplicate the “Hawk-Dove Live Results” spreadsheet template (keep one copy per year; reuse and re-share it each time you teach the course). It needs two data tabs and one dashboard tab: Game1_Data: one row per pair, pre-filled with Pair ID = 1, 2, 3, … (enough rows for number of students / 2). For each of the 15 rounds, two entry columns (R1_P1, R1_P2, R2_P1, R2_P2, … using H/D), plus a formula-computed benefit column per round and a Total_P1_benefit / Total_P2_benefit column, so students never have to do the arithmetic themselves. Keep B and C in two named cells that the benefit formulas refer to, so you can change the payoffs in future years without editing every formula. Game2_Data: one row per student, pre-filled with Player ID = 1, 2, 3, … up to the class size. For each of the 15 rounds, two entry columns (R1_self, R1_opponent, …), the same formula-computed per-round and total benefit columns. Live_Dashboard: charts wired to the data tabs: a line chart of “% Hawk played, by round” for each game, and a scatter chart of “mean hawkishness vs. total benefit” per pair/player for each game (these are the same two charts reproduced from archived data in the Results of the hawk-dove games chapter after class). Set sharing so students can edit without individually logging in (e.g. “anyone with the link can edit”), and share the link at the start of class (projected, or via itsLearning). Assign Pair IDs (Game 1) and Player IDs (Game 2) before class (e.g. by seat number or an attendance list) rather than letting students choose their own names or team labels. This is what lets everyone’s data line up automatically and avoids the messy name-matching problems free-text team names caused in past years. Project the Live_Dashboard tab throughout the activity. After class, keep the spreadsheet (or an exported copy) as this year’s archived dataset for the Results chapter. 25.4.4 How today’s data collection works Instead of filling in a new form after every round, the whole class shares one live spreadsheet, projected on the screen as you play: You’ll be given a Pair ID (Game 1) or a Player ID (Game 2): use it to find your row. Don’t invent your own label; the ID is what lets the spreadsheet combine everyone’s results automatically. You only ever type into your own row. Enter cards as single letters: H for Hawk, D for Dove. The spreadsheet calculates the benefit for you from the payoff table, so there’s no arithmetic to do mid-game. Watch the projected screen: two live charts update automatically as the class enters data, so you can see the round-by-round pattern emerge as you play (see “Watching the results live” below). 25.4.5 GAME ONE: repeated partner Find your assigned partner and note your shared Pair ID. Collect a set of two game cards (Hawk and Dove), one each. Agree who is recorded as “Player 1” and who is “Player 2” for your pair (it doesn’t affect scoring). Conceal your cards. When the instructor gives the signal (“reveal!”), simultaneously show either card to your partner. Agree on which card each of you showed, then enter both (H/D) into your pair’s row for that round (one phone or laptop per pair is enough). Repeat for 15 rounds, waiting for the instructor’s signal each time. Try to strategise how to get the best benefit from every round, but don’t communicate your strategy with your partner beyond the cards themselves. At the end, check your row: the spreadsheet shows each player’s total benefit across all 15 rounds. Divide by 15 to get your mean payoff per round, and compare it with the class average and, later, with Game Two. (Do not just ask who “won” within your pair: the more hawkish player always does, for the reason given under Hypotheses.) No wifi? Jot your results on paper first (round, your card, partner’s card) and enter them all at once at the end; the live chart will simply catch up when you do. 25.4.6 GAME TWO: changing partners every round To swap partners quickly with a large class, use a rotating circle: half the class forms an inner circle facing outward, the other half forms an outer circle facing inward, so everyone starts facing one partner. Find your assigned Player ID and starting position in the circle. Play a round exactly as in Game One: conceal your card, reveal on the instructor’s signal, agree on both cards played. Enter your own card and your opponent’s card (H/D) into your row for that round. When the instructor calls “rotate”, everyone in the outer circle shifts one position to their left. You now face a new partner for the next round. Repeat for 15 rounds. Because you rotate through the circle, you meet a new person every round without any time lost searching for a free partner. A double circle gives each person (class size / 2) different partners, so 15 distinct partners needs at least 30 students. With a smaller class, either play only (class size / 2) rounds, or carry on and note that some partners will be met twice (and discuss whether that matters). 25.4.7 Watching the results live As you play, two charts update automatically on the projected screen: % playing Hawk, by round: lets you see whether hawkish play increases, decreases, or stays flat as the rounds go by. Total benefit vs. mean hawkishness, one point per pair/player: lets you see, once the game finishes, whether being more hawkish or more dovish paid off better. We’ll pause after each game to look at these together before moving on to the next part. 25.5 Summarise and discuss results Before looking at the final numbers, revisit the predictions you wrote down earlier. Did the % Hawk trend in Game One and Game Two match what you predicted? Did the total-benefit-vs-hawkishness pattern support the one-shot theory prediction (Hawk pays off best), or the repeated-game reciprocity argument (Dove pays off best when you keep meeting the same partner)? Which game, if either, better matches what you’d expect from a species whose individuals encounter each other only once versus a species that lives in small, stable social groups? Did you or your partner take turns (Hawk/Dove, then Dove/Hawk)? What happened in round 15? Discuss as a class what would likely happen if you increased or decreased the relative value of the benefit (B) compared with the cost (C): would that change which strategy dominates in a one-off encounter? (Hint: see the box above on \(p^* = B/C\).) The full analysis of the actual class data, including how the live charts you just watched connect to the underlying theory, is worked through in detail in the Results of the hawk-dove games chapter. 25.6 Acknowledgement This exercise is taken from https://www.jove.com/science-education/10611/group-behaviour 25.7 Takeaways With B > C, a single anonymous encounter is won by playing Hawk, but repeated encounters with the same partner change the incentives, because mutual Hawk-Hawk is worse for both players than mutual Dove-Dove. Collecting and displaying data live, as a class, makes it possible to test a theoretical prediction in real time rather than waiting until after the session. Game outcomes depend on the structure of the interaction (one-off vs. repeated), not just on the payoffs themselves. When the cost of fighting exceeds the value of the resource (C > B), the ESS is a mix of Hawks and Doves, with Hawk frequency p* = B/C. 25.7.1 Optional: running a live dashboard in R If you’re comfortable with R, you can draw the “% playing Hawk, by round” chart yourself from the shared spreadsheet using the googlesheets4 package, instead of (or alongside) the spreadsheet’s own charts. This is optional: the built-in spreadsheet charts are enough to run the session. The code assumes the column names in the instructor setup above (R1_P1, R1_P2, … for Game 1). library(googlesheets4) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(ggplot2) # A publicly-editable sheet can be read without signing in: gs4_deauth() sheet_url <- "PASTE_THIS_YEAR'S_LIVE_SHEET_URL_HERE" # Re-run from here every 10-15 seconds during class to refresh the chart. game1 <- read_sheet(sheet_url, sheet = "Game1_Data") # One row per pair, round and player, with the card played (H or D) game1_long <- game1 %>% select(matches("^R[0-9]+_P[12]$")) %>% pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("round", "player"), names_pattern = "R([0-9]+)_(P[12])", values_to = "card") %>% filter(card %in% c("H", "D")) %>% mutate(round = as.numeric(round)) hawk_by_round <- game1_long %>% group_by(round) %>% summarise(percent_hawk = 100 * mean(card == "H")) ggplot(hawk_by_round, aes(x = round, y = percent_hawk)) + geom_point() + geom_line() + ylim(0, 100) + xlab("Round") + ylab("% playing Hawk")
