26 Solutions and “take-home” messages In this section you will find the solutions and/or main take home messages of the practical exercises used in this course. 26.1 How to use this section Use these solutions to check your reasoning after you attempt the tasks. If your answer differs, focus on the logic rather than the final number. 26.2 Solutions: The blind watchmaker Predictions and the default run With selection on, one example run using Dawkins’ 28-character phrase and 27 possible characters reached the target at generation 66. The number varies between runs: in 5,000 simulated runs the median was 98 generations, and 90% of runs finished between about 60 and 166 generations. Compare this with single-step selection, where you would expect to need about \(27^{28} \approx 10^{40}\) attempts. What happens if selection is turned OFF? Each generation is then a completely new random guess (single-step selection), and nothing is kept from one generation to the next. The output stays random nonsense. The chance of hitting the whole phrase in any one generation is \((1/27)^{28} \approx 8 \times 10^{-41}\), so in practice it never happens. Does the number of generations affect whether the target phrase is reached? Yes. With 100 generations, only about half of runs (about 52%) reach this phrase; with 200 generations almost all do (about 99%). The last letters to be fixed are the slow part: each wrong letter has only a 1 in 27 chance of being right in any one generation. Does the speed of reaching the target phrase depend on the length of the phrase? Yes, but much less than you might expect. Longer phrases take more generations, because there are more letters that all have to be fixed, but the increase is small: “I LOVE SCIENCE” (14 characters) takes a median of about 81 generations, the 28-character weasel phrase about 98, and the 53-character “WITH YOUR FEET ON THE AIR AND YOUR HEAD ON THE GROUND” about 117. With single-step selection, every extra character makes success 27 times less likely. How does this simulation differ from real natural selection? Natural selection has no long-term goal or target. Here, every phrase is judged by how close it is to a fixed target that is decided in advance. In nature, individuals are “judged” only by how well they survive and reproduce in their current environment. The intermediate phrases have no use of their own: “METHINKS IT IS LIKE A WXASEL” is only better because it is closer to the target. In evolution, every intermediate form (for example, each stage in the evolution of an eye) must itself work well enough to survive and reproduce. The simulation judges each letter separately, with perfect knowledge of the right answer, and a correct letter can never be lost again. There is no population, no reproduction and no inheritance. Real selection acts on whole organisms in a population, and favourable variants can still be lost by chance. The important lesson still holds: random variation combined with cumulative selection can produce outcomes that would be impossible by chance alone. 26.3 Solutions: Bug hunt camouflage Predictions Typical good predictions: the average colour will move towards the background colour; it will take longer to catch 10 bugs as time goes on; after switching background, catching will suddenly become easy again, and the bugs will then start to evolve towards the new background. Students who predicted that individual bugs would change colour have met a key misconception (see the genotype question below). What happens to the average colour of the bug population with time as you hunt? Was your prediction correct? The colour evolves to become more similar to the background colour because you (the hunter) find it harder to find these better-camouflaged individuals. What happens to your hunting efficiency? Use your measurements. Your hunting efficiency tends to decrease with time because the bugs are evolving to be harder to see. They are evolving camouflaged colours. In your measurements, the time to catch 10 bugs should increase over the first two minutes, drop sharply when you switch background (the bugs are suddenly conspicuous), and then increase again as the bugs adapt to the new background. The exact times differ between students, because each of you is a different predator, but the pattern should usually be the same. Apart from bug evolution, what else could change how long it takes you to catch 10 bugs? Which of the plots gives more direct evidence that the bugs themselves have evolved? You, the predator, also change: you learn where to look and get faster (catch times fall), you get tired or bored (catch times rise), and a new background can be distracting at first, or make you concentrate harder. So catch time mixes changes in the bugs with changes in you, and a student whose times did not rise has not shown that evolution failed. The direct evidence that the bugs evolved is in the colour plots (the histograms of the colour values and the change in average genotype): the distribution of colours in the population shifts towards the background. Would you say that the bug population becomes worse or better adapted to their environment? The population becomes better-adapted to their environment with time. Can you explain how this happens? You (the hunter) kill the most obvious bugs first (i.e. those with contrasting colours to the background). These are the individuals that are not well-adapted to the environment. The survivors have offspring that are similar to them, while the ones you kill leave no offspring. So as time goes on, the population becomes dominated by individuals that are well-camouflaged. After simulating in one environment (e.g. poppy field) for a few minutes, pause then switch to another environment. Are the bugs now well- or poorly-adapted to their environment? Changing the environment means that the individuals are now poorly-adapted to their environment. This is because the individuals now find themselves in an environment that they did not evolve in. Their evolved camouflage does not work so well in a new environment. Do the genotypes of individuals change (e.g. with individual age)? No, individuals’ genotypes are fixed: with “show-genotype?” switched on, each bug keeps the same three numbers for its whole life. The change in the population occurs because of selection of individuals to reproduce. Better-adapted individuals are more likely to reproduce. Increasing the “max-mutation-step” makes bug offspring less like their parents. How do you think this will influence the speed of adaptation of the bugs? Increasing the amount of variation in offspring will tend to speed up adaptation. However, there are limits: too much variation can cause maladaptation of offspring. For example, if a parent is well-adapted (perfectly camouflaged), too much variation in offspring could lead to some offspring being poorly-camouflaged and therefore vulnerable to predation. Where do you see each of the four conditions in the model? Where does new variation come from? Individuals vary in a trait: the bugs differ in colour. Individuals vary in reproductive success: bugs that you catch leave no more offspring; survivors may be chosen to reproduce. The trait affects reproductive success: colours that contrast with the background are caught first, so they are less likely to survive and reproduce. The trait is inherited: offspring get their colour genes from their parent. New variation comes from mutation: each offspring’s colour genes can differ slightly from its parent’s (the “max-mutation-step” slider). Mutation is not one of the four conditions; it supplies the variation that condition 1 needs. Newborn bugs start very small. Could this let some bugs escape for reasons that have nothing to do with their colour? How might that affect the results? Yes. A newborn bug is hard to see because it is small, whatever its colour, so for a short time it escapes for a reason that has nothing to do with camouflage. This adds chance to who survives and weakens selection on colour slightly. It does not stop camouflage evolving, because every bug is small only briefly and colour still matters once it has grown. How does this model differ from a real predator–prey system? Give at least two differences. Possible answers: there is only one predator, and it does not evolve (although you do learn!); reproduction is asexual, with one parent and no recombination; the population size is fixed, so there is no population growth or decline; bugs do not move or choose where to rest; the only selection is predation on colour, whereas real prey face many other pressures (temperature, food, mates); generations overlap in an unusual way, because one offspring is born each time a bug is caught. Optional extension: gene flow and local adaptation With a small “offspring-distance”, offspring stay close to their parents, so bugs in each patch of background are mostly the descendants of bugs that survived in that patch: each patch can evolve its own matching colour (local adaptation). With a large “offspring-distance”, offspring are scattered across the whole background. This is like frequent gene flow between populations: well-camouflaged colours from one patch keep arriving in patches where they stand out, so local adaptation is weaker or absent. Whether gene flow swamps local adaptation depends on how much movement there is compared with the strength of selection. 26.4 Solutions: Geometric growth You can find the completed Excel file here. Take home messages: The rate of exponential/geometric growth depends on the population growth rate. Lambda (\(\lambda\)) values \(<1\) lead to a exponential decrease, while values \(>1\) lead to exponential growth. A \(\lambda\) of 1 indicates no change. Exponential growth is unlimited. This is unrealistic because very soon competition (what Darwin called “The struggle for existence”) will soon take effect as the population runs out of space or resources. Nevertheless, the model is useful and realistic for some limited situations (e.g. early population growth for new invaders) Growth trajectories can be plotted on the natural scale or on a log scale. Exponential growth (or decline) plotted on a log scale is a straight line. This could be useful to infer biological processes (or the lack of them). For example, exponential growth in population size indicates that there are no forces currently limiting the population (e.g. predators/competition/management actions). The slope of the population growth on the natural log scale can tell you what \(\lambda\) is. The “opposite” of ln is exp, so you can ask Excel to calculate =EXP(slope). Answers to the task: Steps 1-2: with \(N_0 = 10\) and \(\lambda = 1.1\), the population reaches 16.1 at \(t = 5\) and 67.3 at \(t = 20\). Plotted against time, N curves upwards ever more steeply. Steps 3-4: plotting ln(N) against time turns the curve into a straight line. A constant proportional increase each time step becomes a constant absolute increase on the log scale. Step 5: with \(\lambda = 1.2\) the curve rises faster (steeper straight line on the log plot); with \(\lambda = 0.8\) the population declines towards zero (straight line sloping downwards on the log plot); with \(\lambda = 1\) the population stays at 10 (flat line). \(\lambda = 1\) is the boundary between growth and decline: the population exactly replaces itself each time step (\(R_m = 0\)). Step 6: the trendline slope is 0.0953 = ln(1.1), and =EXP(0.0953) returns 1.1, the \(\lambda\) you used. The slopes for \(\lambda\) = 0.8, 1 and 1.2 are -0.223, 0 and 0.182. If you get a different slope, check that you fitted the trendline to the logN (natural log) column, not to N on a logarithmic axis. Step 7 (doubling time): with \(\lambda = 1.1\) the population passes 20 between \(t = 7\) (\(N = 19.5\)) and \(t = 8\) (\(N = 21.4\)), and passes 40 about 7 time steps later. The doubling time is \(t_d = \ln 2 / \ln 1.1 = 0.693/0.0953 = 7.27\) time steps. It does not depend on the starting population size: a geometrically growing population doubles at a constant interval, whatever its size. Geometric series: \(N_5 = 10 \times 1.1^5 = 16.1\), the same as the spreadsheet. After 900 generations, \(N_{900} = 10 \times 1.1^{900} \approx 1.8 \times 10^{38}\). That is absurdly large (far more individuals than there are atoms in a human body, around \(10^{27}\)), which shows why unlimited geometric growth cannot continue for long in reality. Answers to the questions: Constant growth rate: the population is multiplied by the same factor each time step, so it grows by the same proportion each step and by ever-larger numbers. For example, with \(\lambda = 1.1\) the population grows by 10% each step: from 10 to 11 in the first step, but from 61.2 to 67.3 between steps 19 and 20. It also doubles at a constant interval: \(\ln 2 / \ln 1.1 \approx 7.3\) time steps. Why unrealistic: it assumes density independence (unlimited resources and space; competition, predation or disease do not increase as the population grows), constant birth and death rates and so a constant \(\lambda\) every year (no environmental variation), no time lags, no age or stage structure (all individuals are identical), and a closed population (no immigration or emigration). Real populations eventually run out of resources and growth slows. Where it might be suitable: the early stages of growth when a population is small relative to its resources, e.g. an invasive species newly arrived in a suitable habitat, a population recovering after a crash or after protection (e.g. some seal or raptor populations), or bacteria in fresh culture medium. Decline of 25% per year: this means \(\lambda = 0.75\), so \(N_4 = 800 \times 0.75^4 = 253.1\), i.e. about 253 individuals. \(\lambda\) per half-year: \(r_m = \ln 1.1 = 0.0953\) per year, so \(r_m = 0.0477\) per half-year, and \(\lambda = e^{0.0477} = 1.049\) per half-year. Check: \(1.049^2 = 1.1\). (Simply halving the 10% increase to 5% would be slightly too much, because growth compounds.) 26.5 Solutions: Estimating Population Growth Rate You can find the completed Excel file here. What does the log-transformed plot of population size over time tell you about the population’s growth trend? Does the population grow exponentially? The log-transformed plot should show a straight line if the population is growing exponentially, because the natural logarithm of an exponentially growing population will linearise the exponential curve. The slope of this line represents the natural log of the population growth rate \(log(\lambda)\). If the line has a positive slope, it indicates the population is growing; if it’s flat, the population is stable; and if it’s negative, the population is shrinking. In this exercise, assuming \(\lambda > 1\), the population is indeed growing exponentially, which will be reflected by a positively sloped line in the log-transformed plot. What is the estimated population growth rate (\(\lambda\)) based on your regression analysis? From the linear regression performed on the log-transformed data, the slope of the line corresponds to \(log(\lambda)\). To find \(\lambda\), exponentiate the slope: \(\lambda = e^{\text{slope}}\). With the data provided, the slope of the regression of ln(N) on year is about 0.070 (0.0696), so \(\lambda = e^{0.0696} \approx 1.07\). The population grows by about 7% per year. (Small differences in the third decimal place are fine; they come from rounding in the trendline label.) In fact, the data were simulated with an average \(\lambda\) of 1.09, with random year-to-year variation in \(\lambda\) and measurement error in the counts. Our estimate is lower than 1.09 for two reasons: year-to-year variation in \(\lambda\) lowers long-run growth (growth follows the geometric mean of \(\lambda\), which is smaller than the arithmetic mean), and with only 25 years of noisy counts the estimate has considerable sampling error. This is a useful reminder that an estimate from real data is never exactly the “true” value. What assumptions does this model make? Discuss any potential real-world factors that might affect the accuracy of your estimate for \(\lambda\). The model assumes a constant growth rate over time. It does not account for environmental changes, resource limitations, or carrying capacity (which would lead to logistic rather than exponential growth). The model also assumes no immigration, emigration, or catastrophic events that might disrupt the population trend. Environmental variability: In reality, populations experience fluctuations due to weather, food availability, disease, and other stochastic factors, which can cause growth rates to change over time. Density dependence: As populations grow larger, they may face resource limitations or increased competition, leading to a slowdown in growth, which would not be captured by a simple geometric model. Measurement errors: In practice, the measurement of population sizes may not be precise, as discussed earlier with the introduction of noise. These errors can lead to inaccuracies in estimating \(\lambda\). 26.6 Solutions: Stochastic population growth You can find the completed Excel file here. Take home messages: Population growth rates are unlikely to be constant through time. Environmental stochasticity will cause changes through time in vital rates (birth/death) which will influence \(\lambda\) (and \(r_m\)). We can model environmental stochasticity using a distribution of population growth rates instead of a single deterministic value. We then can randomly draw growth rate values from this distribution for each time-step in a population projection. The “spread” or uncertainty in the population size at a future time point depends on (i) the spread (variance) of the distribution and (ii) the amount of time elapsed. We can repeatedly simulate a population projection (e.g. in R, or more laboriously in Excel) to get a feel for the likely fate of a population. E.g. “what percent of the projections show extinction within 50 years?”. We can use this relatively simple and “unrealistic” model to nevertheless get an intuition about general trends in population dynamics and extinction risk. Extinction probability increases as (i) initial population size decreases; (ii) variance increases; (iii) growth rates decrease; (iv) the time frame increases. Long-run growth follows the mean of \(r_m\) (the geometric mean of \(\lambda\)), not the arithmetic mean of \(\lambda\). With mean \(r_m\) = 0.05 and variance 0.1, the typical (median) population grows by \(e^{0.05} = 1.051\) per year, but the average \(\lambda\) is \(e^{0.05 + 0.1/2} = 1.105\). In the default R run, after 50 generations the median population size is about 116 (theory: \(10 \times e^{0.05 \times 49} = 116\)), while the mean is about 1,900, pulled up by a few runs that boom. 26.6.1 Things to try Your numbers will differ from these, because each run draws new random numbers. The values below are from the example run shown in the chapter, followed in brackets by the range seen over 100 further runs of 1,000 trials each. Differences of a few percentage points between runs are just chance. Default settings (mean 0.05, variance 0.1, startPop = 10, 50 generations): extinction probability 0.058 (range 0.04 to 0.08). Most trajectories grow, but they spread out enormously: after 50 generations some populations are near 1 and others are in the tens or hundreds of thousands. var.r = 0.5: extinction probability rises to 0.418 (range 0.39 to 0.47), about seven times higher, even though the mean growth rate is unchanged. The trajectories also spread out much more. startPop = 3: extinction probability rises to 0.235 (range 0.21 to 0.28). Starting size matters a lot: a small population needs only a short run of bad years to fall below 1 individual, whereas a larger one has a buffer. mean.r = 0: extinction probability is 0.249 over 50 generations (range 0.24 to 0.30). So extinction is not certain within 50 generations. But it is certain in the long run: with a mean of zero the log population size is a random walk with no upward drift, and such a walk eventually hits any lower boundary. You can see this by increasing nGen: with nGen = 200 the extinction probability is 0.567 (range 0.54 to 0.61), and it keeps rising towards 1 as time increases. Challenge: keep mean.r = 0.05 and increase var.r to 1: extinction probability is 0.576 (range 0.55 to 0.62), so more than half of the populations go extinct even though they grow on average (and the median population still grows in the long run). Other combinations work too (e.g. mean.r = 0.02 with var.r = 0.5 gives about 0.5). This tells us that a positive average growth rate does not guarantee persistence: with enough year-to-year variation, chance runs of bad years drive many populations below the extinction threshold before the positive trend can carry them to safety. The variance matters as much as the mean. If you compare these results with the rule from the lecture (extinction is almost certain if \(\sigma^2 > 2\bar{r}\)), remember that the rule uses \(\bar{r}\) on the \(\lambda\) scale and describes the very long run. In this simulation \(r_m\) is drawn on the log scale, so the long-run growth rate is \(\bar{r}_m\) itself, and certain long-run extinction needs \(\bar{r}_m \leq 0\) (see the box in the chapter). 26.6.2 Questions Deterministic vs. stochastic: a deterministic model always gives the same trajectory for the same parameters; a stochastic model draws the growth rate at random each time step, so each run gives a different trajectory and the model predicts a distribution of possible outcomes (including a probability of extinction) rather than a single number. Why more realistic: real growth rates vary from year to year with weather, food supply, disease and so on, and small populations are also affected by chance births and deaths. A stochastic model captures this variation, and so shows the uncertainty in forecasts and the risk of extinction, which a deterministic model cannot. Two populations with identical growth rates: run the R code (or the Excel sheet) twice with the same settings, or look at any two of the trajectories in the plot. With mean 0.05 and variance 0.1, one population may grow into the thousands while another, with exactly the same parameters, falls below 1 and goes extinct. The implication is that the fate of a single real population is partly a matter of luck, so we should describe it with probabilities, and that two populations that differ in outcome need not differ in their underlying biology. Extinction risk and population size: small populations are at much higher risk (in the default runs, about 0.06 for 10 individuals against about 0.24 for 3), because a short run of bad years can take them below the threshold. Extinction risk and environmental variation: more variable environments (higher variance in \(r_m\)) increase extinction risk, even if the average growth rate does not change (about 0.06 at variance 0.1 against about 0.42 at variance 0.5). This is why increasing environmental variability, for example more frequent extreme weather, is a conservation concern. 26.7 Solutions: Basic logistic population growth You were asked to use the Excel sheet to explore the logistic growth model by changing its parameters and examining the two graphs. 26.7.1 Graph 1: Population size through time Step 1 (default settings: Initial N = 10, \(r_m\) = 0.8, \(K\) = 200). The maximum population size is the carrying capacity, \(K = 200\). The population grows quickly at first and then slows as it approaches \(K\), giving an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve. It reaches about 99% of \(K\) after around 9 time steps. Step 2 (\(K\) = 300). The maximum population size increases to 300, but the time taken to approach it stays roughly the same (around 10 time steps). \(K\) sets where the population ends up. It does not change how fast it gets there. Step 3 (\(r_m\) = 0.4). The population grows more slowly and takes roughly twice as long to approach \(K\) (around 18 time steps rather than 9). The time taken to approach \(K\) is related to \(r_m\): as you increase \(r_m\) this time decreases, and halving \(r_m\) roughly doubles it. Step 4 (\(r_m\) = 1.8). The population overshoots the carrying capacity (to about 218), then oscillates around \(K\) with damped oscillations that gradually converge on \(K\). It is a common misconception that \(K\) is the maximum population size. When \(r_m\) is markedly greater than 1, the population grows so fast that it can exceed \(K\). This means that if a population has even a moderate population growth rate and density dependence, it can fluctuate in numbers without any extrinsic factor (like weather) acting. Step 5 (higher \(r_m\)). As you increase \(r_m\), the nature of the oscillations changes. In fact, this is predictable: \(r_m < 1\): the population approaches \(K\) smoothly. \(1 < r_m < 2\): damped oscillations of decreasing amplitude around \(K\). \(2 < r_m < 2.449\): a stable 2-point limit cycle, in which the population bounces between two values around \(K\) (e.g. \(r_m\) = 2.1 or 2.4). \(2.449 < r_m < 2.57\): the cycle doubles to 4 points (e.g. \(r_m\) = 2.5), then 8 points, and so on (period doubling). \(r_m > 2.57\): the population fluctuates chaotically, with no repeating pattern (e.g. \(r_m\) = 2.8, 2.9 or 3.0). Within the chaotic region there are narrow windows of regular cycles (for example a 3-point cycle near \(r_m = 2.83\)), but you are unlikely to hit one by chance. \(r_m\) above 3 (e.g. 3.1): the population overshoots so far that a later time step gives \(N \leq 0\) (with Initial N = 10 and \(K\) = 200, at \(t = 4\)), i.e. extinction. In the spreadsheet this shows up as negative population sizes, which are a mathematical artefact of the model. At exactly \(r_m\) = 3.0 the population stays positive and chaotic. So yes, there is a limit to how high \(r_m\) can be. Step 6 (sensitivity). When \(r_m\) is high (\(> 2.57\)) the dynamics are chaotic, and the population becomes extremely hard (in practice impossible) to predict. Changing \(r_m\) from 2.8 to 2.81, or changing the initial population size by 1, produces trajectories that soon become completely different. Because a change this small could simply be measurement error, this would cause big problems for a population manager. Many pest species have very high population growth rates, for example outbreak insects such as locusts and some forest moths. High growth rates with density dependence are one reason why it can be hard to predict when the next pest outbreak will happen (real outbreaks are also driven by weather and other external factors). Chaos is not the same as randomness. The model contains no random element: run it again with exactly the same parameters and you get exactly the same trajectory. The unpredictability comes from extreme sensitivity to the starting conditions and parameter values. 26.7.2 Graph 2: Per capita growth rate vs. population size Step 1. The per capita growth rate declines linearly as population size increases. It crosses the x-axis (population size) at \(K\) (here, 200) and crosses the y-axis at \(r_m\) (here, 0.8). Step 2 (\(K\) = 300). The x-axis intercept moves to 300. The y-axis intercept stays at \(r_m\), so the line becomes shallower. The line always crosses the x-axis at \(K\), whatever the growth rate. Step 3 (\(r_m\) = 1.8). The y-axis intercept rises to 1.8 and the line becomes steeper, but it still crosses the x-axis at \(K\) = 200. Step 4. The two parameters control the two intercepts: \(r_m\) sets the y-axis intercept (the per capita growth rate of a very small population) and \(K\) sets the x-axis intercept (the population size at which per capita growth is zero). The slope of the line is \(-r_m/K\). 26.7.3 Reflection Step 5. The two graphs are different views of the same model. As the population in Graph 1 approaches \(K\), the per capita growth rate in Graph 2 approaches zero, so population growth slows and levels off. When \(N\) is above \(K\), the per capita growth rate is negative and the population shrinks. For exponential growth, the per capita growth rate does not depend on population size, so the equivalent of Graph 2 would be a horizontal line at \(r_m\). Graph 1 would show unlimited, ever-accelerating (J-shaped) growth with no levelling off. 26.8 Solutions: Deeper into logistic growth 26.8.1 Relationship between Logistic and Exponential growth equations The logistic growth equation simplifies to become the exponential growth equation if you set \(K\) to be infinite (\(\infty\)). The simplification goes like this: \(\frac{dN}{dt}=r_m N\left(1-\frac{N}{K}\right)\) \(\frac{dN}{dt}=r_m N\left(1-\frac{N}{\infty}\right)\) \(\frac{dN}{dt}=r_m N\left(1-0\right)\) \(\frac{dN}{dt}=r_m N \times 1\) \(\frac{dN}{dt}=r_m N\) This simplification also works with the discrete version of the equation used in the Excel workbook, \(N_{t+1}=N_{t}+r_{m} N_{t}\left(1-\frac{N_{t}}{K}\right)\), which becomes \(N_{t+1}=N_{t}+r_{m} N_{t}\). The discrete version uses the same \(r_m\) but applies it once per whole time step. It is therefore an approximation of the continuous model: a small population is multiplied by \(1 + r_m\) each time step rather than by \(\lambda = e^{r_m}\). The approximation is good for small \(r_m\) and poor for large \(r_m\). This is why the discrete logistic model can overshoot \(K\), oscillate and become chaotic at high \(r_m\), while the continuous logistic model always approaches \(K\) smoothly. 26.8.2 Task 1: Type of dynamics depends on \(r_m\) As you increase \(r_m\), the dynamics of the population change. At low \(r_m\) (\(< 1\), e.g. 0.8) population size (\(N\)) simply converges smoothly on the carrying capacity, \(K\). As \(r_m\) increases (\(1 < r_m < 2\), e.g. 1.2 or 1.8) you will see damped oscillations, whereby \(N\) overshoots \(K\) and then oscillates and converges to \(K\). Then (\(2 < r_m < 2.57\)) you will see stable cycles where the population size oscillates around \(K\) indefinitely. Between 2 and 2.449 (e.g. 2.4) these are 2-point cycles, where \(N\) bounces between two values. Between 2.449 and 2.57 they are 4-point, then 8-point (and so on) cycles. Above \(r_m \approx 2.57\) (e.g. 2.7) the dynamics are chaotic: they never repeat and are unpredictable in practice. The critical values of \(r_m\) that define the type of dynamics are fixed: if we know \(r_m\) we can predict the type of dynamics. The type of dynamics depends only on \(r_m\), not on \(K\) or starting population size (\(N_0\)) (as long as \(0 < N_0 < K\)). 26.8.3 Task 2: Per capita growth rate vs. population size (Figure 2) The line crosses the x-axis at \(K\) and the y-axis at \(r_m\). The y-intercept is the per capita growth rate of a very small population, which is the maximum per capita growth rate \(r_m\). The x-intercept is the population size at which per capita growth is zero, which is the carrying capacity \(K\). The slope of the line is \(-r_m/K\). Increasing \(r_m\) raises the y-intercept and makes the line steeper. Increasing \(K\) moves the x-intercept to the right and makes the line shallower. For \(r_m = 1.5\) and \(K = 250\), your sketch should be a straight line falling from 1.5 on the y-axis to 250 on the x-axis. Having some information about the parameters therefore allows you to sketch the dynamics. Conversely, if you have a graph showing aspects of the population dynamics, you can work out the parameters of the logistic equation. 26.8.4 Task 3: Population growth rate vs. population size (Figure 3) The population growth rate is zero (\(dN/dt = 0\)) at \(N = 0\) and at \(N = K\). At \(N = 0\) there are no individuals to reproduce. At \(N = K\) the per capita growth rate is zero (Figure 2), so births balance deaths. Between these two points \(dN/dt\) is positive, and above \(K\) it is negative (the population shrinks). The curve is a parabola because \(dN/dt\) is the population size multiplied by the per capita growth rate: \(dN/dt = N \times r_m\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right) = r_m N - \frac{r_m}{K}N^2\). When \(N\) is small there are few individuals, so growth is slow even though each individual reproduces quickly. When \(N\) is close to \(K\) there are many individuals, but each reproduces slowly. Growth is fastest in between, at exactly \(N = K/2\), where \(dN/dt = r_m K/4\). Changing \(K\) moves the peak (always to \(K/2\)). Changing \(r_m\) changes the height of the peak, but not its position. The peak of this curve is the maximum sustainable yield (MSY): the largest number of individuals that could be harvested each time step without the population declining. For \(r_m = 0.8\) and \(K = 200\), MSY = \(0.8 \times 200/4 = 40\) individuals per time step, achieved by holding the population at \(N = 100\). Harvesting at exactly MSY is risky because \(r_m\) and \(K\) are only estimates and vary between years. If the true MSY is lower than estimated, or the population falls below \(K/2\), the harvest exceeds what the population can replace and the population declines further. 26.8.5 Task 4: Comparison with exponential growth For exponential growth, population size is unlimited and will grow exponentially if \(r_m > 0\) (or \(\lambda > 1\)). Logistic growth always shows some kind of limit (smooth convergence, damped oscillation, cycles or chaos), as the population size is attracted to \(K\) in some way. The equivalent figures for exponential growth are: Fig 1 (\(N\) vs. \(t\)): a J-shaped curve that accelerates without levelling off. Fig 2 (per capita growth rate vs. \(N\)): a horizontal line at \(r_m\). The per capita growth rate is constant and unaffected by \(N\), unlike the negative slope of the logistic model. Fig 3 (\(dN/dt\) vs. \(N\)): a straight line through the origin with slope \(r_m\). The more individuals there are, the faster the population grows, unlike the logistic parabola. In the Exponential worksheet the parameter labelled “r_m intrinsic growth rate” (0.1) is applied once per time step, \(N_{t+1} = N_t(1 + 0.1)\), so it acts as the per-step rate \(R_m\) (geometric growth with \(\lambda = 1.1\)). \(dN/dt\) increases linearly with \(N\) (Figure 3) but exponentially with time. 26.8.6 Task 5: Time lag Time-lagged density dependence results in oscillations. With the default \(r_m = 0.6\), the ordinary logistic model converges smoothly on \(K\). With a 1-step lag, the population overshoots \(K\) and then shows damped oscillations. At \(r_m\) above about 1 (e.g. 1.2), the oscillations become sustained cycles. This happens because the population responds to its density one time step ago. It keeps growing after it has passed \(K\), and keeps declining after it has fallen below \(K\). The lecture’s thresholds for lags (\(r_m\tau < e^{-1}\) smooth, up to \(\pi/2\) damped, above that cycles with a period of about \(4\tau\)) apply to the continuous-time lag model. In this discrete version with a 1-step lag the approach is smooth only for \(r_m\) below about 0.25, oscillations are damped between about 0.25 and 1, and above 1 there are sustained cycles with a period of about 6 to 7 time steps (7 at \(r_m = 1.2\), where \(N\) cycles between about 67 and 647 with \(K = 400\)). The message is the same: lags cause overshoot and cycles. Therefore, if we see oscillations in population dynamics, they could be due to a high \(r_m\) value or to lagged density dependence. Time lags make populations harder to predict and manage, because the population’s response to a change (e.g. a harvest or a cull) is delayed. 26.8.7 \(N_{t+1}\) vs. \(N_t\) Because \(N_{t+1} = N_t + dN/dt\), a plot of \(N_{t+1}\) against \(N_t\) is also a parabola: it is the Figure 3 parabola with the line \(N_{t+1} = N_t\) added to it. It passes through the origin and crosses the line \(N_{t+1} = N_t\) at \(N_t = 0\) and \(N_t = K\). These are the equilibria, where \(dN/dt = 0\) and the population does not change from one time step to the next. How steeply the parabola crosses the line at \(K\) depends on \(r_m\). This slope determines whether the population approaches \(K\) smoothly, oscillates, or behaves chaotically. The slope at \(K\) is \(1 - r_m\): for \(r_m < 1\) it is between 0 and 1 and the population approaches \(K\) smoothly; for \(1 < r_m < 2\) it is between \(-1\) and 0 and the population overshoots and oscillates back towards \(K\) (damped oscillations); for \(r_m > 2\) it is steeper than \(-1\), so \(K\) is unstable and the population cycles or behaves chaotically. This one rule explains all the dynamics in Task 1. 26.8.8 Chaotic dynamics Chaotic dynamics are deterministic in the sense that if you have the same initial conditions you will get the same results (dynamics). However, small changes in any parameters (\(N_0\), \(K\), or \(r_m\)) will lead to very different dynamics. In that sense, because of measurement error, the population dynamics would be very hard to predict in practice. 26.9 Solutions: Life tables and survivorship types The take home messages for this exercise are that life tables are a rich source of information on the life history of a population or species. From a simple accounting of survivors and fertility at each age we can obtain information about the “shape” of the survivorship trajectory: do most deaths happen early or late? Is mortality risk constant with age? We can also calculate measures including life expectancy, generation time, \(R_0\) and population growth rate. You should know what these measures mean. Life table. For the cohort in the Life table sheet: \(R_0 = \sum l_x m_x = 4.06\) daughters per female, so the population is growing. \(T = \sum x l_x m_x / R_0 = 15.35/4.06 = 3.78\) years. \(r_c = \ln(R_0)/T = \ln(4.06)/3.78 = 0.37\) per year (\(\lambda \approx e^{r_c} = 1.45\)). The exact intrinsic rate of increase from the Euler-Lotka equation is \(r_m = 0.41\) (\(\lambda = 1.50\)): the capacity for increase, \(r_c\), slightly underestimates \(r_m\) when generations overlap. Life expectancy at birth is \(e_0 = 3.76\) years. It rises to \(e_1 = 4.14\) years: once the risky first year is survived, an individual can expect to live longer than a newborn. \(p_x\) and \(q_x\) for each age, e.g. \(p_2 = 254/298 = 0.852\) and \(q_2 = 0.148\); \(q_9 = 0.88\) (only 5 of 43 nine-year-olds survive to age 10). Declining force of selection (optional task). Adding one daughter at age \(x\) (ages 1 to 10) raises \(R_0\) by exactly \(l_x\): by 0.70 (17%) at age 1, 0.60 (15%) at age 2, 0.13 (3%) at age 8 and 0.01 (0.2%) at age 10. Population 1 is Type I (\(q_x\) rises with age, from 0.02 to over 0.6); Population 2 is close to Type II (\(q_x\) stays roughly between 0.25 and 0.4, so \(\ln(l_x)\) falls in a nearly straight line); Population 3 is Type III (\(q_x\) falls from 0.73 in the first year to about 0.1 in old age). The completed Excel spreadsheet is here. 26.9.1 Answers to the questions 1. What are the three main types of survivorship curves, and which organisms typically exhibit each type? Type I curves show high survival in early life and high mortality at older ages (e.g. humans in developed countries, zoo and domestic animals). Type II curves show roughly constant mortality throughout life (e.g. many small birds). Type III curves show high juvenile mortality, followed by lower mortality for the few that survive the vulnerable early period (e.g. many fish and trees). 2. What does a net reproductive rate (\(R_0\)) of less than 1 signify for a population? On average, each female is replaced by fewer than one daughter over her lifetime, so the population is declining. 3. How does the shape of a survivorship curve reflect trade-offs in life history strategies, typically? Type I curves suggest heavy investment in each offspring, with low juvenile mortality: typical of species with few offspring and much parental care. Type III curves reflect species that produce many offspring but give each one little care, leading to high early mortality. 4. How is survivorship (\(l_x\)) different from survival probability (\(p_x\))? Survivorship (\(l_x\)) is the proportion of newborns that survive from birth to age \(x\). It is cumulative across all the age classes up to \(x\), starts at \(l_0 = 1\) and can only fall with age. Survival probability (\(p_x\)) is the probability that an individual alive at age \(x\) survives to age \(x+1\). It measures survival over a single time step, and can rise or fall with age. The two are linked: \(l_{x+1} = l_x \times p_x\). In the worked example, \(l_2 = 0.4\) and \(p_2 = 0.25\), so \(l_3 = 0.4 \times 0.25 = 0.1\). 5. How does altering reproduction or survival/mortality at different ages affect \(R_0\) and population growth rate? Changes early in life have a larger effect on \(R_0\) and population growth rate than changes later in life, because fewer individuals survive to experience late-life changes (adding one daughter at age \(x\) raises \(R_0\) by \(l_x\)). This is the declining force of selection. 6. Two populations have the same \(R_0\), but one has a shorter generation time. Which grows faster per year, and why? The one with the shorter generation time. \(R_0\) is growth per generation, and \(r_c = \ln(R_0)/T\) is (approximately) growth per year, so a shorter \(T\) means the population multiplies by \(R_0\) more often. For example, with \(R_0 = 2\): \(T = 1\) year gives \(r_c = 0.69\) per year; \(T = 2\) years gives \(r_c = 0.35\) per year. 7. The probability of dying in a year, \(q_x\), can never be greater than 1, but the force of mortality, \(\mu_x\), can. Why? \(q_x\) is a probability over an interval, so it lies between 0 and 1. \(\mu_x\) is an instantaneous rate per individual still alive (like a speed), so it has no upper limit. For a rate that is constant over a year, \(q_x = 1 - e^{-\mu_x}\): at low mortality \(q_x\) is close to \(\mu_x\), but as \(\mu_x\) increases, \(q_x\) approaches 1 without reaching it (e.g. \(\mu_x = 2\) gives \(q_x = 0.86\)). 26.10 Solutions: Matrix population modelling The main take home messages for this class are that you should: (1) understand, and be able to draw or interpret, a life cycle diagram; (2) be able to (roughly) parameterise a model shown in the life cycle diagram, remembering that a reproduction entry must include the survival needed for newborns to be counted at the next census; (3) be able to write out a matrix model (the square of numbers) for a given life cycle diagram (and vice versa); (4) understand how population projection works, and therefore be able to interpret a figure or description showing a population projection; (5) understand what an elasticity matrix tells us (the relative influence of a proportional change in each transition on population growth), and how it differs from sensitivity (the effect of an absolute change); (6) understand the logic of in silico experiments (changing the matrix and comparing \(\lambda\)) to investigate management options. 26.10.1 Model answers for the matrix modelling practical Does the starting population matter? The early (transient) dynamics depend strongly on the starting population structure, and the lines may zigzag or even decline temporarily. Eventually the lines become parallel and straight on the log scale, with the same slope as before. The slope is the same because the long-term growth rate (\(\lambda\)) depends only on the matrix, not on the starting population. The gaps between the lines are also the same, because the stage proportions converge to the same stable stage distribution. Starting structure affects the short term, but not the long-term growth rate or structure (given constant vital rates). An evolutionary experiment (homework). For the example matrix, \(\lambda = 1.346\). A mutant that has one extra baby as an adult (fecundity 8 to 9) but lower juvenile-to-adult survival (0.10 to 0.08) has \(\lambda = 1.295\), so the mutant has lower fitness and would not spread: the small loss of juvenile survival outweighs the extra baby. If juvenile-to-adult survival only falls to 0.09, the mutant’s \(\lambda\) is 1.3466, almost exactly the same as the original (1.3458), so selection on this trade-off would be very weak. Juvenile-to-adult survival has the highest elasticity in this matrix, which is why a small proportional cost there matters so much. Your own organism will give different numbers, but the logic is the same: compare \(\lambda\) for the original and mutant matrices. Question 1. On a log scale, straight lines mean the population is growing (or shrinking) exponentially at a constant rate, i.e. the growth rate has stabilised at \(\lambda\) once the transient phase has passed. Question 2. Elasticity measures the proportional change in \(\lambda\) caused by a small proportional change in each matrix element. It identifies which transitions have the greatest influence on population growth. If adult survival has the highest elasticity, conservation might focus on protecting adults (e.g. habitat protection, reducing human-induced mortality). If juvenile survival has a high elasticity, efforts might target juveniles (e.g. habitat restoration or predator control). Managers can then allocate limited resources to where they are likely to matter most, bearing in mind that high elasticity does not mean a rate is easy to change in practice. Question 3. Key assumptions include: constant vital rates (no environmental variation from year to year); no density dependence (vital rates do not depend on population size); a closed population, with no immigration or emigration; all individuals within a stage are identical; only females are modelled, and there is no shortage of mates; a fixed time step (here one year) with the census at a fixed point in the annual cycle. Several of these are shared with the exponential/geometric growth models. 26.11 Solutions: Pre- and Post-reproduction census Why A1 and A2 give the same \(\lambda\). Both give \(\lambda = 1.0703\) (to 4 decimal places), and they are exactly identical, not just equal to rounding error. Both matrices have the same characteristic equation, \(\lambda^3 = p_0 p_1 m_2 \lambda + p_0 p_1 p_2 m_3\): each term is one route from birth to reproduction (survive to age 2 and breed, or survive to age 3 and breed), and each route contains the same survival and reproduction terms in both census types. The net reproductive rate is also the same in both: \(R_0 = p_0 p_1 m_2 + p_0 p_1 p_2 m_3 = 0.54 + 0.648 = 1.188\). Census timing only changes when we count the population (and so which age classes are in the matrix), not what the animals do, so it cannot change how fast the population grows. What does change is anything that depends on the classes counted: the stable age distribution (post-breeding: 74% newborns of age 0; pre-breeding: 43% age 1, with no newborns counted), the reproductive values and the sensitivities. A2 vs A3. The matrices differ only in the top row (the fertilities): A2 has \(m_2 p_0 = 0.6\) and \(m_3 p_0 = 1.2\), whereas A3 has \(m_2 p_1 = 2.7\) and \(m_3 p_2 = 3.6\). In A3, first-year survival \(p_0\) appears nowhere in the matrix: it was removed from the sub-diagonal (correctly) but never added to the fertilities. So every newborn is effectively assumed to survive its first year, and \(p_0 = 0.2\) is the lowest survival rate in the whole life cycle. Instead, the parent’s survival (\(p_1\) or \(p_2\)) is counted twice: once on the sub-diagonal and once in the fertility. The result is \(\lambda = 1.864\) instead of 1.070: a rapidly growing population instead of a slowly growing one. (The mistaken matrix also gives \(R_0 = 4.374\) instead of 1.188.) Changing a survival probability. The correct conversion always agrees, whatever values you use, because the characteristic equations are identical. The error from the mistake depends on which parameter you change: Change \(\lambda\) for A1 and A2 \(\lambda\) for A3 (mistake) Error None (\(p_0 = 0.2\), \(p_1 = 0.9\)) 1.070 1.864 0.79 \(p_1 = 0.7\) 0.969 1.562 0.59 \(p_1 = 0.5\) 0.850 1.266 0.42 \(p_0 = 0.5\) 1.548 1.864 0.32 Lowering \(p_1\) shrinks the error a little, because \(p_1\) is counted twice in A3, but the error stays large (at \(p_1 = 0.5\) the correct matrices say the population is declining, while the mistake says it is growing by 27% per year). Changing \(p_0\) shows what really drives the error: A3 does not respond to \(p_0\) at all (its \(\lambda\) stays at 1.864), and the error shrinks as \(p_0\) gets closer to 1. The mistake is equivalent to assuming that all newborns survive their first year, so it does the most damage in species with low first-year survival, which is most birds, mammals, fish and plants. 26.12 Solutions: Life Table Response Experiments Predicting the contributions. Each contribution is (treatment element − reference element) × (sensitivity at the midpoint matrix). Sensitivities are always positive here, so the sign of each contribution is the sign of the difference in the element: Element Difference (treatment − reference) Sensitivity at midpoint Contribution Juvenile stasis (top left) 0 0.336 0 Fertility (top right) 1.3 − 2.3 = −1.0 0.208 −0.208 Juvenile → adult (bottom left) 0.2 − 0.5 = −0.3 1.071 −0.321 Adult survival (bottom right) 0.7 − 0.6 = +0.1 0.664 +0.066 The largest difference in an element is in fertility, but the largest contribution is from maturation (juvenile → adult), because \(\lambda\) is about five times more sensitive to maturation than to fertility. Checking the sum. The contributions sum to −0.463, while the observed difference is \(\lambda_{\mathrm{treat}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{ref}} = 0.992 - 1.451 = -0.460\). They are close but not identical, because the LTRE is a linear approximation: it assumes \(\lambda\) changes in a straight line with each element, with the slope (sensitivity) taken from the midpoint matrix, whereas in reality the sensitivities change as the elements change. Changing one element of A_treat. For example: Treatment fertility 1.8 instead of 1.3: the fertility difference halves (−0.5 instead of −1.0), so the fertility contribution roughly halves, to −0.098. The maturation and adult survival contributions change slightly (−0.345 and +0.065), because the midpoint matrix, and therefore the sensitivities, have changed. The sum is −0.378 (observed \(\Delta\lambda\) = −0.380). Treatment maturation 0.4 instead of 0.2: the maturation difference falls from −0.3 to −0.1, so its contribution drops to −0.096, and fertility (−0.239) becomes the largest contribution. The sum is −0.270 (observed \(\Delta\lambda\) = −0.270). In both cases the element you changed shows the biggest change in contribution, and the change can be explained as (new difference) × (sensitivity), with small knock-on changes in the other contributions because the sensitivities are recalculated at the new midpoint matrix. Interpretation. The Location B population has a lower \(\lambda\) (0.99, slowly declining) than Location A (1.45) mainly because fewer juveniles survive and mature into adults; lower fertility is the second most important reason; and slightly higher adult survival at Location B partly offsets these. Negative contributions lower \(\lambda\) at Location B relative to Location A, positive ones raise it. Why LTRE alone does not tell a manager what to target. LTRE is retrospective: it explains an observed difference in \(\lambda\) that has already happened. A contribution is large if the element did differ a lot between the populations and/or if \(\lambda\) is sensitive to it. A vital rate can make a large contribution because it varied a lot for reasons managers cannot influence (e.g. spring weather), and a rate with a high sensitivity (here juvenile stasis, 0.336) can make no contribution at all because it did not differ. To ask what would happen if a vital rate were changed, use prospective tools (sensitivity, elasticity, in silico experiments), together with knowledge of which rates can realistically be changed, by how much, and at what cost. 26.13 Solutions: How many eggs should a bird lay? You can find a completed Excel spreadsheet here. The expected numbers of surviving chicks for clutches of 1 to 10 eggs are 0.9, 1.7, 2.46, 2.8, 2.5, 1.8, 1.54, 1.2, 0.9 and 0.5, so the optimum is 4 eggs. Laying 10 eggs gives only 0.5 surviving chicks on average. The take-home message is that the trade-off between number of eggs and juvenile survival leads to an optimum number of eggs required to maximise reproductive success (i.e. number of surviving chicks). You can move this optimum if the trade-off is changed. For example, if you increase survival of the chicks from larger clutches, then the optimum number of eggs will increase. This fact reminds us that the environment (e.g. predation risk and resource abundance) will be an important factor in determining the evolution of life history parameters (like average number of babies). 1. What is Lack’s hypothesis? Does the big bird’s optimum support it, given that most big birds lay 3 eggs? Lack’s hypothesis is that clutch size evolves to the number from which, on average, the most young survive. For the big bird that is 4 eggs (4 × 0.70 = 2.8 surviving chicks). But most big birds lay only 3 eggs (2.46 surviving chicks), one fewer than the single-season optimum, so these data do not fully support Lack’s hypothesis. Many real birds also lay slightly fewer eggs than the clutch that produces the most young in one season. Question 3 shows one reason why. 2. A good food year. Survival in clutches of 5 or more rises by 0.2, so the expected numbers of surviving chicks for 4 to 8 eggs become 2.8, 3.5, 3.0, 2.94 and 2.8. The optimum rises to 5 eggs. When food is plentiful, chicks in larger broods are fed better and survive better, so larger clutches pay. Many birds do lay more eggs in good years or rich habitats. 3. A cost to the parents. Parent survival is 0.72, 0.64, 0.56, 0.48 and 0.40 for 1 to 5 eggs, so the expected number of breeding seasons (counting this season as the first) is 3.57, 2.78, 2.27, 1.92 and 1.67. Multiplying by the surviving chicks per season gives lifetime totals of 3.21, 4.72, 5.59, 5.38 and 4.17. The optimum falls from 4 eggs to 3 eggs, which is exactly the clutch that most big birds lay. Lack counted the young raised in a single season. Once the cost to the parents’ future breeding is included, the best clutch is smaller than the one that produces the most surviving young in one season. This is the argument behind the kestrel brood manipulations in the lecture: parents given extra chicks paid for them later. Neal’s chapter Evolution of Life Histories discusses the same idea. 4. Egg number versus egg size. You would need a second relationship, describing how the size of an egg (or offspring) affects its chance of survival, and a fixed amount of resources to divide among the eggs, so that more eggs means smaller eggs. The best combination is the one that maximises the number of surviving offspring (Smith & Fretwell 1974). 26.14 Solutions: Trade-offs and the force of selection Simulate this by adding 1 to fertility (mx) at age 1 (the benefit), but setting Survival to 0 in the age-25 row, so that all die before age 25 (the cost). Questions The declining force of selection. A change in survival or reproduction at age \(x\) only affects the individuals still alive at that age, so its effect on fitness shrinks as survivorship (\(l_x\)) falls and as less of the lifetime’s reproduction remains. Selection therefore acts strongly on early life and weakly on late life. Early reproduction, and genes with early benefits and late costs, are favoured, and senescence can evolve. Age-related disease in humans. Many diseases of old age (e.g. many cancers, heart disease, dementia) have their main effects after most reproduction has happened, so selection against them is weak. Harmful mutations with late effects can build up (mutation accumulation), and some genes that cause late disease may have been favoured for their early benefits (antagonistic pleiotropy). Predation risk. Where predation is high, an individual is unlikely to survive to old age whatever it invests in its body, so resources spent on maintenance and repair are less valuable. Selection should favour putting more into early reproduction and less into maintenance. Survival after reproduction. Older individuals can raise inclusive fitness by helping relatives. Post-reproductive killer whale females lead their groups to salmon when food is scarce, and in humans, grandmothers can improve their grandchildren’s survival (the grandmother hypothesis). 26.15 Solutions: Matrix Population Models (MPMs): Projection and Simulation The simulation results below come from 2,000 replicates per scenario. They are stochastic: in another set of runs, probabilities of extinction typically change by about ±0.02 and medians by a few individuals. Your results with 200 replicates will vary more. The deterministic \(\lambda\) values are exact. Exercise 1: Projection interval. \(\Delta t = 1\) year means that one multiplication by \(\mathbf{A}\) moves the population forward by one year, so every entry in the matrix is a rate per year (e.g. \(P_A = 0.8\) is the probability that an adult survives one whole year). With \(\Delta t = 1\) month, \(P_A\) would be the probability of surviving one month. If mortality is spread evenly through the year, the monthly survival that gives the same annual survival is \(0.8^{1/12} = 0.982\). \(F_A\) would be the number of new juveniles (counted at the next monthly census) per adult per month. For most animals and plants this is not constant: reproduction happens in a breeding season, so \(F_A\) would be zero in most months, and the matrix would have to change from month to month (a seasonal model). Growth probabilities (\(G_J\), \(G_S\)) would also have to be per month. For example: the species is short-lived or breeds several times a year (insects, rodents), so a year is too coarse; you want to model seasonal events such as a breeding season, a hunting season or a harsh winter; or management (e.g. culling) happens at a particular time of year.
