The average adult survival is unchanged, but the spread of outcomes is wider, because in a run of bad years all adults have low survival at the same time. Variation between years also tends to reduce the long-run growth rate slightly (the stochastic growth rate \(\lambda_s\) is lower than the \(\lambda\) of the average matrix); see the chapter “Stochastic population growth”. 26.16 Solutions: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium Answers to the Hardy-Weinberg questions. Remember the basic formulas: \(p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1\) and \(p + q = 1\) \(p\) = frequency of allele A (where there is dominance, A is the dominant allele) \(q\) = frequency of allele a \(p^2\) = frequency of homozygous AA individuals \(q^2\) = frequency of homozygous aa individuals \(2pq\) = frequency of heterozygous Aa individuals A general rule for all these problems: keep full precision in your calculator and round only at the end. Rounding \(p\) or \(q\) early can change the final answer in the second decimal place, which matters on a multiple-choice exam. 26.16.1 Problem 1 The frequency of allele a: Since \(p + q = 1\) and \(p = 0.8\), \(q = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2\). The expected genotype frequencies: AA = \(p^2 = 0.8 \times 0.8 = 0.64\) (64%) Aa = \(2pq = 2 \times 0.8 \times 0.2 = 0.32\) (32%) aa = \(q^2 = 0.2 \times 0.2 = 0.04\) (4%) Check: \(0.64 + 0.32 + 0.04 \approx 1\) (displayed frequencies are rounded). The phenotype frequencies if A is completely dominant over a: Both AA and Aa individuals show the dominant phenotype, so its frequency is \(0.64 + 0.32 \approx 0.96\) (96%). Only aa individuals show the recessive phenotype, so its frequency is 0.04 (4%). Heterozygotes cannot be distinguished from AA homozygotes by phenotype alone. There are approximately 8 times as many heterozygotes as recessive homozygotes. 26.16.2 Problem 2 Assuming HWE at birth, the frequency of SS babies is \(q^2 = 0.09\). The HbS allele frequency is therefore \(q = \sqrt{0.09} \approx 0.3\), and the HbA allele frequency is \(p = 1 - q \approx 0.7\). The expected frequency of carriers (AS) is \(2pq \approx 2 \times 0.7 \times 0.3 \approx 0.42\), so about 42% of babies are expected to be carriers. 26.16.3 Problem 3 The allele frequencies: 200 diploid individuals carry 400 allele copies. Each AA individual carries two copies of A and each Aa individual carries one, so the number of A copies is \(2 \times 90 + 70 = 250\). \(p = 250 / 400 \approx 0.625\), and \(q = 1 - p \approx 0.375\). (Check: the number of a copies is \(2 \times 40 + 70 = 150\), and \(150 / 400 \approx 0.375\).) The expected counts under HWE are the expected frequencies multiplied by the sample size, 200: Genotype Observed Expected under HWE AA 90 \(p^2N \approx 0.625^2 \times 200 \approx 78.125\) Aa 70 \(2pqN \approx 2 \times 0.625 \times 0.375 \times 200 \approx 93.75\) aa 40 \(q^2N \approx 0.375^2 \times 200 \approx 28.125\) Comparison: There are fewer heterozygotes than expected, and more of both homozygotes: a heterozygote deficit. There are 70 observed heterozygotes, compared with 93.75 expected. Possible explanations include inbreeding or other non-random mating, combining partly separated subpopulations (the Wahlund effect), selection against heterozygotes, or genotyping errors. The comparison alone does not identify a cause. In the Inbreeding lecture you will quantify departures in heterozygosity with \(F = 1 - H_o/H_e\), here \(1 - 0.35 / 0.46875 \approx 0.253\). Optional extension: the \(\chi^2\) test. Genotype \(O\) \(E\) \((O - E)^2/E\) AA 90 78.125 1.8 Aa 70 93.75 6.02 aa 40 28.125 5.01 Total 200 200 \(\chi^2 \approx 12.84\) There are three classes, so you might expect \(3 - 1 = 2\) degrees of freedom (one is lost because the expected counts are forced to add up to the sample size, 200). But we also estimated one parameter, \(p\), from the data to calculate the expected counts, which costs another degree of freedom. So df \(= 3 - 1 - 1 = 1\). Using the unrounded statistic, \(\chi^2 \approx 12.84\) gives \(P \approx 0.0003\). The test provides evidence of a departure from HWE at the 5% significance level. It does not identify the cause. 26.16.4 Problem 4 Since white is recessive (genotype bb), \(q^2 = 0.4\). Take the square root: \(q = \sqrt{0.4} \approx 0.632456\). Then \(p = 1 - q \approx 0.367544\). Keep full precision for subsequent calculations; the displayed values are rounded. The heterozygote frequency is \(2pq \approx 2 \times 0.367544 \times 0.632456 \approx 0.464911\), or about 46.5%. The homozygous dominant frequency is \(p^2 \approx 0.367544^2 \approx 0.135089\). Extension: Brown butterflies have genotype BB or Bb, so their frequency is \(1 - 0.4 = 0.6\). The proportion of brown butterflies that are heterozygous is \(2pq / (1 - q^2) \approx 0.464911 / 0.6 \approx 0.774852\), or about 77.5%. Compare this with 46.5% in the population as a whole: the denominator here includes only brown butterflies. 26.17 Solutions: Gene pool model 26.17.1 Part 2: Drift through time How does population size affect the variation through time in allele frequencies? Why do you see these patterns? Each generation is a random sample of 2N alleles from the previous gene pool. The smaller the sample, the larger the sampling error, so allele frequencies fluctuate much more in small populations. With N = 20 the frequency of A wanders widely and usually hits 0 or 1 within 100 generations; with N = 1000 it stays close to 0.5 over the same period. With 20 individuals, does A always end up fixed, or is it sometimes lost? Both happen, roughly equally often. Drift has no direction: starting from 0.5, A is fixed in about half of the populations and lost in the other half. When the population size is large (say 1000), can you see an allele become fixed within 100 generations? Could it happen if you ran the simulation for much longer? Not within 100 generations: in large populations drift is slow. But yes, given enough time an allele is eventually fixed even in a large population. Starting from p = 0.5, the expected time until one allele is fixed is about \(2.8N\) generations (more precisely \(-4N[p \ln p + q \ln q]\)), i.e. around 55 generations for N = 20 and around 2,800 generations for N = 1000. With n_gen <- 3000 you will see fixation in some runs but not all. (This is a different quantity from the time a new mutation that does fix takes to get there, which is about \(4N\) generations, as in the mutation lecture.) 26.17.2 Part 3: Many populations What proportion of the populations have lost one of their alleles by generation 100 for N = 20, 100 and 1000? Roughly 90% for N = 20, around 10 to 15% for N = 100, and essentially none for N = 1000 (exact numbers will vary between runs). Of the populations where one allele was fixed, in what proportion was it A? Does this depend on population size? About half, at every population size. Starting from a frequency of 0.5, A and a have equal chances of being fixed. So what does population size change: which allele is fixed, or how quickly variation is lost? How quickly. For a neutral allele, the probability of fixation equals its starting frequency whatever the population size. Population size determines the speed of drift: small populations lose variation quickly, large populations slowly. Are rare alleles more or less likely to be lost than common ones? More likely. A neutral allele at frequency \(p\) is eventually fixed with probability \(p\) and lost with probability \(1 - p\). So an allele at 0.1 is lost 90% of the time, and an allele at 0.75 is lost only 25% of the time. Compare the proportion of populations where the new allele was fixed with \(1/(2N)\). What does this tell you about the fate of most new mutations? With N = 20, a single new copy starts at \(1/40 = 0.025\), and roughly 2 to 3% of populations end up fixed for it (with 200 replicates you might see anywhere from about 0.5% to 5%). This matches \(1/(2N)\). Most new neutral mutations, about 39 out of 40 here and 1,999 out of 2,000 in a population of 1000, are lost by chance, usually within a few generations. This is the “Model 1” result from the lecture. Can you find a simple rule linking starting frequency to probability of fixation? The probability of fixation of a neutral allele equals its starting frequency. For example, one run of the template with 200 replicates gave 0.095 for \(p_0 = 0.1\), 0.26 for 0.25 and 0.675 for 0.75. Your numbers will differ by a few percentage points from run to run (the standard error with 200 replicates is about 0.02 to 0.03), but they cluster around the starting frequency. Going further: does the simulated decline in \(H_e\) agree with \(H_t = H_0 (1 - 1/(2N))^t\)? Yes. Averaged over 500 populations, \(H_e\) declines smoothly and follows the theoretical curve closely. With N = 20 it falls by 2.5% per generation, from 0.5 to about 0.04 after 99 generations of drift (theory: \(0.5 \times (1 - 1/40)^{99} = 0.041\); repeated runs of the code give between about 0.03 and 0.05). Individual populations are noisy, which is why the average is needed. Note that \(H_e\) declines in every case, even though the average allele frequency across populations stays at about 0.5: drift removes variation within populations while creating differences between them. 26.17.3 Part 4: Bottlenecks and founder effects How does a genetic bottleneck influence the genetic composition of the population? During the bottleneck the population is small, so drift is strong and allele frequencies can change a lot in a few generations. One allele may be lost altogether. The genetic composition after the bottleneck is therefore often quite different from that before it, and genetic diversity is usually reduced. How might a genetic bottleneck affect the probability that one allele is fixed and the other lost? It greatly increases it. With 10 individuals for 21 generations, roughly half of all runs lose one allele during the bottleneck, whereas in a constant population of 1000 this essentially never happens within 100 generations. Which allele is fixed is still a matter of chance. What happens to allele frequency after the bottleneck? Does the population “recover” its original allele frequency? No. Once the population is large again, drift is weak, so the frequency stays close to wherever the bottleneck left it. Nothing pulls it back to 0.5. If an allele was lost, it cannot return without mutation or migration. The effects of a bottleneck persist long after the population has recovered in size. Does the severity of the bottleneck (i.e. length and population size) matter? Yes. Smaller and longer bottlenecks cause larger changes and a higher chance of losing an allele. Each generation of the bottleneck multiplies heterozygosity by \(1 - 1/(2N)\), so 21 generations at N = 10 leaves about \((1 - 1/20)^{21} \approx 0.34\) of the original heterozygosity, whereas 21 generations at N = 100 leaves about 0.90. Optional: effective population size. What are the arithmetic and harmonic means of N over the bottleneck run? The arithmetic mean is 792.1 (79 generations at 1000 and 21 at 10), but the harmonic mean is only about 46 (1 / mean(1 / N) = 45.9). So the population loses diversity as if it had about 46 individuals throughout, not 790. A few generations at small size dominate the long-term effect of drift: \(N_e\) is much closer to the smallest population sizes than to the average. (Compare the lecture’s example, 1,000, then 10, then 1,000, which gives \(N_e \approx 29\) against an arithmetic mean of 670.) This is one reason why \(N_e\) is usually much smaller than the census size in real populations. Founder effects: how different are the new populations from the source population, and from each other? How would this change with 50 founders? Although the source population has a frequency of 0.5, the founded populations typically range from about 0.3 to 0.7, and some are further off. They also differ from each other. The spread reflects sampling only 20 alleles (standard deviation about \(\sqrt{0.5 \times 0.5 / 20} \approx 0.11\)). With 50 founders (100 alleles), the spread is smaller (standard deviation about 0.05), so the new populations resemble the source population more closely. 26.17.4 Conclusions What are the limitations of this simulation? The model makes the assumptions listed at the start, and each is a limitation: No selection: in reality, some alleles affect survival or reproduction. No mutation: new alleles never arise, so variation can only be lost. In real populations, mutation replenishes variation (mutation-drift balance). No migration: real populations exchange genes, which can restore lost alleles and counteract drift. Random mating: real populations may show inbreeding or assortative mating. Constant population size and non-overlapping generations: real populations fluctuate in size and have overlapping generations, and not all individuals breed. The relevant population size for drift (the effective population size) is usually much smaller than the census size. One locus with two alleles: real genomes have many loci, many with more than two alleles, and linked loci are not independent. Why is genetic diversity important to a population, for example in a conservation context? Genetic diversity is crucial for the adaptability and survival of a population. In a conservation context: Resilience to diseases: a genetically diverse population is less likely to be wiped out by a single disease, as some individuals might have resistance. Adaptation to changing environments: diversity provides the variation that selection needs if conditions change. Reduced inbreeding: high genetic diversity reduces the chance that individuals inherit two copies of harmful recessive alleles, which lowers fitness (inbreeding depression). Long-term survival: small populations lose diversity through drift, which is why conservation programmes try to keep populations large and connected. Can you think of real-life scenarios where understanding gene pool dynamics would be valuable? Conservation biology: managing captive breeding and reintroductions to retain genetic diversity, or moving individuals between isolated populations (“genetic rescue”). Medical genetics: founder effects explain why some genetic disorders are unusually common in particular populations descended from small founding groups. Agriculture: maintaining diversity in crop and livestock breeding programmes. Challenge: how could you simulate a population that is steadily shrinking through time? Inside the loop, set the population size as a function of the generation number before sampling, for example pop_size <- round(1000 * 0.95^(i - 1)) for a 5% decline per generation, or pop_size <- max(10, 1000 - 10 * i) for a linear decline to a floor of 10. As the population shrinks, drift becomes stronger and the frequency of A fluctuates more and more until one allele is fixed. 26.18 Solutions: Neutral or adaptive evolution in humans There is no single correct ordering: groups can defend different placements. What matters is the reasoning. A good answer for each trait goes through three questions: Is the variation heritable? If not, the trait cannot evolve by drift or by selection. How strongly does the trait affect survival or reproduction, in this environment? Strong effects put the trait at the selection end of the continuum; weak or no effects put it at the drift end. Is the population large enough for that selection to beat drift? Selection is effective only when \(s\) is clearly larger than about \(1/(2N_e)\). The take-home message is that whether a trait evolves adaptively or neutrally depends on the environment (and on population size), not just on the trait. A useful comparison is antibiotic resistance in bacteria. With antibiotics, resistance genes are strongly selected for. Without antibiotics they are not neutral: resistance usually has a fitness cost, so it is usually selected against (which is why resistance can decline when an antibiotic is used less, although compensatory mutations can reduce the cost). The environment can change both the strength and the direction of selection. Humans are still evolving. In industrialised societies such as Denmark, almost everyone survives to adulthood, so selection now acts mainly through differences in the number of children people have (and the age at which they have them), rather than through survival. Studies of modern populations have measured selection on traits such as height, age at first birth and cholesterol in exactly this way (e.g. Byars et al. 2010, PNAS; Sanjak et al. 2018, PNAS). 26.18.1 Suggested placements Trait Heritable variation? As foragers In Denmark today Where on the drift-selection continuum, and why Metabolic efficiency Yes, partly Probably important: food was often scarce, so efficient use of energy aided survival and reproduction Weak, possibly reversed: food is abundant, and very efficient storage may contribute to obesity and type 2 diabetes Towards selection as foragers; weaker today. Debatable: the “thrifty gene” idea has weak direct genetic support Eyesight acuity Partly Probably important for hunting and gathering Weak: glasses correct poor vision Towards selection as foragers; near the drift end today Height Yes, highly heritable (many genes) Probably selected, but the optimum depends on environment Modern studies detect weak selection, mainly through number of children, with differences between the sexes (e.g. Stulp et al. 2015, Proc. R. Soc. B) In the middle: weak but measurable selection Birth canal (pelvic) shape Yes Stabilising selection: the canal must allow birth of a big-brained baby while still allowing efficient walking Weaker: caesarean section reduces the cost of a mismatch Selection keeps the shape within limits, but much of the variation between populations fits drift during serial founder effects as humans spread out of Africa (Betti & Manica 2018, Proc. R. Soc. B; see the drift lecture). A good example of both acting together Resistance to bubonic plague Yes, partly (immune genes) Weak: plague is a disease of dense agricultural and urban societies, not of small foraging groups Weak: plague is rare and treatable Strongly selected in medieval Europe during the Black Death (Klunk et al. 2022, Nature, immune genes such as ERAP2), not in foragers and not today. A clear example of environment-dependent selection Eye colour Yes, strongly (mainly OCA2/HERC2) Probably weak, except perhaps through mate choice Weak Blue eyes rose quickly in Europe, which suggests some selection (on pigmentation in general, or sexual selection), but drift and “hitch-hiking” with selected pigmentation alleles are possible. Debatable Earwax type (ABCC11) Yes, simple (one DNA change) Unknown; a selection signal exists, perhaps linked to sweat or body odour Weak Some evidence of past selection (Ohashi et al. 2011, Molecular Biology and Evolution), but the trait it acted on is uncertain. Debatable Face symmetry Weakly; much is developmental noise Possibly via mate choice, as a cue of health Weak Mostly not heritable, so it can evolve little by either process Examples of traits that cannot evolve much because their variation is mostly not heritable: the fine texture of the iris, the detailed ridge minutiae of fingerprints (these differ between identical twins), and much of the variation in face symmetry. 26.18.2 Gene flow between populations Differences that gene flow would erase: neutral variation (most DNA differences, and traits close to the drift end of the continuum). Very few migrants per generation are enough to prevent large neutral differences between populations, which is one reason why most human genetic variation is found within populations rather than between them. Differences that local selection can maintain against gene flow: traits where the selection coefficient is large compared with the migration rate. Examples are skin pigmentation (UV intensity differs with latitude), lactase persistence (dairying history), and HbS and Duffy-null (malaria). These traits vary between populations much more than most neutral markers do. 26.18.3 Discussion questions Traits categorised differently between the two societies. Eyesight acuity and metabolic efficiency were probably more strongly selected in foraging societies than in Denmark today. Others (e.g. plague resistance) were strongly selected only in particular historical environments. In both settings, though, selection still acts, especially through the number of children. Traits with little heritable variation. Iris texture, fingerprint detail and much of face symmetry: they can vary a lot but cannot evolve much by either process. Gene flow vs local selection. See above. Preconceived notions. Common ones are that “evolution has stopped in humans” (it has not), that “every trait is an adaptation” (many traits drift, and some barely vary heritably), and that “drift only matters in tiny populations” (it acts in every finite population; it dominates whenever \(s\) is small compared with \(1/(2N_e)\)). Other traits to add. Sense of smell (many olfactory receptor genes have become non-functional, consistent with relaxed selection and drift), lactase persistence, skin pigmentation, blood groups, alcohol flush reaction, ability to taste bitter compounds (TAS2R38), and wisdom teeth are all good candidates with some genetic evidence. 26.19 Solutions: Heritability Predictions. If offspring were on average exactly like their parents, the slope would be 1 (\(h^2 = 1\)). If offspring were no more like their own parents than like any other bird, the line would be flat (slope 0, \(h^2 = 0\)). A slope in between means that offspring resemble their parents partly: on average, they lie part of the way between their parents’ value and the population mean (“regression towards the mean”). After downloading the file, you can read in the data like this (or use the “Import Dataset” wizard in RStudio): pop_1 <- read.csv("data/heritability_pop1.csv") Plot the data and fit the model as follows. # Plot the relationship plot(pop_1$Midparent_value, pop_1$Offspring_value, xlab = "Mid-parent wing length (mm)", ylab = "Offspring wing length (mm)") # Fit the linear regression model mod1 <- lm(Offspring_value ~ Midparent_value, data = pop_1) # Add the regression line to the plot abline(mod1, col = "red") # Summarise the model, and get the 95% confidence interval of the slope summary(mod1) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = Offspring_value ~ Midparent_value, data = pop_1) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -4.7982 -1.0608 0.0486 1.1242 3.2360 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) ## (Intercept) 20.1633 9.1736 2.198 0.0303 * ## Midparent_value 0.7342 0.1220 6.018 3.06e-08 *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ## ## Residual standard error: 1.663 on 98 degrees of freedom ## Multiple R-squared: 0.2699, Adjusted R-squared: 0.2624 ## F-statistic: 36.22 on 1 and 98 DF, p-value: 3.059e-08 confint(mod1)[2, ] ## 2.5 % 97.5 % ## 0.4921315 0.9763443 What is your estimate of \(h^2\), and how precise is it? The heritability is the slope of the relationship: 0.73, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.49 to 0.98. This is a high heritability, but the interval is wide: anything from about 0.5 to nearly 1 is compatible with the data. (The data were simulated with a true value of 0.70.) What does this heritability tell us about the variation in wing length in this population? What does it not tell us about any one bird? About 73% of the variation in wing length among birds in this population is due to additive genetic differences between them. It does not mean that 73% of any one bird’s wing length “comes from its genes”: heritability describes variation in a population, not individuals. It also applies only to this population in this environment. What else might explain the remaining variation? The remaining 27% or so is due to differences in the environment that the birds grew up in (for example food supply, brood size, weather during the nestling period, parasites), to chance events during development, to measurement error, and to any non-additive genetic effects (dominance and interactions between genes). Calculate \(V_P\) and \(V_A\). VP_1 <- var(pop_1$Offspring_value) VA_1 <- coef(mod1)[2] * VP_1 VP_1 ## [1] 3.7496 VA_1 ## Midparent_value ## 2.753098 \(V_P\) = 3.75 mm² and \(V_A = h^2 \times V_P\) = 0.73 × 3.75 = 2.75 mm². We use the offspring values for \(V_P\) because each offspring value is a single bird’s phenotype. Each mid-parent value is the mean of two birds, and averaging two independent values halves the variance, so var(pop_1$Midparent_value) (here 1.88 mm²) is only about half of \(V_P\). Predict the response to selection with \(S\) = 2 mm. \(R = h^2 S\) = 0.73 × 2 = 1.47 mm: the mean wing length of the next generation should increase by about 1.5 mm. Do the two confidence intervals overlap? For this population the heritability is 0.18 (95% confidence interval -0.09 to 0.46), much lower than in population 1 (0.73). The two confidence intervals only just fail to overlap, and the interval for population 2 includes zero. That does not mean that \(h^2\) is zero: the data are compatible with anything from no additive variance up to about 0.46. (The true values used in the simulation were 0.18 and 0.70.) Note how wide both intervals are, even with 100 families: heritability is hard to estimate precisely, and estimates from a few dozen families are very uncertain. Report the uncertainty, not just the slope. (Non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals are a conservative, informal check, not a formal test of the difference.) Compare \(V_A\) and \(V_P - V_A\) between the populations. Population 1 Population 2 \(h^2\) 0.73 0.18 95% confidence interval 0.49 to 0.98 -0.09 to 0.46 \(V_P\) (mm²) 3.75 15.87 \(V_A\) (mm²) 2.75 2.91 \(V_P - V_A\) (mm²), an estimate of \(V_E\) 1.00 12.95 The estimates of the additive genetic variance are similar (both data sets were simulated with \(V_A\) = 2.8 mm²), but they are uncertain. Multiplying the confidence limits for \(h^2\) by \(V_P\) gives roughly 1.85 to 3.66 mm² in population 1 and -1.48 to 7.30 mm² in population 2 (a variance cannot really be negative; this just shows how wide the interval is). So these data alone cannot show that \(V_A\) is equal. The clear difference is in the phenotypic variance: population 2 is about four times as variable. Because we simulated the data, we know that all of the extra variance is environmental, so heritability is lower in population 2 not because it has less genetic variation, but because its environment is more variable. With real data, this would be the most likely explanation rather than a certainty. Either way, heritability is a property of a population in an environment, not of a trait. Can you suggest environmental differences that could explain this? Anything that makes the conditions in which chicks grow up more variable in population 2 would do it. For example: Food supply: in a patchy habitat, some territories are rich and others poor, so chicks in different nests get very different amounts of food. Weather: cold, wet spells during the nestling period reduce growth in some broods but not others, especially if breeding is spread over a long season. Brood size and competition: chicks in large broods get less food each. Parasites and disease: infection during growth reduces final size in some individuals. In each case \(V_E\) increases, so \(V_P\) increases and \(h^2 = V_A/V_P\) falls, even though \(V_A\) is unchanged. For the same selection differential, which population would respond faster to selection? Population 1. With \(S\) = 2 mm, \(R\) = 0.73 × 2 = 1.47 mm in population 1 but only 0.18 × 2 = 0.37 mm in population 2. In population 2, most of the difference between the selected parents and the rest of the population is environmental, and is not passed on. Can you think of any real-world applications where understanding heritability would be important? Agriculture: plant and animal breeding programmes use heritability to predict how fast yield, disease resistance or growth rate will respond to selection. Conservation biology: the heritability of traits linked to survival and reproduction (for example breeding time, or tolerance of heat) indicates how fast a population might adapt to environmental change. Fisheries and hunting: harvesting the largest individuals is a form of selection; heritability predicts how fast body size or age at maturity will evolve in response (compare the bighorn sheep example from the lecture). Medicine: heritability estimates indicate how much of the variation in a disease risk is genetic, which guides the search for the genes involved (but a heritable condition can still be prevented or treated by changing the environment). Violation of assumptions Shared environment, correct parentage and measurement accuracy are the three set in class; the others are the optional extension. Additive genetic effects: dominance and interactions between genes are not passed on predictably, so the slope estimates only the additive part; genotype-by-environment interactions mean that the estimate applies only to the environment studied. These limit what the estimate means, rather than making it too high or too low. No shared environment: if parents and offspring share a good or a poor territory, they resemble each other for non-genetic reasons, and \(h^2\) is overestimated. Cross-fostering removes this bias. Correct parentage: extra-pair paternity means that some chicks are not the offspring of their social father, which weakens the resemblance and underestimates \(h^2\). Linearity: if the relationship is curved (for example because of dominance, or because extreme parents produce offspring that do poorly), a straight line is a poor summary, with no fixed direction of error. Measurement accuracy: errors in measuring the parents make the slope shallower (heritability is underestimated); errors in the offspring add noise and widen the confidence interval. Random mating: if birds choose mates of similar size (assortative mating), the mid-parent values vary more than under random mating, but their covariance with the offspring rises in step, so the slope on the mid-parent value still estimates \(h^2\). This is an advantage of using both parents: the slope on a single parent would be steeper than \(h^2/2\), so doubling it would overestimate \(h^2\). Representative sample: it matters which birds are filtered. If selection acts on the offspring before they are measured (for example, only those that survived a harsh winter, with survival depending on wing length), the slope is too shallow and \(h^2\) is underestimated. Choosing parents on the basis of the trait does not bias the slope, although a narrower range of parents gives a less precise estimate. Independence: if the same parent appears in several families, or several chicks from one nest are entered as separate points, the data points are not independent and the confidence interval will be too narrow. 26.20 Solutions: Lotka-Volterra competition You can find a completed Excel spreadsheet here. The full answers from the worksheet are here. Brief answers are given below. They use Neal’s notation (Interspecific Competition): \(\alpha\) is the PDF’s \(\alpha_{12}\) (effect of species 2 on species 1) and \(\beta\) is the PDF’s \(\alpha_{21}\) (effect of species 1 on species 2). The general rule. Ask whether each species can invade when it is rare and the other species is at its carrying capacity: When species 2 is at \(K_2\), a rare species 1 experiences crowding equivalent to \(\alpha K_2\) of its own individuals. It can grow if this is less than its own carrying capacity: \(\alpha K_2 < K_1\), or \(\alpha < K_1/K_2\). On the isocline graph, this means \(K_2 < K_1/\alpha\). In the same way, a rare species 2 can grow when species 1 is at \(K_1\) if \(\beta K_1 < K_2\), or \(\beta < K_2/K_1\). On the isocline graph, \(K_1 < K_2/\beta\). Species 1 can invade? Species 2 can invade? Outcome (question) Yes No Species 1 excludes species 2 (Q1) No Yes Species 2 excludes species 1 (Q2) Yes Yes Stable coexistence (Q3) No No Either species can win, depending on the starting densities (Q4) Q1. For example \(R_1 = 0.25\), \(K_1 = 3000\), \(\alpha = 1.25\); \(R_2 = 0.5\), \(K_2 = 1000\), \(\beta = 0.5\); start \(N_1 = 50\), \(N_2 = 100\). Species 1 goes to 3000 and species 2 to zero (after 50 time steps the sheet shows about 2979 and 2.4). Species 1 can invade (\(\alpha = 1.25 < K_1/K_2 = 3\)) but species 2 cannot (\(\beta = 0.5 > K_2/K_1 = 0.33\)). This happens even though species 2 grows faster, starts larger and has the larger per capita effect (\(\alpha > \beta\)). Changing \(R\) or the starting numbers does not change the outcome. In ecological terms, species 1 can keep growing even when species 2 is at its own carrying capacity, but not the other way round. Q2. For example \(R_1 = 0.25\), \(K_1 = 3000\), \(\alpha = 2.25\); \(R_2 = 0.25\), \(K_2 = 2000\), \(\beta = 0.25\); start 50 and 50. Species 2 goes to 2000 and species 1 to zero, even though \(K_1 > K_2\): species 1 cannot invade (\(\alpha = 2.25 > K_1/K_2 = 1.5\)) but species 2 can (\(\beta = 0.25 < K_2/K_1 = 0.67\)). Q3. For example \(R_1 = 0.75\), \(K_1 = 2500\), \(\alpha = 0.75\); \(R_2 = 0.5\), \(K_2 = 2000\), \(\beta = 0.5\). Both species can invade (\(0.75 < 1.25\) and \(0.5 < 0.8\)), and the populations settle at \(N_1 = 1600\), \(N_2 = 1200\). You can check this with the equilibrium formulae \(N_1^* = (K_1 - \alpha K_2)/(1 - \alpha\beta)\) and \(N_2^* = (K_2 - \beta K_1)/(1 - \alpha\beta)\). The equilibrium is stable: starting from (1000, 1), (1, 1000), (500, 2500), (1000, 3000) or (250, 3000), the populations always return to (1600, 1200). The worksheet’s default values also give stable coexistence, at (720, 640). In ecological terms, each species limits its own growth more than it limits its competitor’s, once you allow for differences in carrying capacity. If the carrying capacities are similar, this means \(\alpha < 1\) and \(\beta < 1\): each individual competes more strongly with its own species than with the other species, for example because the two species partly use different resources (niche differences). Q4. For example \(R_1 = R_2 = 0.5\), \(K_1 = K_2 = 1000\), \(\alpha = \beta = 1.25\). Neither species can invade (\(1.25 > 1\)), so the isoclines cross at an unstable equilibrium, \(N_1 = N_2 = 444.4\). Starting at (50, 50) the populations go to this point and stay there, but whichever species starts larger wins: (100, 50) and even (445, 444) end at (1000, 0); (50, 100) and (444, 445) end at (0, 1000). The growth rates matter too: starting at (50, 50) with \(R_1 = 0.8\), \(R_2 = 0.4\), species 1 wins, and with the \(R\) values swapped species 2 wins. In ecological terms, each species affects the other more than it affects itself: interspecific competition is stronger than intraspecific competition, for example through interference or mutual predation. Fifth case. If the isoclines lie exactly on top of each other (\(K_1 = K_2/\beta\) and \(K_2 = K_1/\alpha\)), every point on the line is an equilibrium. For example, with identical species (\(\alpha = \beta = 1\), \(K_1 = K_2 = 1000\), \(R_1 = R_2 = 0.5\)), starting at (100, 300) the populations end at (250, 750) and starting at (300, 100) they end at (750, 250): they keep their starting ratio. So the basic model does not predict that identical species exclude each other; that conclusion comes from Gause’s experiments (see Neal, Interspecific Competition). Q5 (optional). (a) Rhizopertha and Oryzaephilus: both can invade (\(\alpha = 0.235 < K_1/K_2 = 0.75\); \(\beta = 0.12 < K_2/K_1 = 1.33\)), so they coexist, at \(N_1 = 233\), \(N_2 = 412\). Neal reports that this is what Crombie observed. (b) Tribolium confusum and T. castaneum: neither can invade (\(\alpha = 1 > 0.65\); \(\beta = 2.2 > 1.55\)), so the winner depends on the starting densities. With \(R_1 = R_2 = 0.5\), starting at (100, 20) T. confusum wins (220, 0), and starting at (20, 100) T. castaneum wins (0, 340). Park found the same in his experiments, with an “indeterminate zone” of starting densities where either species could win by chance. Note that comparing a coefficient with 1 is not enough when the carrying capacities differ. In Q1, species 1 wins even though \(\alpha = 1.25 > 1\), because its carrying capacity is three times larger. 26.21 Solutions: Lotka-Volterra predator-prey dynamics You can find a completed Excel spreadsheet here. The worksheet’s own answers are here. One of them is wrong: the answer to question 3 says that smaller values of \(f\) delay extinction and larger values hasten it. That is not what the spreadsheet does (see below). Use the answers here instead. All numbers come from the spreadsheet model (\(V_{t+1} = V_t + RV_t - aC_tV_t\), \(C_{t+1} = C_t + afV_tC_t - qC_t\), with populations not allowed to go below zero), with the default values \(R = 0.25\), \(a = 0.01\), \(f = 0.008\), \(q = 0.1\), starting at \(V = 1000\), \(C = 20\), copied down far enough to see the prey hit zero. In Neal’s notation, \(V = H\), \(C = P\), \(R = r\), \(af = c\) and \(q = d\). Change from default Time step at which the prey hit zero None 220 \(R\) = 0.15 / 0.4 416 / 55 \(q\) = 0.05 / 0.2 398 / 58 \(f\) = 0.004 / 0.006 / 0.010 / 0.012 / 0.016 129 / 173 / 200 / 203 / 154 \(a\) = 0.005 / 0.0075 / 0.015 / 0.02 78 / 122 / 257 / 175 R. A larger prey growth rate makes the system less stable: the cycles grow faster and extinction comes sooner. Faster prey growth allows faster predator growth, and each population responds one whole time step late, so the overshoot is bigger. q. Predators that starve faster also make the system less stable (extinction sooner); slower starvation delays it. With high \(q\) the predators crash when prey are scarce, so the prey recover to very high numbers; the predators then explode and wipe them out. f. The effect of conversion efficiency is not simple. From the default start, both the smallest (\(f = 0.004\)) and the largest (\(f = 0.016\)) values give the earliest extinction, and intermediate values the latest. The reason is that \(f\) only moves the predator isocline (\(V = q/(af)\): 2500 prey at \(f = 0.004\), 1250 at the default, 625 at \(f = 0.016\)). It does not change how fast the discrete model spirals outwards. What changes is how far the fixed starting point (1000, 20) is from the new equilibrium: the further away it is, the bigger the first cycle and the sooner the crash. If you start at the same relative position (80 % of the equilibrium numbers), \(f = 0.004\), 0.008 and 0.016 all give extinction at time step 220. a. The attack rate moves both isoclines (\(C = R/a\) and \(V = q/(af)\)), so its effect also depends on where you start: from the default start, both a much lower (\(a = 0.005\)) and a somewhat higher (\(a = 0.02\)) attack rate bring extinction forward, but \(a = 0.015\) delays it. Starting numbers. Yes. Starting exactly where the isoclines cross (\(V = 1250\), \(C = 25\)), nothing changes. The further from that point you start, the larger the cycles and the sooner the extinction. Ultimate outcome. In the spreadsheet, both species always go extinct in the end: the cycles grow until the prey hit zero, and then the predators starve. With the defaults this takes 220 time steps, longer than the 100 steps in the original sheet, but the growing cycles show it coming. This is caused by the discrete time steps (each population responds to the other one step late), not by the biology: in the continuous-time model the cycles keep the same size for ever (see the solutions to the continuous- and discrete-time R chapters). Near the equilibrium, the distance from the equilibrium grows by a factor of about \(\sqrt{1 + Rq}\) per time step. This contains \(R\) and \(q\) but not \(a\) or \(f\), which is why \(R\) and \(q\) have simple effects in the table and \(a\) and \(f\) do not. Real predator and prey populations rarely show either growing or perfectly constant cycles. Factors missing from the model include prey carrying capacity, refuges for the prey, predators that become satiated (a Type II functional response), alternative prey, predator interference or territoriality, spatial structure and environmental variation. Parts 2 to 4 of the worksheet add some of these: refuges stop the prey going extinct, and a prey carrying capacity turns the expanding oscillations into damped ones that settle at an equilibrium (Neal discusses this in Predator-Prey Interactions). 26.22 Solutions: Continuous-time Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model in R All numbers below come from the chapter code with the default parameters (\(R = 0.25\), \(a = 0.01\), \(f = 0.008\), \(q = 0.1\)), start \(V = 1000\), \(C = 20\), run to time 200, unless stated otherwise. 1. Oscillations Both populations cycle regularly and for ever. The prey peak first (at \(t \approx 13.7, 53.8, 93.9, \ldots\)) and the predators peak about a quarter of a cycle later (\(t \approx 22.4, 62.5, 102.6, \ldots\)). Prey increase while predators are scarce; predators then increase because food is plentiful; the larger predator population pushes the prey down; the predators then starve and decline, and the cycle repeats. With prey on the x-axis the orbit runs anticlockwise. Below the prey isocline (\(C < R/a = 25\)) prey increase (move right); above it they decrease (move left). To the right of the predator isocline (\(V > q/(af) = 1250\)) predators increase (move up); to the left they decrease (move down). Following these arrows round the four regions gives right, up, left, down: anticlockwise. 2. Neutral stability and starting numbers Starting exactly at \(V = 1250\), \(C = 25\) nothing changes: this is the equilibrium. Starting just next to it (\(V = 1300\), \(C = 25\)) gives a very small cycle (prey 1201 to 1300, predators 24.4 to 25.6), which does not grow or shrink. Further away, the cycles are bigger: from \(V = 2000\), \(C = 20\) the prey range is 632 to 2180; from \(V = 1000\), \(C = 40\) it is 475 to 2601 (predators 14 to 41). In every case the size of the cycle stays the same for the whole run: the oscillations neither grow nor die away. This is neutral stability: the model has no tendency to return to the equilibrium or to move away from it, so the size of the cycles is set entirely by where you start. The period changes a little with the size of the cycle: about 39.7 time units for the tiny cycle, about 40 at the default start, about 40.5 to 41.5 for the larger ones. For small cycles the period is \(2\pi/\sqrt{Rq} = 2\pi/\sqrt{0.025} \approx 39.7\). 3. Equilibrium and time-averages \(V^* = q/(af) = 0.1/(0.01 \times 0.008) = 1250\) and \(C^* = R/a = 0.25/0.01 = 25\). The populations never settle there, but mean(output_df$V) = 1250.6 and mean(output_df$C) = 25.01: the averages over the cycles equal the equilibrium (the small difference is because the run does not end at the end of a complete cycle). 4. Moving the isoclines Doubling \(R\) (to 0.5) raises the prey isocline to \(C = 50\) (more predators are needed to stop the prey growing). Doubling \(a\) (to 0.02) lowers the prey isocline to \(C = 12.5\) and moves the predator isocline left to \(V = 625\). Doubling \(f\) (to 0.016) moves only the predator isocline, to \(V = 625\). Doubling \(q\) (to 0.2) moves the predator isocline right, to \(V = 2500\). Because the starting point (1000, 20) is now a different distance from the new equilibrium, the cycles also change size. With \(R = 0.2\) and \(q = 0.12\) the equilibrium moves to \(V^* = 1500\), \(C^* = 20\). The run gives average prey 1511 and average predators 19.95. So killing both species increases the average number of prey and decreases the average number of predators. This is Volterra’s principle: an indiscriminate mortality factor (pesticide, fishing) can benefit the prey because it hits their predators. 5. Extinction and reality From \(V = 1000\), \(C = 100\) the predators fall to about 2.0 and the prey to about 8. In the model neither population can ever reach exactly zero (the growth rates are proportional to population size, so the populations approach zero but never reach it). In a real population, a handful of individuals, or a fraction of one, means extinction, and chance events (demographic stochasticity) would make it very likely. Unrealistic assumptions include: prey grow exponentially without predators (no carrying capacity); each predator eats in proportion to prey density without limit (no handling time or satiation, i.e. a Type I functional response); predator death rate is constant; no time lags, no refuges, no other prey or predators; individuals meet at random; populations are large enough to treat as continuous. Prey carrying capacity, predator satiation, refuges, alternative prey, spatial structure and environmental noise will all change the cycles: some damp them, others destabilise them, so real cycles are rarely neutrally stable. 26.23 Solutions: Discrete-time Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model in R All numbers below come from the chapter code with the default parameters (\(R = 0.25\), \(a = 0.01\), \(f = 0.008\), \(q = 0.1\)), start \(V = 1000\), \(C = 20\) and total_time = 300. The model is deterministic, so you should get exactly these numbers. Default run (\(\Delta t = 1\)). Instead of a closed loop, the phase plot spirals outwards: each cycle is a little larger than the one before. By the last cycle the prey reach about 16,000 and the predators about 230. The prey hit zero at \(t = 220\); after that the predators have nothing to eat and dwindle towards zero (about 0.05 by \(t = 300\)). The populations “react one step too late”: the change over each step is calculated from the numbers at the start of the step, so the prey keep growing for a whole step after predators have become numerous enough to stop them, and so on round the cycle. Smaller time steps. With \(\Delta t = 0.1\) the spiral still grows, but much more slowly: over 300 time units the prey stay between about 670 and 2120 and neither population goes extinct. With \(\Delta t = 0.01\) the orbit is almost closed (prey up to about 1850), very close to the continuous-time model (prey 812 to 1823). Small time steps are just a more accurate way of calculating the continuous model. Larger time step. With \(\Delta t = 2\) the spiral grows faster and the prey hit zero earlier, at \(t = 142\). Which parameters control the spiral? \(R\) and \(q\). Doubling \(R\) (to 0.5) brings the prey crash forward from \(t = 220\) to \(t = 64\); doubling \(q\) (to 0.2) brings it forward to \(t = 58\). Doubling \(a\) or \(f\) also changes the time of the crash from the default start (\(t = 175\) and \(t = 154\)), but only because the equilibrium moves and the start is then a different distance from it. If you start the same relative distance from the equilibrium (e.g. at 80 % of \(V^*\) and \(C^*\)), doubling \(a\) or \(f\) makes no difference (crash at \(t = 220\), as with the defaults), while doubling \(R\) (\(t = 79\)) or \(q\) (\(t = 132\)) still speeds it up. Why. Near the equilibrium, each step multiplies the distance from the equilibrium by about \(\sqrt{1 + \Delta t^2 R q}\). With the defaults this is \(\sqrt{1 + 0.025} \approx 1.012\), about 1 % growth per step. The factor contains \(R\), \(q\) and \(\Delta t\) but not \(a\) or \(f\), and it is always bigger than 1, so the discrete model always spirals out eventually; it gets closer to 1 (no growth, as in the continuous model) as \(\Delta t\) gets smaller. 26.24 Solutions: Game theory: Hawks and doves Your own class results will differ from year to year. A worked analysis of real class data (2022) is in the Results of the hawk-dove games chapter. Predictions before playing Game Two (new partner every round): with B = 4 and C = 3, Hawk earns more than Dove whatever the opponent plays (4 > 2 against a Dove, 0.5 > 0 against a Hawk), so theory predicts mostly Hawk play, and that more hawkish players earn more. Game One (same partner for 15 rounds): a good prediction is that Hawk play will be less common than in Game Two, and that pairs who settle into mutual Dove (2 each per round) will earn far more than pairs stuck in mutual Hawk (0.5 each per round). Taking turns (Hawk/Dove, then Dove/Hawk) also averages 2 per round each, so it is just as good as mutual Dove with these payoffs. In round 15 there is no future round in which to be punished, so theory predicts more Hawk play in the last round. (In practice people often keep cooperating; in the 2022 class, Hawk play in round 15 was no higher than average.) Did the % Hawk trend in Game One and Game Two match what you predicted? Compare your class’s charts with your predictions. In the 2022 class, neither game showed a trend in Hawk play across rounds (p = 0.9 for Game 1 and 0.72 for Game 2), and Hawk play was only slightly lower in Game 1 (0.62 vs 0.69 per player; not significant). A flat line does not mean nothing happened: many pairs settle on a pattern within the first few rounds and then keep to it. Did the total-benefit-vs-hawkishness pattern support the one-shot theory prediction (Hawk pays off best), or the repeated-game reciprocity argument (Dove pays off best when you keep meeting the same partner)? Both, depending on the game and on how you look at it. Within a pair in Game 1, the more hawkish player always earns at least as much as their partner, because Hawk earns more than Dove in every round against the same opponent. So comparing partners always favours Hawk. Across pairs in Game 1, more hawkish pairs earn less: escalation provokes escalation, and both players end up with 0.5 per round instead of 2. This supports the reciprocity argument (2022 class: pair mean payoff fell by about 2 per round from an all-Dove to an all-Hawk pair). In Game 2, more hawkish individuals earned more (2022 class: slope 1.21 per round, p = 0.006), as the one-shot theory predicts. Which game, if either, better matches what you’d expect from a species whose individuals encounter each other only once versus a species that lives in small, stable social groups? Game 2 is like a species in which individuals rarely meet the same opponent twice: the one-shot logic applies, and selection should favour Hawk when B > C. Game 1 is like a small, stable social group in which the same individuals meet repeatedly: restraint can pay because escalation is answered in later encounters (reciprocity, the “shadow of the future”). Being able to recognise individuals and remember past encounters is required for this. Did you or your partner take turns? What happened in round 15? Taking turns gives each player (4 + 0)/2 = 2 per round, exactly the same as mutual Dove, so it is a perfectly good way to cooperate in this game. (With Neal’s payoffs, which include a display cost, taking turns is actually better than mutual Dove.) In round 15, a player who has cooperated so far gains by switching to Hawk (4 instead of 2) because the partner cannot retaliate. If your class showed a jump in Hawk play in the last round, that is the end-game effect; if not, people cooperated beyond what strict theory predicts. What would happen if you increased or decreased the value of the benefit (B) relative to the cost (C)? Would that change which strategy dominates in a one-off encounter? Yes. Let p be the frequency of Hawks in the population (with no display cost, D = 0). The average payoffs are: Hawk: \(p\frac{B-C}{2} + (1-p)B\) Dove: \((1-p)\frac{B}{2}\) If B > C (as in the class game), Hawk always earns more than Dove, so Hawk is the ESS: a population of Hawks cannot be invaded by Doves. Making B larger relative to C only strengthens this. If C > B, Hawks do well when rare (they beat the Doves) but badly when common (they keep meeting and injuring each other), and Doves do the opposite. Neither pure strategy is stable. Setting the two payoffs equal and solving gives the mixed ESS: \[p^* = \frac{B}{C}\] Worked example: B = 4, C = 8. Then \(p^* = 4/8 = 0.5\). Check: Hawk earns \(0.5 \times (4-8)/2 + 0.5 \times 4 = -1 + 2 = 1\); Dove earns \(0.5 \times 4/2 = 1\). The payoffs are equal, so neither strategy can do better by becoming more common. If Hawks were more common than 0.5, Doves would earn more and increase, and vice versa. The more costly fighting is relative to the prize, the fewer Hawks there are at equilibrium (with B = 4: C = 5 gives \(p^* = 0.8\), C = 8 gives 0.5, C = 16 gives 0.25). Neal’s version, which includes a cost of display D for Doves, gives \(p^* = (B/2 + D)/(C/2 + D)\); with B = 50, C = 100 and D = 10 this is 7/12, the example used in the lecture. Note that the ESS is not the best outcome for the group: at the mixed ESS with B = 4, C = 8, everyone earns 1 per encounter, whereas a population of Doves would earn 2 each. A population of Doves cannot resist invasion by Hawks. Take-home messages: In a one-off contest with B > C, Hawk is the ESS, even though everyone would do better as Doves. When C > B, the ESS is a mix of Hawks and Doves with Hawk frequency p* = B/C. Repeated interaction with the same partner changes the incentives: escalation is answered in kind, so restraint can pay. 26.25 Solutions: The legend of Ambalappuzha You can find the completed Excel file here. How much rice? The 64 squares hold \(2^{64} - 1 = 1.84 \times 10^{19}\) grains of rice. At 25 mg (0.000025 kg) per grain, that is about \(4.6 \times 10^{14}\) kg (461 billion tonnes): hundreds of times the world’s annual rice production. Great tits (optional exercise). Each female lays about 6 eggs, so she produces about 3 daughters per year. We start with 100 females (one per breeding pair). If every female survives every year, and daughters breed the year after they hatch, each female this year becomes herself plus 3 daughters next year: \(F_{t+1} = F_t + 3F_t = 4F_t\), so \(\lambda = 4\). After 5 years there are \(100 \times 4^5 = 102{,}400\) females. If instead adults die after breeding once, only the 3 daughters per female are left next year, so \(\lambda = 3\) and after 5 years there are \(100 \times 3^5 = 24{,}300\) females. Either way, numbers explode within a few years. The answer depends strongly on the assumptions, which is the point of the discussion prompts: real great tits have far from 100% survival (most fledglings die in their first year), and density dependence (territories, food, nest sites) stops growth long before these numbers are reached. Take home messages: Exponential/geometric growth is extremely powerful and can very quickly lead to very large numbers. The multiplication rate, \(\lambda\), depends on both reproduction and survival, and on assumptions about the life cycle (e.g. whether adults survive to breed again). 26.26 Solutions: From population biology to fitness The matrix model with a trade-off (increased juvenile survival, but old-adult survival reduced to 0.05) looks like this. A3 <- matrix(c(0.00, 4.00, 2.00, 0.11, 0.80, 0.00, 0.00, 0.10, 0.05), byrow = TRUE, nrow = 3) eigs(A3)$lambda We can compare the \(\lambda\) value from this model (1.187) with the original one (1.166) to ask whether the large cost is worth paying for the small benefit. It turns out that it is. You can then ask how MUCH cost would be worth bearing, by repeating the exercise and slowly reducing old-adult survival until you reach the original \(\lambda\) value. You should find that the cost can be huge, and still worth bearing. In fact, you could reduce old-adult survival to 0 and it is still worth doing (\(\lambda = 1.186\))! You can even reduce old-age adult reproduction without much effect on fitness: with old-adult survival at 0.05 and old-adult reproduction set to 0, \(\lambda\) is 1.175, still above the original. HOWEVER, changes to prime-age adults are much more important. With juvenile survival at 0.11, you can only reduce prime-age adult survival to about 0.76 (from 0.8) before the cost is not worth bearing (population growth rate falls below that of the baseline model). Thus, old-age costs are “worth it” while prime-age costs are much more important. This finding is central to the evolution of senescence and life span, which you met in the practical Trade-offs and the declining force of selection (the declining force of selection). 26.27 Solutions: From plain English to a matrix model Matrix. With stages hatchling (H), juvenile (J) and adult (A), and the census once a year: Fertilities (top row): juveniles 1, adults 3 hatchlings per year (the text says these are hatchlings, so we treat them as already counted at the next census). Hatchling to juvenile: 0.20. Juveniles survive with probability 0.70 (30% mortality). Of the survivors, 5% stay juvenile and 95% become adults: stasis \(0.70 \times 0.05 = 0.035\), growth \(0.70 \times 0.95 = 0.665\). A_hawk <- matrix(c(0.00, 1.000, 3.00, 0.20, 0.035, 0.00, 0.00, 0.665, 0.82), byrow = TRUE, nrow = 3) popdemo::eigs(A_hawk, what = “lambda”) # 1.172 pr <- popdemo::project(A_hawk, vector = c(1000, 150, 5), time = 20) Assumption about juvenile stasis. “5% of juveniles fail to transition” can also be read as 5% of all juveniles: stasis 0.05 and growth 0.65 (so survival is still 0.70). This gives \(\lambda = 1.171\), almost the same as 1.172, so the assumption barely matters here. What matters is that you state it, and that stasis plus growth for juveniles does not exceed their survival of 0.70. After the transient period (the starting population is dominated by hatchlings), the projection settles into steady exponential growth, reaching about 14,300 individuals after 20 years. 26.28 Solutions: Continuous traits from discrete genes Shape of the histograms. Both the classroom histogram and the R histogram should be roughly bell-shaped and centred near 47.5 (35 + 12.5). With only 30 individuals the classroom histogram will be lumpy; with 100 it is smoother. With genes alone, every value is a whole number, so the distribution has many classes but is still discrete. Does the environment make the trait continuous? Yes. After adding the environmental effect, the values are no longer whole numbers, and the gaps between the genetic classes are filled in: individuals with the same number of ON genes now differ slightly, and individuals with different numbers of ON genes overlap. This is exactly Neal’s point about wheat kernel colour: with little environmental effect there are only a few discrete classes, but environmental (and other small genetic) effects blur them into a continuous distribution. Variances. In the example run shown in the chapter, var(trait_value) is 6.29 (expected 6.25) and var(trait_value_env) is 8.24 (expected \(6.25 + 2.25 = 8.5\)). These values vary a lot between runs: with 100 individuals, the genetic variance typically lies between about 4.7 and 8.0, and the phenotypic variance between about 6.3 and 11.1. Heritability. All the genetic variance here is additive, so \(h^2 = V_A/V_P = 6.25/8.5 = 0.74\). With an environmental standard deviation of 4, \(V_E = 16\), \(V_P = 22.25\) and \(h^2 = 6.25/22.25 = 0.28\). The genes are exactly the same, but the more variable environment lowers the heritability, just as for the two bird populations in the heritability practical.

27 Results of the hawk-dove games This section summarises class outcomes for Game 1 (same partner) and Game 2 (changing partners). Use it to compare with your own observations and results. These results are from the 2022 class, who played both games. 27.1 Game 1: the same partner for 15 rounds The average hawkishness in Game 1 (the proportion of rounds in which Hawk was played) was 0.62 (averaged over players), but players differed. Is this more spread than we would expect by chance? The lecture showed that a mixed ESS can be reached in two ways: a mixture of pure Hawks and pure Doves, or every individual playing Hawk with the same probability. If every player had played Hawk with the same probability (0.62) in each of their 15 rounds, chance alone would give a standard deviation in hawkishness among players of about 0.13. The observed standard deviation is 0.22, so these players really did differ in strategy: some were consistently hawkish, others consistently dovish. Did the level of hawkishness change as the game went on? No: there is no detectable trend across the 15 rounds (p = 0.9). Nor was there a jump in Hawk play in the final round (round 15: 0.62), even though there was no next round in which to be punished. 27.1.1 Does being hawkish pay with a fixed partner? With the payoffs used in this game (B = 4, C = 3), a single, anonymous encounter has a simple answer. Because B > C, Hawk beats Dove regardless of what your opponent plays (Hawk-vs-Dove gives 4 > 2 for Dove-vs-Dove, and Hawk-vs-Hawk gives 0.5 > 0 for Dove-vs-Hawk), so the one-shot ESS here is pure Hawk, not an intermediate mix. (The stable mix of Hawks and Doves, with Hawk frequency p* = B/C, only arises when the cost of fighting, C, exceeds the value of the resource, B: the opposite of the situation here. With B > C, the payoff ranking Hawk-vs-Dove > Dove-vs-Dove > Hawk-vs-Hawk > Dove-vs-Hawk has the same structure as the classic Prisoner’s Dilemma, with Hawk playing the role of “Defect”.) This has an important consequence: within a pair, the more hawkish player always earns at least as much as their partner, because in every round Hawk earns more than Dove against the same opponent. So asking “who won in each pair?” always favours Hawk. The interesting question for Game 1 is a different one: do pairs that play Hawk a lot end up worse off, both of them, than pairs that hold back? To answer it, we look at each pair as a unit: the pair’s mean hawkishness (both players’ cards) against the pair’s mean payoff per player per round. The relationship is strongly negative (slope -1.96 per round): pairs that escalated a lot got stuck in Hawk-Hawk rounds worth only 0.5 each, while pairs that held back earned close to the 2 per round of mutual Dove. (The data file records players rather than pair IDs, so most pairs appear twice in this plot, once from each partner’s records, and the two points usually lie on top of each other. Because of this duplication we do not quote a p-value.) That is the pattern expected if hawkishness provokes hawkishness: with a fixed partner, playing Hawk does not make you lose to your partner, but it lowers what both of you earn. Reciprocity in repeated games This idea is not covered in the lecture, but it explains why repeated play can change the outcome. When you meet the same partner again and again, what you do now affects how they treat you later. This is sometimes called the shadow of the future. A simple strategy that does well in repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma games is tit-for-tat: cooperate (Dove) in the first round, then copy whatever your partner did in the previous round. Tit-for-tat is never the first to escalate, punishes escalation immediately, and forgives as soon as the partner returns to Dove (Axelrod & Hamilton 1981, Science 211: 1390-1396). Two caveats. First, in a game of known, fixed length, defecting (Hawk) in the last round always pays, because there is no future to protect, so cooperation is not guaranteed in theory (in practice people often cooperate anyway). Second, with the class payoffs, taking turns (Hawk/Dove, then Dove/Hawk) pays exactly as well as mutual Dove, 2 per round each, so there is more than one way to cooperate. 27.2 Game 2: a new partner every round The students were asked to compete against a new opponent every round. The idea was that this would make it much harder to learn your opponent’s strategy, and harder to come to an agreement that reduces aggression. The average hawkishness in Game 2 was 0.69, a little higher than in Game 1 (0.62). Again, hawkishness did not change systematically over the game (p = 0.72). Finally, we can look at what the best strategy is in Game 2. Here each point is one player, and we use the mean payoff per round, because a few players missed some rounds. The best strategy has changed: now the more hawkish players earned more (slope 1.21 per round, p = 0.006). This matches the one-shot theoretical prediction much better than Game 1 did. In Game 2 you faced a new partner every round, so there was no opportunity to build reciprocity, and no way to be “punished” for playing Hawk against the same individual again. With no repeated interaction, no “shadow of the future”, the game reduces to the simple one-shot logic, and since B > C, Hawk pays off best. In this setting we might expect natural selection to drive towards the evolution of more aggressive individuals. 27.3 Comparing the two games Our hypothesis was that, compared with Game 2, players in Game 1 would play Hawk less often and earn more per round. In this class, hawkishness was slightly lower in Game 1 (0.62 vs 0.69 per player; p = 0.34), but mean payoff per round was not higher (1.25 vs 1.4; p = 0.36). Neither difference is statistically significant, so with one class of 18 players we cannot reject the null hypothesis. Remember too that Game 2 was always played after Game 1, so any difference between the games could also reflect learning or fatigue. What did differ clearly between the games was which strategy paid: within Game 1, pairs that held back did best, while within Game 2, individual Hawks did best. Put together, the two games illustrate a general result from game theory: repeated interaction with the same partner can favour restraint even in a game where Hawk wins any single encounter, while anonymous, one-off interactions favour the individually dominant strategy. This is one reason why reputation, memory, and repeated encounters matter so much for the evolution of cooperation, both in nature and in human societies. Think about what this means in terms of human cooperation and conflict avoidance. Can you see the value of understanding your opponent/competitor?

28 Exponential growth in detail 28.1 Discrete time model 28.2 Real-World Application: Breeding Pairs of Merlin (Falco columbarius) 28.3 Continuous time model

28 Exponential growth in detail One of the foundational concepts in population dynamics is the exponential growth model. This model is a simplified representation of how populations grow when resources are not limiting. While it’s rare for populations to experience uninhibited growth for extended periods, understanding this basic model is crucial for understanding more complex dynamics that include factors like resource limitations, predation, and disease. In this chapter, we will explore the mathematical framework that describes exponential growth in both discrete and continuous time settings. We will introduce key parameters such as the per-capita birth rate, death rate, and intrinsic rate of increase. We will also demonstrate how to apply these models using R programming, offering a practical dimension to these theoretical concepts. Learning outcomes: Understand the fundamental equations that underpin exponential growth in populations. Differentiate between discrete and continuous time models. Interpret the role and significance of various parameters in exponential growth models. Use R programming to analyse exponential growth scenarios with real data. 28.0.1 Nomenclature Symbol Meaning Alternatives \(R_m\) Per capita rate of increase per time step, per capita population growth rate (discrete time) \(R\), \(r_d\) (Gotelli) \(r_m\) Intrinsic rate of increase (continuous time) \(r\). From a life table, \(r_m \approx \ln(R_0)/T\), which Neal calls \(r_c\), the capacity for increase \(\lambda\) Population growth rate, population multiplication rate \(R_0\) Net reproductive rate: the expected number of female offspring per female, per generation (\(\sum l_x m_x\)) Not the same as the “basic reproduction number” of epidemiology, which uses the same symbol 28.1 Discrete time model We’ll first look at discrete population growth, which is the population growth that is considered to grow over distinct time steps (e.g., 1 year intervals). This is also called Geometric Population Growth. A population at time \(t\) has size \(N\): \(N_t\). After one time interval, there will be some births (\(B\)), and some deaths (\(D\)). Births will have the effect of increasing the population size at time \(t+1\) while deaths will decrease population size. The population at the next time step (\(N_{t+1}\)) is thus: eqn. 1. \(N_{t+1} = N_t + B - D\) We can think about the birth/death processes on a per-individual basis, and use per-capita birth rate (\(b\)) and per-capita death rate (\(d\)). We can think of \(b\) as the average number of offspring produced by an individual during the time interval starting at \(N_t\) and ending at \(N_{t+1}\). Similarly, \(d\) is the probability that an individual alive at \(N_t\) will die at some point during the interval. The total number of births within a time interval depends on the number of individuals there are at the start of the interval (\(N_t\)), and the total number of births in the population during the time interval is \(bN_t\). Similarly, the total number of deaths is \(dN_t\). Thus: eqn. 2. \(N_{t+1} = N_t + bN_t - dN_t\). This equation can be simplified to: eqn. 3. \(N_{t+1} = N_t + (b-d)N_t\). Furthermore, because the expression \((b-d)\) is important, we can give it its own symbol, \(R_m\) (as in Neal). \(R_m\) is called the per capita rate of increase. (Note that the nomenclature varies depending on the book/paper! In other places this is called \(R\) or \(r_d\).) So we now have: eqn. 4. \(N_{t+1} = N_t + R_m N_t\). Or, if we are only interested in the change in population size: eqn. 5. \(\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta t} = R_m N_t\). Equation 4 can be simplified again, by factoring out the \(N_t\) on the right hand side: eqn. 6. \(N_{t+1} = (R_m + 1)N_t\). The quantity \((R_m+1)\) is given its own symbol: \(\lambda\), the population multiplication rate (also known as the “finite rate of increase”). eqn. 7. \(N_{t+1} = \lambda N_t\). By rearranging this equation (eqn. 7) we can see that \(\lambda\) is simply the ratio of population size at time \(t+1\) and \(t\): eqn. 8. \(\lambda = N_{t+1}/N_t\). It follows, therefore, that when the population is neither growing nor declining (when \(N_{t+1}=N_t\)), \(\lambda = 1\) (and \(R_m = 0\)). 28.1.1 Calculating N for any future time point Assuming the population growth rate remains constant, we can calculate the population at any time in the future. As a starting point, consider equation 7: \(N_{t+1} = \lambda N_t\). If we want to calculate \(N_{t+2}\), we would need to plug in \(N_{t+1}\) instead of \(N_t\): \(N_{t+2} = \lambda N_{t+1}\), and, since we know that \(N_{t+1} = \lambda N_t\),: \(N_{t+2} = \lambda \lambda N_t\). Similarly, if we wanted to calculate \(N_{t+3}\), we’d end up with: \(N_{t+3} = \lambda \lambda \lambda N_t\). This can be simplified by raising \(\lambda\) to a suitable power, and using the starting population at time = 0, \(N_0\): eqn. 9. \(N_{t} = \lambda ^tN_0\). This should be familiar to those of you that did (or remember!) the concept of geometric series which was covered in MM554 Mathematics for Biology. 28.1.2 Applying the model If we plot exponential growth on a log scale we can see that it is straight line. For example, in the plot below I show the sequence for a population with a starting population of 1 and a \(\lambda\) (population multiplication rate) of 1.2 (i.e., the population increases by 20% each year). In (A) the time series is plotted on the natural scale while in (B) it is plotted on the log scale. # Set initial population and lambda startPop <- 1 lambda <- 1.2 # Create a data frame with time and corresponding population df1 <- data.frame(time = 0:20) df1$N <- lambda^df1$time * startPop # Plotting the data par(mfrow=c(1,2)) # Plot on natural scale plot(df1$time, df1$N, type = "b", xlab = "time", ylab = "N") title("A") # Plot on log scale plot(df1$time, log(df1$N), type = "b", xlab = "time", ylab = "log(N)") title("B") In fact, we can linearise the relationship by log transforming both sides of equation 9: \(\ln{N_t} = \ln(\lambda ^tN_0)\), which can be re-written as: \(\ln{N_t} = \ln(\lambda )t + \ln(N_0)\). This looks familiar. Indeed, the equation of a straight line (\(y = ax + b\)) maps onto this. In this equation, the slope \(a\) is equivalent to \(\ln(\lambda )\) and the intercept (\(b\)) is equivalent to \(\ln(N_0)\). This is very convenient because now we can use simple regression methods to estimate \(\ln(\lambda)\) (the slope) of the relationship, and therefore the value of \(\lambda\) (or \(R_m\), which is \(\lambda - 1\)). 28.2 Real-World Application: Breeding Pairs of Merlin (Falco columbarius) To bring these mathematical concepts to life, let’s consider an example from the Neal textbook that focuses on the population of breeding pairs of Merlin, a species of small falcon. The data spans from 1970 to 1982 and shows the following population sizes (breeding pairs): 1,1,2,4,2,3,5,6,7,10,12,14,16 This is not much data, so we can simply put it into R manually, and plot it, like this: df1 <- data.frame(year = 1970:1982, N = c(1,1,2,4,2,3,5,6,7,10,12,14,16)) plot(df1$year,df1$N, type = "b") 28.2.1 Observations and Context It is clear from the graph that the number of breeding pairs is increasing over the years, albeit with some fluctuations. These fluctuations could be due to various factors such as changes in food availability, predation, or human activity. However, the general trend suggests growth. 28.2.2 Applying the Exponential Growth Model To analyse this data, we’ll use the exponential growth model. We’ll plot the data on a log scale and fit a regression model: df1$logN <- log(df1$N) plot(df1$year,df1$logN) mod1 <- lm(logN~year,data = df1) abline(mod1) Model summary output: ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = logN ~ year, data = df1) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -0.32858 -0.13684 -0.01967 0.10104 0.60054 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) ## (Intercept) -464.77072 36.12270 -12.87 5.66e-08 *** ## year 0.23596 0.01828 12.91 5.48e-08 *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ## ## Residual standard error: 0.2466 on 11 degrees of freedom ## Multiple R-squared: 0.9381, Adjusted R-squared: 0.9324 ## F-statistic: 166.6 on 1 and 11 DF, p-value: 5.478e-08 Interpretation The summary of the model indicates that the slope of the relationship between year and logN is 0.236. This slope is \(\ln(\lambda)\), so the population multiplication rate (\(\lambda\)) is \(e^{\text{slope}}\) = 1.266, the intrinsic rate of increase (\(r_m\)) is the slope itself = 0.236, and the per capita rate of increase (\(R_m = \lambda - 1\)) is 0.266. Strictly, this slope is the realised average growth rate over 1970-1982. It equals the intrinsic rate \(r_m\) only if growth was not slowed by density dependence during that period (Neal returns to the merlins in the chapter Logistic Growth). This suggests that the number of breeding pairs is indeed growing exponentially over the time period studied, with a specific rate of increase. Understanding this rate is crucial for conservation efforts, because it provides insights into the population’s resilience, its demands on the ecosystem, and how it might respond to future changes in environmental conditions or conservation policies. 28.3 Continuous time model In contrast to the discrete time model, the continuous time model allows us to understand population growth without the constraint of clear time intervals. This is particularly useful for studying populations that don’t have breeding seasons or for those that experience continuous births and deaths (e.g. bacteria, humans). In continuous time, the population changes smoothly according to eqn. 10. \(\frac{dN}{dt} = r_m N\), where \(r_m\) is the intrinsic rate of increase: the instantaneous per capita birth rate minus death rate (\(r_m = b - d\), with \(b\) and \(d\) now instantaneous rates rather than per time step). Solving this equation gives the population size at any time \(t\): eqn. 11. \(N_t = N_0 e^{r_m t}\). Compare this with the discrete-time result, eqn. 9: \(N_t = \lambda^t N_0\). The two describe the same growth if \(\lambda = e^{r_m}\), or equivalently eqn. 12. \(r_m = \ln(\lambda)\): “\(r_m\) is the natural log of lambda”, which is the same as saying \(r_m = \ln(N_{t+1}/N_t)\) for a population growing at a constant rate. To back-transform from a natural log, we use the exponential. Therefore, \(\lambda = e^{r_m}\): “lambda is the exponential of \(r_m\)”. This allows us to relate \(\lambda\) and \(r_m\) directly. From the discrete model (above), we know that \(\lambda = 1 + R_m\), so: \(1 + R_m = e^{r_m}\) \(R_m = e^{r_m} - 1\) 28.3.1 Doubling time A useful way to express a growth rate is the time it takes the population to double. Setting \(N_t = 2N_0\) in eqn. 11 gives \(2 = e^{r_m t_d}\), so the doubling time is eqn. 13. \(t_d = \ln(2)/r_m = \ln(2)/\ln(\lambda)\). For the merlins, \(t_d\) = ln(2)/0.236 = 2.9 years. r_m <- as.vector(coef(mod1)[2]) # slope of the merlin regression log(2) / r_m # doubling time in years ## [1] 2.937516 28.3.2 Changing the time scale Because \(r_m\) is a rate per unit time, it is easy to convert between time scales: just divide or multiply by the number of time units. For example, a population with \(\lambda = 2\) per week has \(r_m = \ln(2) = 0.693\) per week, which is \(0.693/7 = 0.099\) per day, so \(\lambda\) per day is \(e^{0.099} = 1.104\). (You cannot simply divide \(\lambda\) by 7.) 28.3.3 Zero population growth When the population is steady with zero growth, \(r_m = 0\) and \(\lambda = 1\). It’s important to note that the relationship \(\lambda = r_m + 1\) only holds true when the population is not growing or shrinking, and approximately when \(r_m\) is small (e.g. \(r_m = 0.05\) gives \(\lambda = 1.051\)). It should not be generalised. Do not make the common mistake to think that \(\lambda\) is simply \(r_m + 1\)!
