29 The legend of Ambalappuzha Exponential growth is a powerful concept. To help us grasp it better let’s use an ancient Indian chess legend as an example. Learning outcomes Use of Excel formulae for mathematical modelling. Understanding the multiplicative process of exponential/geometric growth. According to legend, Lord Krishna once appeared in the form of a wise man in the court of the king and challenged him to a game of chess. The king was a chess enthusiast and naturally accepted the invitation. The king asked the wise man to choose a prize in case he won. The old man told the king that he had few material needs and that all he wished was a few grains of rice. He added that the amount of rice itself should be determined using the chessboard in the following manner: one grain of rice would be placed in the first square, two grains in the second square, four in the third square, and so on. Every square would have double the number of grains of its predecessor. Upon hearing this, the king was unhappy, since the man requested only a few grains of rice instead of any of the other riches of the kingdom, which the king would have been happy to donate (he was a generous guy). He requested the old man to add other items to his prize, but the man declined. So the game of chess started and, needless to say, the king lost the game so it was soon time to pay the old man his prize. As he started adding grains of rice to the chessboard, the king soon realised the true nature of the wise man’s demand. The royal granary soon ran out of rice and the king realised that even if he provided all the rice in his kingdom and even the whole of India, he would never be able to fulfil the promised reward. He was distraught that he could not fulfil his promise! Seeing the king upset, the wise man appeared to the king in his true form, that of Lord Krishna. He told the king that he did not have to pay the debt immediately but could pay him over time. The king would serve rice in the temple freely to the pilgrims every day until the debt was paid off. And that is why the Ambalappuzha Temple in India still serves rice pudding (palpayasam) to pilgrims: the debt is still being paid off. Use the Excel sheet RiceOnAChessboard.xlsx to calculate the quantity of rice that the king owed. A grain of rice weighs 25mg, what weight of rice did the king owe in total, in kg? 29.1 Animals/plants, not grains of rice Imagine that instead of rice, we were talking about population growth (e.g. bacteria or rabbits) reproducing every time step. 29.1.1 Quick exercise (optional) We have ~100 breeding pairs of great tits (Parus major, musvit) in woodland around SDU. Each female lays ~6 eggs per year with an assumed 50:50 sex ratio, so each female produces 3 daughters per year. If survival were 100%, how many females would there be after 5 years? Assume that every female (adults and all their daughters) survives every year, that daughters breed in the year after they hatch, and that every female breeds every year. What is \(\lambda\) for the females? How does your answer change if, instead, adults die after breeding once (so only the daughters are left to breed next year)? Now relax that assumption: allow realistic survival and recruitment. How do your answers change? 29.1.2 Discussion prompts Is this simple multiplicative model realistic? Why / why not? Key processes to consider: Survival < 100%; age/stage-specific survival and fecundity Density dependence (resources, territories, disease, predation) Carrying capacity and feedbacks on reproduction/survival Variation over time and space: Stochasticity (good/bad years), seasonality, environmental drivers Dispersal, immigration/emigration Model structure: Age/stage structure (e.g. juvenile vs adult), sex ratio, mating system Time-step choice (daily/weekly/annual) and what processes occur within a step 29.2 Optional: Try these calculations in R You can do this kind of calculation easily in R. Try this. myData <- data.frame(Squares = 1:64,nRice = NA) myData$nRice[1] <- 1 for (i in 2:64){ myData$nRice[i] <- myData$nRice[i-1]*2 } Now we can look at the top and bottom of the 64 row data frame like this: head(myData) ## Squares nRice ## 1 1 1 ## 2 2 2 ## 3 3 4 ## 4 4 8 ## 5 5 16 ## 6 6 32 tail(myData) ## Squares nRice ## 59 59 2.882304e+17 ## 60 60 5.764608e+17 ## 61 61 1.152922e+18 ## 62 62 2.305843e+18 ## 63 63 4.611686e+18 ## 64 64 9.223372e+18 Output preview: ## Squares nRice ## 1 1 1 ## 2 2 2 ## 3 3 4 ## 4 4 8 ## 5 5 16 ## 6 6 32 ## Squares nRice ## 59 59 2.882304e+17 ## 60 60 5.764608e+17 ## 61 61 1.152922e+18 ## 62 62 2.305843e+18 ## 63 63 4.611686e+18 ## 64 64 9.223372e+18 And we can sum up the total number of grains of rice on the 64 squares of the board like this: sum(myData$nRice) ## [1] 1.844674e+19 Output: ## [1] 1.844674e+19 To put that HUGE number in context, if a grain of rice weighs 25mg (0.000025kg), then we’d have 461,168,601,842,739 kg. That’s 461 gigatonnes, or roughly 600 to 900 times annual world rice production (depending on whether you use paddy or milled weight)!

30 From population biology to fitness 30.1 An in silico experiment 30.2 The link to fitness 30.3 Introducing a trade-off

30 From population biology to fitness The purpose of this practical is to draw clear links between the first part of the course (population biology) and the second part of the course (evolution). Learning outcomes: Understanding the relationship between population growth and the concept of fitness. Understanding the concept of an evolutionary trade-off. We will focus on the concept of fitness. Fitness is a slippery concept, but it is widely accepted that it is closely related to population growth rate. In this class you will explore this concept using some mathematical modelling. This practical uses RStudio (R). It is similar to the previous exercise on matrix population models, but ask for help if you get stuck! 30.1 An in silico experiment As you learned in the classes on age- and stage-structured population dynamics, differences in survival and reproduction can be modelled using matrix population models (MPMs). These models can be simple or complex, and can be thought of as mathematical descriptions of the life history of the species (or population) in a particular environment. Earlier in the course you will have played with construction and analyses of these models by creating MPMs for species with different life histories such as high juvenile survival, or low juvenile survival etc. We will first need to load the popdemo package like this. Note that if you have not installed this package you should first install it with the command install.packages("popdemo"). Let’s set up our baseline model. This model describes a population of some mammal species which we have divided into 3 stages: juvenile, adult and senescent (old). You can “read” the matrix by looking at the columns and rows: a value in column j and row i tells you the “transition” from stage j to stage i. For example, column 2, row 1 says that an individual in the adult age class produces an average of 4 babies, and column 3, row 1 says that one from the senescent age class produces 2 babies. Juveniles have a probability of 0.1 (10% chance) to survive to adulthood (and they reach maturity in 1 year, so there is no “stasis” where they can remain being juveniles). Adults can survive in 2 ways, they can survive and remain as adults (probability = 0.8) or they can survive and transition to being in the senescent age class (probability = 0.1). Therefore, the total survival probability is 0.9. Senescent adults survive less well (probability = 0.4). We can project a population like this: Take a look at pr, the projected population. This gives you the total population size, and below that the population sizes in each stage. ## 1 deterministic population projection over 8 time intervals. ## ## [1] 18.00000 32.70000 31.18000 37.51200 42.93080 50.15272 58.36605 68.04116 ## [9] 79.29730 You can access the population sizes of the different stages using vec(pr). ## S1 S2 S3 ## [1,] 10.00000 5.00000 3.000000 ## [2,] 26.00000 5.00000 1.700000 ## [3,] 23.40000 6.60000 1.180000 ## [4,] 28.76000 7.62000 1.132000 ## [5,] 32.74400 8.97200 1.214800 ## [6,] 38.31760 10.45200 1.383120 ## [7,] 44.57424 12.19336 1.598448 ## [8,] 51.97034 14.21211 1.858715 ## [9,] 60.56588 16.56672 2.164697 Let’s plot this… Check out how, after a “transient” period, there is exponential growth in all stages of the population. The population is growing steadily with a fixed population growth rate (\(\lambda\)). You can see that the population is increasing and we can calculate the precise population growth rate (\(\lambda\)) like this: ## [1] 1.165587 Thus, the population is growing at 16.56% per year. So where does evolution come in? 30.2 The link to fitness In this population consider that suddenly a mutation arises in an individual parent that causes it to give more care to their offspring. For example, maybe they provide milk with a higher fat content, or build a safer nest. Whatever the mechanism, let’s assume that it results in a small increase in juvenile survival. We can simulate this by increasing the juvenile survival in the matrix model from 0.10 to 0.11. What effect does that have on population growth rate? ## [1] 1.192317 The small increase in juvenile survival has resulted in a small increase in population growth rate, from 16.56% to 19.23% per year. If you consider that the original population now consists of two genotypes – “ordinary” and “caring” – what do you think will happen to the percentage of the two genotypes through time? You can be sure that the proportion of the caring genotype will grow faster than the ordinary genotype. It is the FITTER genotype. (Treating each genotype’s \(\lambda\) as its fitness assumes that offspring inherit their parent’s life history exactly, and that growth is density-independent, as in this model.) 30.3 Introducing a trade-off It is common that apparently beneficial behaviours or innovations come at a cost. In evolutionary biology these are called trade-offs. Let’s explore such a trade-off now and see how it might affect fitness. We’ll stick with the same example above, but we’ll introduce a new genotype that has a trade-off between juvenile survival and old-adult survival. The benefit is clear: a change in adult behaviour or physiology increases juvenile survival a little bit. But such changes often come with a cost: The new genotype allocates extra resources to babies but this exhausts the adults causing older adults to have very small survival probability. Is this new genotype viable? In other words, is the fitness of the genotype greater than that of the original genotype? If so, the new genotype will come to dominate the population. Modify the matrix to reduce old adult survival to, say 0.05 (5% survival) and re-calculate the population growth rate. Is this “trade-off genotype” fitter than the original one? i.e. is the small benefit worth the large cost? Try doing the same thing for the prime-age adults. How much can you reduce survival before the cost is not worth bearing?

31 From plain English to a matrix model 31.1 Background This activity is designed for quick in-class practice translating a verbal life-history description into a matrix population model. It connects directly to the workflow in the chapter Matrix population modelling. Learning outcomes: Convert a verbal life-history description into a matrix population model. Build and interpret a simple projection from initial stage abundances. 31.2 Worked example 31.2.1 Inputs Suppose juveniles do not reproduce, each adult contributes 2 offspring per year that survive to be counted as juveniles at the next census, juvenile survival is 0.4, and adult survival is 0.7. A simple stage matrix would be: 31.2.2 Steps Put fecundity terms in the top row (when all newborns enter stage 1). A fecundity term is the number of offspring counted at the next census per individual now, so it must include any survival needed to get there (see the fecundity box in the chapter “Matrix population modelling”). If a description gives you the number of babies born, multiply by the survival needed to reach the next count. Put survival/transition terms in the subdiagonal/diagonal entries. Assemble the matrix in row = stage at \(t+1\), column = stage at \(t\) form. 31.2.3 Output and interpretation \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 0.4 & 0.7 \end{bmatrix} \] The key idea is to map each biological statement to a matrix entry: fecundity goes in the top row, survival and stage transitions go on the sub-diagonal or main diagonal. 31.3 Your task Read this description of the life history of the red-tailed hawk (Buteo jamaicensis): We assumed that the Red-tailed hawk life history could be described in terms of three major life stages: hatchling, juvenile, and adult (generally the third year of life and beyond). Adults are the primary reproductive stage, and produce an average of 3 new hatchlings each year. Juveniles tend to produce only 1 new hatchling per year on average. We assumed that adults experienced an average of 18% mortality each year. Juvenile mortality was set at 30% per year. Approximately 5% of juveniles fail to transition to adults, remaining in the juvenile phase. Finally, hatchlings had a 20% chance of surviving and transitioning to become juveniles. We initialized the population with 1000 hatchlings, 150 juveniles, and 5 adults. Assume that the population is counted once a year, and that the numbers of “new hatchlings” per juvenile and per adult are already the numbers counted as hatchlings at the next census (so they can go straight into the matrix as fertilities). Draw a 3-stage life cycle diagram (hatchling, juvenile, adult). Translate the verbal description into a 3x3 projection matrix. State any assumptions you make about the juvenile stasis and transition rates. Use the initial population sizes given (1000 hatchlings, 150 juveniles, 5 adults) and project the population for 20 time steps. Calculate the dominant eigenvalue and interpret whether the population grows or declines. Compare your approach with the workflow in the chapter Matrix population modelling. 31.4 Takeaways Verbal life-history descriptions can be translated directly into matrix entries with clear assumptions. Simple projections reveal whether the implied population is growing or declining.

32 Continuous traits from discrete genes 32.1 Background 32.2 Worked example 32.3 Your task 32.4 Takeaways

32 Continuous traits from discrete genes 32.1 Background This activity uses a fast classroom simulation to show how many small genetic effects, together with some environmental variation, can generate a continuous, approximately normal trait distribution. It connects to the heritability practical in Chapter 20. Reading: Neal, chapter Polygenic Inheritance and Quantitative Genetics (Nilsson-Ehle’s wheat kernel colour example makes the same point). Learning outcomes: Explain how many genes with small additive effects create many trait classes, and how environmental variation blurs these classes into a continuous distribution. Compare a classroom simulation with a simple R simulation. Relate the simulation to the partition \(V_P = V_G + V_E\) and to heritability. 32.2 Worked example 32.2.1 Inputs Baseline trait value: 35 Number of genes: 25 Each gene contributes 1 unit when ON, and each gene is ON with probability 0.5 32.2.2 Steps Compute expected number of ON genes under 50:50 ON/OFF: 25 * 0.5 = 12.5. Add expected genetic contribution to baseline. 32.2.3 Output and interpretation Expected trait value is 35 + 12.5 = 47.5. Individual values vary around this because each gene is ON or OFF at random. The genetic variance is \(25 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 = 6.25\) (the variance of a binomial distribution). Notice that, with genes alone, every trait value is a whole number: there are many classes (35 to 60), but they are still discrete. 32.3 Your task You will need the instructions and the Excel spreadsheet (download them): Continuous_Traits_From_Discrete_Genes.docx (instructions) Continuous_Traits_From_Discrete_Genes.xlsx (spreadsheet: each time you press Enter, it re-randomises 25 ON/OFF genes and gives the trait value of a new individual) Classroom simulation. Each student is a gene. In each round, every student flips a coin: heads = ON (1), tails = OFF (0). Count the number of ONs in the class and add it to a baseline of 35. That is the trait value of one individual. Repeat for at least 30 rounds (30 individuals), and record each value. (Alternatively, use the spreadsheet to generate at least 30 individuals.) Plot a quick histogram of the observed trait values. Describe the shape. Now simulate the same process in R for 100 individuals and 25 genes (first chunk below). Compare your histogram with the classroom version. Real traits are also affected by the environment (food, temperature, chance events during development). Add a small random environmental effect to each individual (second chunk below) and compare the two histograms. Relate the outcome to the concepts of genetic and environmental variance in Chapter 20. baseline <- 35 n_genes <- 25 n_individuals <- 100 gene_on <- rbinom(n_individuals, size = n_genes, prob = 0.5) trait_value <- baseline + gene_on hist(trait_value, breaks = seq(min(trait_value) - 0.5, max(trait_value) + 0.5, 1), col = "gray80", main = "Genes only", xlab = "Trait") Now add an environmental effect, drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.5 (so the environmental variance, \(V_E\), is \(1.5^2 = 2.25\)): environment_effect <- rnorm(n_individuals, mean = 0, sd = 1.5) trait_value_env <- trait_value + environment_effect hist(trait_value_env, breaks = 15, col = "gray80", main = "Genes + environment", xlab = "Trait") var(trait_value) # genetic variance (expected 6.25) ## [1] 6.290404 var(trait_value_env) # phenotypic variance, V_P = V_G + V_E (expected 8.5) ## [1] 8.240729 Are the trait values in the second histogram still whole numbers? Why does the environment make the distribution continuous? In this model all the genetic variance is additive. What is the expected heritability, \(h^2 = V_A/V_P\)? (Use the expected variances: 6.25 and 8.5.) What happens to the heritability if you increase the standard deviation of the environmental effect to 4? 32.4 Takeaways Many genes with small additive effects produce many trait classes and a roughly bell-shaped distribution; environmental variation blurs the classes into a continuous distribution. (Normality is an approximation, not a law.) Phenotypic variance is the sum of genetic and environmental variance (\(V_P = V_G + V_E\)), so the same genes give a lower heritability in a more variable environment. Random genetic variation produces a spread of trait values even with identical environments.

33 Building a phylogenetic tree 33.1 Background 33.2 Key idea 33.3 Worked example 33.4 Your task 33.5 Takeaways

33 Building a phylogenetic tree 33.1 Background This activity builds intuition for phylogenetic trees by using discrete morphological characters. It follows the classroom activity by Wojciech Grajkowski, Building a phylogenetic tree (Bioscience Explained 6(2)), which you can download here as a PDF. The PDF includes the organism cards and a worksheet. Reading: Neal, chapter Darwin’s Evolutionary Theories (common descent and Darwin’s “tree of life”). Learning outcomes: Build a simple character table for a set of organisms. Compute pairwise differences and translate them into a tree. Relate morphology-based trees to the idea of evolutionary relatedness, and recognise when similarity may not reflect relatedness. 33.2 Key idea With six organisms and seven characters, you can compute a pairwise difference table, then group the most similar organisms first. The internal nodes of the tree represent inferred common ancestors: the pairs joined first represent the most recent common ancestors, and the deeper splits represent older ones. A caveat: similarity is not the same as relatedness. Grouping organisms by overall similarity (the method used here, which is called UPGMA when done by computer) recovers the true tree only if characters change at a roughly constant rate in all lineages and the same character state never evolves more than once. In reality, unrelated organisms can evolve the same feature independently (convergence, e.g. wings in birds and bats, or loss of thorns in several plant lineages), and features can be lost again (reversal). Some shared features are also simply inherited from a distant ancestor of the whole group (ancestral states) and say nothing about who is most closely related. Modern phylogenetics therefore groups organisms by shared derived characters (new features that arose in their common ancestor), uses an outgroup to decide which states are ancestral, and increasingly uses DNA sequences. Keep this in mind when you interpret your tree. 33.3 Worked example The PDF’s example has six beetle-like organisms (A to F), described by seven characters: beetles <- data.frame( row.names = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"), body_shape = c("Oval", "Oval", "Round", "Oval", "Round", "Round"), colour = c("Yellow", "Yellow", "Orange", "Pink", "Pink", "Orange"), head_colour = c("White", "Black", "Black", "White", "Black", "Black"), antennae = c("No", "No", "No", "Yes", "Yes", "No"), jaws_visible = c("Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "No", "Yes"), spots = c("Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "No", "Yes"), spot_colour = c("Black", "Black", "Black", "None", "None", "White") ) beetles ## body_shape colour head_colour antennae jaws_visible spots spot_colour ## A Oval Yellow White No Yes Yes Black ## B Oval Yellow Black No Yes Yes Black ## C Round Orange Black No Yes Yes Black ## D Oval Pink White Yes No No None ## E Round Pink Black Yes No No None ## F Round Orange Black No Yes Yes White Next, count the number of characters that differ between each pair of organisms. This is the “data matrix” in the PDF: n <- nrow(beetles) differences <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = n, dimnames = list(rownames(beetles), rownames(beetles))) for (i in 1:n) { for (j in 1:n) { differences[i, j] <- sum(beetles[i, ] != beetles[j, ]) } } differences ## A B C D E F ## A 0 1 3 5 7 4 ## B 1 0 2 6 6 3 ## C 3 2 0 7 5 1 ## D 5 6 7 0 2 7 ## E 7 6 5 2 0 5 ## F 4 3 1 7 5 0 Finally, join the most similar organisms first (Figure 33.1). The function hclust with method = "average" does this automatically: at each step it joins the two closest groups, measuring the distance between groups as the average number of differences between their members. tree <- hclust(as.dist(differences), method = "average") plot(tree, main = "", xlab = "", sub = "", ylab = "Average number of differences") Figure 33.1: Tree for the six beetle-like organisms in the PDF, built by joining the most similar organisms first (UPGMA). The height of each join is the average number of character differences between the two groups. A and B differ in only one character, as do C and F, so these pairs are joined first (at a height of 1): they share the most recent common ancestors. D and E (2 differences) are joined next, then the A+B and C+F groups (an average of 3 differences), and finally the two main groups. This is the same tree as the one drawn by hand in the PDF. Now look back at the character table. On this tree, no single change can explain body shape or head colour. E is round like C and F, but groups with D, and A has a white head like D, but groups with B. At least one of these characters must have changed more than once (convergence or reversal). Which one, and in which direction, cannot be decided without knowing the ancestral states, for example from an outgroup. 33.4 Your task Use the PDF as a guide for the classroom activity. Pick six organisms (use the cards in the PDF: plants, birds or butterflies, or invent six organisms with clear traits). Identify seven discrete characters that differ among the organisms (presence/absence, colour class, tail length category, etc.). Fill in a character table and then compute a pairwise difference table. Draw a phylogenetic tree by grouping the most similar organisms first, then adding deeper splits. Identify any characters that look convergent on your tree (the PDF’s “Additional questions”). Optional: compare your hand-drawn tree with an R result, by replacing the beetles table in the worked example with your own character table. 33.5 Takeaways Morphological characters can be converted into a simple distance matrix. The most similar pairs in the distance matrix are joined first, and represent the most recent common ancestors in the tree. Overall similarity is not the same as relatedness: convergence and reversals can mislead, which is why phylogenetics relies on shared derived characters and on many characters, including DNA.
